title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
1. What is the stereocentre?
Locate it in CH₃CH(OH)COOH and list its four substituents.






Check your answer





The CH(OH) carbon bears OH, H, CH₃ and COOH. They are different, so it is a tetrahedral stereocentre.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
2. Does proton loss invert it?
For hydroxide removing the carboxyl OH proton of lactic acid, does that step invert the alcohol-bearing centre?






Check your answer





No. The drawn proton transfer does not change the bonds or spatial arrangement at that centre. It produces lactate and water.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
3. What does oxidation change?
Oxidise lactic acid’s secondary alcohol to a ketone. Is the original centre still R/S?






Check your answer





The product is CH₃C(=O)COOH, pyruvic acid. The former centre is trigonal planar, so it is not assigned R/S.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
4. Which mechanism returns C=O?
Compare an aldehyde addition product with an acyl substitution product.






Check your answer





Addition opens the carbonyl pi bond and produces a tetrahedral product after appropriate protonation. Acyl substitution first adds, then eliminates a viable leaving group to reform C=O.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
section: 5. What does a large mass prove?
text:
5. What does a large mass prove?
A plausible high isolated yield conflicts with major unexpected NMR signals. Which observation should be ignored?






Check your answer





Neither. The apparent yield depends on the identity/purity assumption, while unexpected NMR signals call that assumption into question. Investigate the discrepancy before claiming pure product.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
6. What makes a conclusion inspectable?
Give the ingredients of an evidence-based conclusion and a reproducible report.






Check your answer





State a chemical claim, observations, a reason connecting them, a limitation and a next test. Save raw inputs and code so a fresh R session can recreate tables and plots; separately check chemical validity.



Return to the exercises for any reasoning you could not reconstruct. Explain one corrected mistake in your own words.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
Connect structure, stereochemistry, reaction mechanisms and experimental evidence in each case.
Core exercises 1–10: begin here. Transfer 11–16: apply the same ideas to new cases. Further checks 17–20: use these to investigate mistakes and revise. Allow roughly 2–3 hours across the unit, with more time for complete mechanism drawings. Attempt each problem before opening its hint, then compare your reasoning with the worked explanation.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
Working refresher
Use the same checks on every case: identify functional groups, draw explicit atoms and charges at the changing site, follow electron pairs, and test a proposed structure against observations. In wedge/dash drawings, solid wedge points toward the observer and dashed wedge away. For a tetrahedral centre rank CIP priorities by atomic number, break ties with next attached atoms and treat multiple bonds by duplicated-atom bookkeeping; with priority 4 away, clockwise 1→2→3 is R and anticlockwise S. For the simple C/H/O spectra use DBE=(2C+2−H)/2 and the supplied first-order n +1 rule. Amount=n=m/M; theoretical product comes from balanced limiting extent; apparent yield=100×isolated/theoretical mass. The local lecture provides the chemical drawings used in these exercises.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
section: 1. Read lactic acid without a pathway
text:
1. Read lactic acid without a pathway
For CH₃CH(OH)COOH, identify both oxygen-containing functional groups, alcohol type and the possible stereocentre. Supply the four groups attached to that centre.






Hint





The CH(OH) carbon, rather than the carbonyl carbon, is tetrahedral.









Worked explanation





The molecule has a secondary alcohol and carboxylic acid. CH(OH) bears OH,H,CH₃ and COOH, four different groups, so it is a stereocentre. No metabolic knowledge is needed to infer those features.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
2. Rank the carbon substituents
At the lactic acid centre, compare COOH with CH₃ using supplied CIP multiple-bond bookkeeping: duplicate a doubly bonded atom in the attached-atom comparison. Give the complete priority order.






Hint





The directly attached atoms tie at C; compare their next atoms.









Worked explanation





COOH carbon compares as O,O,O while methyl compares H,H,H, so COOH outranks CH₃. Complete order is OH>COOH>CH₃>H. Atomic identities, not group size or drawn length, determine priority.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
section: 3. Assign a view with lowest priority away
text:
3. Assign a view with lowest priority away
In a tetrahedral drawing H(4) points away. OH(1) is at upper left, COOH(2) upper right and CH₃(3) lower left. Determine R/S and explain what reverses if H points toward you instead.






Hint





Read 1→2→3 with the lowest-priority group away.









Worked explanation





The sequence is clockwise in this stated view, so R. If the same apparent sequence is viewed with H toward the observer, invert the result to S or reorient a model. A page rotation alone does not change configuration.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
4. Distinguish mirror and rotation
Two lactic-acid drawings have identical connectivity but opposite tetrahedral arrangement at their sole stereocentre. State their relationship and whether R/S predicts the sign of optical rotation.






Hint





Configuration and a measured optical property are distinct labels.









Worked explanation





They are enantiomers and cannot be superimposed by rigid rotation. R/S does not determine positive or negative optical rotation; that sign must be measured or otherwise supplied.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
5. Draw one acid–base mechanism
For lactic acid plus OH⁻, draw removal of the carboxyl OH proton with both curved arrows. Give products and state whether that step inverts the alcohol-bearing centre.






Hint





Start an arrow at the base pair and the other at the acid O–H bond.









Worked explanation





CH₃CH(OH)COO⁻ and H₂O form. The proton-transfer step does not break or rearrange the bonds at CH(OH), so it does not itself invert that centre. Other conditions could cause other chemistry, but that is not this drawn event.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
6. Check atom conservation quantitatively
For CH₃CH(OH)COOH+OH⁻→CH₃CH(OH)COO⁻+H₂O, count C,H,O and total charge on each side. Explain why dropping the water product would fail the audit.






Hint





Lactic acid is C₃H₆O₃ and lactate is C₃H₅O₃⁻.









Worked explanation





Each complete side has C₃H₇O₄ and total charge −1. Omitting water loses H₂O from the inventory and hides the proton recipient; electron-flow bookkeeping alone cannot permit atoms to disappear.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
7. Use a supplied ionisation model
For a dilute monoprotic acid with pKa 3.86, use fraction_Aminus=1/(1+10^(pKa−pH)). Calculate fractions at pH3.86 and 4.86 and interpret the population.






Hint





At one pH unit above pKa the ratio A⁻/HA is 10.









Worked explanation





Fractions are 0.5 and 10/11≈0.909. They describe relative populations of acid and conjugate-base species, not molecules each losing half or 90.9% of a proton.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
8. Predict oxidation and geometry
Oxidise the secondary alcohol in CH₃CH(OH)COOH to a ketone while retaining the carbon skeleton. Write the product and explain what happens to the original stereocentre.






Hint





A secondary alcohol becomes a ketone at its OH-bearing carbon.









Worked explanation





The product is CH₃C(=O)COOH, pyruvic acid. The changing carbon becomes trigonal planar, so the original tetrahedral R/S centre no longer exists.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
9. Check the oxidation-state change
At the changing carbon of lactic acid assign +1 per C–O bond order,−1 per C–H and 0 per C–C. Compare the ketone product carbonyl.






Hint





The alcohol centre has one C–O and one C–H; ketone has C=O and no C–H.









Worked explanation





The alcohol centre is +1−1=0; the ketone carbon is +2. The increase by 2 confirms oxidation. This conclusion does not require adding an oxygen atom to the molecular formula.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
10. Choose a target ester site
The selected target from lactic acid and ethanol is CH₃CH(OH)COOCH₂CH₃. Identify the functional-group change and state a condition-related limitation of this target drawing.






Hint





The drawn secondary OH remains; the carboxylic acid becomes ester.









Worked explanation





Acid-group esterification is the intended net change. The drawing does not guarantee selective reaction under arbitrary conditions, since the starting molecule has more than one reactive oxygen function. Actual conditions and competing pathways must be assessed.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
11. Track the alcohol oxygen
In standard esterification, ethanol is labelled at oxygen as CH₃CH₂OH. Write the labelled ethyl-lactate target and identify the two atoms directly bonded to O.






Hint





The incoming alcohol O forms the new bond to acyl carbon.









Worked explanation





CH₃CH(OH)C(=O)OCH₂CH₃. O is bonded to the acid-derived carbonyl carbon and the ethyl CH₂ carbon. Atom identities follow the pathway rather than being inferred from final drawing positions.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
12. Choose addition versus substitution
Compare CH₃CHO and CH₃COOCH₃ reacting with a suitable nucleophile. State the shared first bond changes and the key reason their later pathways can differ.






Hint





Both initial attacks move the carbonyl pi pair, but the ester has an oxygen-based substituent at acyl carbon.









Worked explanation





Both form C–Nu and move C=O pi electrons to O. The ester can undergo a viable leaving-group step to restore C=O; ordinary aldehydes lack the corresponding group, since H⁻ is not a normal leaving group here.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
13. Read amino-acid charges
For H₃N⁺CH(CH₃)COO⁻, identify individual formal charges and net charge. Does net zero make it equivalent to an entirely uncharged hydrocarbon in water?






Hint





Sum the charges without deleting their local presence.









Worked explanation





N is +1 and carboxylate −1, net 0. The molecule is zwitterionic and contains strongly polar charged sites, so net neutrality does not make its interactions hydrocarbon-like.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
14. Predict high-pH deprotonation
Starting from H₃N⁺CH(CH₃)COO⁻, draw OH⁻ accepting one ammonium proton. Give the product formula, N bond count and net charge.






Hint





The N–H bonding pair returns to N.









Worked explanation





H₂NCH(CH₃)COO⁻ and water form. N has three bonds and a lone pair, neutral; carboxylate remains −1. Net −1 on each complete side is conserved.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
15. Assign a complete unknown dataset
U1 has C₄H₈O₂, carbonyl IR without broad OH, proton peaks 1.25 t 3H,2.05 s 3H,4.12 q 2H. Assign CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ and link each observation to a structural part.






Hint





Join the ethyl quartet/triplet, then place the acetyl singlet and carbonyl.









Worked explanation





O–CH₂ gives 4.12 q 2H and terminal ethyl CH₃ gives 1.25 t 3H. Acetyl CH₃ gives 2.05 s 3H because adjacent carbonyl C has no H. Ester carbonyl explains IR and lack of acid/alcohol OH; all atoms fit the formula.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
16. Test a hydroxyketone alternative
For the same U1 dataset, compare CH₃COCH(OH)CH₃. Explain two predicted differences without using filenames or expected reaction products as evidence.






Hint





The proposed O-bearing carbon is CH, not CH₂.









Worked explanation





The hydroxyketone predicts an OH-bearing 1H environment and a methyl adjacent to CH, commonly a doublet in the simple model. It also predicts OH functionality. U1 instead has O–CH₂2H quartet and ethyl 3H triplet, favouring the ester among these candidates.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
section: 17. Calculate yield while stating its assumption
text:
17. Calculate yield while stating its assumption
A1:1 teaching reaction has 0.0100 mol limiting reagent, product M180.16 g/mol and isolate 1.70 g. Calculate theoretical mass and apparent yield, then state why neither number proves purity.






Hint





Theoretical amount comes from starting reagents; isolated mass enters separately.









Worked explanation





Theoretical mass is 1.8016 g and apparent yield 94.4%. The calculation assumes isolated mass is product; impurities, residual solvent or wrong identity can invalidate that interpretation. Purity requires separate evidence.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
18. Resolve contradictory observations
A sample gives 94% apparent yield and one TLC spot, but full NMR has an unexpected major signal group. Give a defensible interpretation and two possible explanations without identifying a unique impurity.






Hint





A single separation feature can hide co-migration, and mass can include other components.









Worked explanation





The sample may not be pure despite its plausible mass. Residual solvent or another organic component could contribute; incorrect assignment is also possible. Investigate with complete spectral assignments or a discriminating separation rather than ignoring the contradiction.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
section: 19. Critique a reproducible but invalid calculation
text:
19. Critique a reproducible but invalid calculation
An Rmd file always reproduces 100×isolated_mass/starting_reagent_mass and calls the result percent yield. Explain why reproducibility alone does not make this formula chemically correct.






Hint





Mass yield must use theoretical product mass from balanced stoichiometry and molar masses.









Worked explanation





The denominator is generally wrong because starting and product molar masses and coefficients can differ. Correctly compute theoretical product amount from limiting extent, convert using product molar mass, then compare isolated product mass. Repeating an invalid formula is reproducibly wrong.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
20. Write a final evidence-based conclusion
You have a formula-consistent ester candidate, matching simulated IR/NMR, an apparent 66.6% yield from teaching masses and no actual measured isolate spectra. Write a supported claim, limitation and useful next observation for a real sample.






Hint





Keep model demonstration and real measurement separate.









Worked explanation





The supplied simulated evidence supports the ester candidate and the teaching mass calculation gives 66.6% apparent yield under its assumptions. It does not identify or establish purity of a real isolate. Appropriate measured sample spectra and independent purity assessment would test that real-sample claim.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
Consolidate your work
Choose one corrected error and explain what changed in your reasoning. Then complete the self-check. Reading is optional; all practice above is self-contained.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
Explore
Question: can you reach a target while justifying each functional-group change and accounting for the extra reacting molecules?
Allow 10 minutes: plan for 2, build and revise for 5, then explain one accepted and one rejected step for 3. This is a reasoning tool, not a laboratory protocol.

Enable JavaScript to select a target, propose transformations and inspect accepted bond changes.




Predict
Starting with ethanol, propose a route to ethyl ethanoate through ethanoic acid. The acid-derived and alcohol-derived fragments cannot both arise from one two-carbon molecule without another carbon source. Identify the needed separate ethanol portion before building the route.


Explore

Select a transformation and press Apply. A rejected step leaves the current structure unchanged and explains the mismatch.
Reach the acid, then esterify using a separate ethanol portion. Inspect the explicit ethanol reactant and water product.
Undo a step and try oxidation via the aldehyde instead.
Hydrolyse the ester in base. Why does the current structure become carboxylate rather than neutral acid? Apply acid work-up separately.
Reset and try the shorter acid target.



Worked route and accounting
One accepted route is ethanol → ethanoic acid → ethyl ethanoate. Esterification uses the balanced net comparison
\[\mathrm{CH_3COOH+CH_3CH_2OH\rightleftharpoons CH_3COOCH_2CH_3+H_2O}.\]
It therefore supplies the added two-carbon fragment explicitly. A longer route can go through ethanal before further oxidation. Base-promoted ester hydrolysis gives ethanoate and ethanol; a later hydronium transfer gives the neutral acid and water.


Model limits
Only the listed small toolkit is implemented. An unsupported choice means that it is not justified by this supplied toolkit, not that chemistry can never achieve any related change. [O] is a net oxidation equivalent, not an identified reagent. H:⁻ represents hydride-equivalent delivery from a suitable reagent, not free hydride persisting in water; proton donation is explicitly included afterward. Actual selectivity, conversion, equilibrium and isolated yield need suitable conditions and observations. Review local synthesis reasoning.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
section: A chemical route through this session
text:
A chemical route through this session
Connect reaction planning to recorded amounts and evidence. Keep theoretical product, isolated yield, conversion, identity and purity as separate claims.

45-minute budget: retrieval 4 min; route planning 5 min; amount/limiting-reagent calculations with paper checks 12 min; theoretical and isolated yield 8 min; TLC and spectral evidence 10 min; report critique and exit 6 min. Total 45 min, including calculation and discussion.
Suggested 30 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Plan 45 minutes including short drawing and discussion intervals. Routine visual frames take roughly 40 seconds; worked checks need longer and some resolutions can be quicker. Treat timings as guidance, with room for questions.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence

Write amount = mass / molar mass with units. What quantity results from g divided by g/mol?

Suggested 30 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Give students a short individual attempt. Worked answer: Mol. Calculate amounts before comparing reagents and include balanced coefficients.

Two simple transformations connect an alcohol and an esterWhich two transformations connect ethanol to the ester through an acid?

Suggested 40 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Ask students to inspect the indicated molecular feature rather than read the answer caption. Worked answer: Oxidation gives ethanoic acid; acid-catalysed esterification with another ethanol portion gives ethyl ethanoate.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text:
1. What does C₄H₈O₂ imply?
Calculate degree of unsaturation for an ordinary closed-shell C/H/O molecule and state one limitation.






Check your answer





(2×4+2−8)/2 = 1. A carbonyl, another double bond or a ring could account for it; formula alone does not establish an ester.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text:
2. Which IR direction means absorption?
In a transmittance plot, do stronger absorptions point up or down?






Check your answer





They are dips to lower transmittance. An absorbance plot uses a different ordinate. Always inspect the axis label.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
section: 3. Which part of an ethyl group is a quartet?
text:
3. Which part of an ethyl group is a quartet?
For O–CH₂–CH₃ in the simple first-order model, give the two multiplicities and integrations.






Check your answer





CH₂ is a quartet integrating to 2H because it sees three adjacent equivalent H. CH₃ is a triplet integrating to 3H because it sees two adjacent H.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
section: 4. Why is acetyl methyl a singlet?
text:
4. Why is acetyl methyl a singlet?
In CH₃C(=O)OCH₂CH₃, explain the 3H signal near 2 ppm using neighbouring atoms.






Check your answer





The carbonyl carbon directly adjacent to that methyl has no H. The distant O–CH₂ hydrogens are not vicinal neighbours of the acetyl methyl in this introductory splitting model.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text:
5. Can NMR height replace integral?
A schematic triplet is taller than a singlet. Can you conclude that the triplet represents more H?






Check your answer





No. Integral is area over the whole signal, not the tallest line. Use supplied integration or measured integrated area; schematic heights are not quantitative proton counts.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text:
6. What rejects the acid candidate?
State two observations in U1 supporting ethyl ethanoate over butanoic acid.






Check your answer





No evident broad acid O–H in a suitable complete IR trace, and a 2H O–CH₂ quartet with matching terminal CH₃ triplet. The acetyl CH₃ singlet supplies additional support.



Return to the exercises for any reasoning you could not reconstruct. Explain one corrected mistake in your own words.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
Use molecular formulas, IR observations and NMR patterns to test proposed structures.
Core exercises 1–10: begin here. Transfer 11–16: apply the same ideas to new cases. Further checks 17–20: use these to investigate mistakes and revise. Allow roughly 2–3 hours across the unit, with more time for complete mechanism drawings. Attempt each problem before opening its hint, then compare your reasoning with the worked explanation.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
Working refresher
All numerical spectra below are simulated teaching examples. For ordinary closed-shell C/H/O formulas use DBE=(2C+2−H)/2; O is omitted from this simple count. IR transmittance dips indicate absorption: broad alcohol O–H is often near 3200–3600 cm⁻¹, acid O–H can extend broadly around 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ and carbonyls occupy roughly 1650–1800 cm⁻¹ depending on structure. In our simple first-order proton NMR model, n equivalent adjacent H give n +1 lines; integral gives relative total H area. A singlet/triplet/quartet has 1/3/4 lines. These shortcuts do not describe all real coupling or exchange. Chemical shifts are in ppm; supplied values are illustrative. Candidate tests and drawings are available in the lecture.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
1. Calculate one formula constraint
For an ordinary closed-shell C/H/O molecule C₄H₈O₂, calculate DBE=(2C+2−H)/2. State two structural possibilities consistent with that degree without claiming a unique structure.






Hint





O does not enter this simplified expression.









Worked explanation





DBE=1. One double bond, such as C=O, or one saturated ring could supply it. The formula alone does not establish ester, acid or any unique connectivity.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
2. Check two proposed formulas
Count the atoms in CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ and CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH. Verify whether both can be U1 with C₄H₈O₂ and name their functional-group difference.






Hint





Write the carbonyl explicitly before counting.









Worked explanation





Each is C₄H₈O₂. Ethyl ethanoate is an ester, while butanoic acid is a carboxylic acid. Both include one C=O, satisfying DBE1, but the oxygen/hydrogen connectivity differs.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
3. Reject a formula mismatch
A proposed candidate for C₄H₈O₂ is ethanol CH₃CH₂OH. Count its atoms and explain why a plausible-looking O–H IR band would not rescue it as the whole U1 structure.






Hint





A matched functional group does not replace the molecular formula constraint.









Worked explanation





Ethanol is C₂H₆O, not C₄H₈O₂. Even if it shared an OH feature with some spectrum, it would not account for U1’s total composition. A full candidate must satisfy all supplied constraints.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
4. Read a transmittance trace
A simulated IR trace falls from 95% to 30% transmittance near 1740 cm⁻¹. Which position indicates stronger absorption, and why must you inspect the y-axis label?






Hint





Transmittance measures the fraction of incident light passing through.









Worked explanation





30% transmittance means less light transmitted and therefore stronger absorption than 95% at the comparison region. In an absorbance plot stronger absorption would normally be higher; the same curve direction cannot be assumed without reading the axis.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
5. Use an acid-region prediction
Candidate A is ethyl ethanoate and B is butanoic acid. The supplied complete simulated IR has C=O but no broad O–H envelope across the usual acid region. Which candidate is challenged, and what experimental limitation could weaken that argument?






Hint





Ask what each candidate predicts in a measured, sufficiently sensitive region.









Worked explanation





Butanoic acid predicts broad acid O–H, so its absence challenges B. Missing spectral coverage, weak signal or obscuration would weaken absence evidence. Ester A fits this functional-group comparison but still needs other evidence.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
6. Compare alcohol and carbonyl evidence
A teaching trace has broad O–H near 3300 cm⁻¹ and no evident C=O region band. Compare ethanol and ethanal as candidates, assuming adequate coverage and sensitivity.






Hint





Ethanol contains OH; ethanal contains C=O but no OH.









Worked explanation





The trace supports ethanol over ethanal for this pair. It does not uniquely prove ethanol against all possible alcohols; the carbon skeleton still requires further constraints.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
7. Avoid a unique-peak claim
A student assigns a whole molecule solely because its IR has a band near 1740 cm⁻¹. Explain why this is too strong and name two independent kinds of additional information used here.






Hint





Functional-group regions occur in many related molecules.









Worked explanation





A carbonyl-region band constrains a functional group rather than uniquely specifying connectivity. Molecular formula and proton/carbon NMR supply independent information about composition and atom environments.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
8. Interpret a quartet and integral
A simulated signal at 4.12 ppm is a quartet integrating to 2H. Under the supplied simple first-order n +1 model, give the number of neighbouring equivalent H and a plausible fragment.






Hint





Line count and integral describe different things.









Worked explanation





Four lines imply three neighbouring equivalent H. The 2H integral supports CH₂ beside CH₃; a downfield O–CH₂–CH₃ environment is consistent with the shift. That fragment still needs to fit the whole formula.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
9. Interpret a triplet and integral
A simulated signal at 1.25 ppm is a triplet integrating to 3H. Under the same simple model, state adjacent-H count and how it can pair with a 2H quartet.






Hint





A triplet has n +1=3, so n=2.









Worked explanation





A CH₃ next to CH₂ can give three lines and 3H integration. Paired with a 2H quartet, it supports an ethyl fragment. The triplet alone does not say whether the remote atom is O, C or another group.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
10. Explain a singlet structurally
For CH₃C(=O)OCH₂CH₃, explain why the acetyl CH₃ can be a 3H singlet near 2 ppm while the ethyl CH₃ is a triplet. Ignore small long-range couplings.






Hint





Identify the atom directly adjacent to each methyl.









Worked explanation





Acetyl CH₃ is adjacent to carbonyl carbon with no attached H, so no ordinary vicinal splitting is expected. Ethyl CH₃ is adjacent to CH₂ with two H, giving a triplet in this simple model.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
11. Normalise integrals
A spectrum reports integral areas 6, 6 and 4 for the three signal groups of a candidate with eight H. Normalise the ratio and explain why quartet line count is not a hydrogen count.






Hint





Divide by a common factor and compare the total.









Worked explanation





The ratio reduces to 3:3:2, totalling eight H. Splitting distributes a signal’s area across lines; a quartet can represent two equivalent H. Its four lines do not mean four H.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
section: 12. Avoid using peak heights as areas
text:
12. Avoid using peak heights as areas
One line of a singlet is twice as tall as one line of a triplet. Can you infer relative H counts? State what quantitative information is required.






Hint





A multiplet spreads total area over several lines.









Worked explanation





No. Use integrated area over the full signal group, with a consistent integration scale. Individual line heights are not proton counts, especially when signal shapes or widths differ.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
section: 13. Assign all proton environments in U1
text:
13. Assign all proton environments in U1
U1 is C₄H₈O₂ with 1.25 ppm triplet 3H, 2.05 ppm singlet 3H and 4.12 ppm quartet 2H. Assign every group to CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, explicitly connecting multiplicity and integral.






Hint





Start with the linked CH₂–CH₃ pair, then place the remaining methyl.









Worked explanation





The terminal ethyl CH₃ is 1.25 t 3H; O–CH₂ is 4.12 q 2H. The acetyl CH₃ is 2.05 s 3H, with no H on adjacent carbonyl carbon. The groups account for all eight H and the ester connectivity.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
14. Assign four carbon environments
A simulated decoupled ¹³C spectrum for CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ gives 14,21,60 and 171 ppm. Assign them and state why line height is not normally a quantitative carbon count.






Hint





Separate carbonyl, O-bound methylene and the two methyl environments.









Worked explanation





171 is ester C=O, 60 is O–CH₂, 14 terminal ethyl CH₃ and 21 acetyl CH₃. Routine ¹³C intensities depend on measurement/relaxation effects, so do not count atoms from heights.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
15. Interpret signal count with symmetry
A candidate has six total carbons but only four ¹³C environments. Is that automatically impossible? Explain using the distinction between atoms and equivalent environments.






Hint





Equivalent carbons can share a resonance.









Worked explanation





No. Symmetry or equivalence can make several carbon atoms share one signal. Four environments do not always mean four total carbons. The formula, structure and measurement conditions determine whether that equivalence is plausible.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
section: 16. Reject butanoic acid with two clues
text:
16. Reject butanoic acid with two clues
Use U1’s complete simulated IR (C=O, no broad OH) and proton peaks 1.25 t 3H,2.05 s 3H,4.12 q 2H. State two observations conflicting with CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH, rather than citing the sample name.






Hint





An acid lacks O–CH₂ and predicts acid OH.









Worked explanation





The acid predicts broad carboxylic O–H and no O–CH₂ quartet. It also lacks the isolated acetyl methyl singlet arrangement. A terminal methyl triplet could fit both structures, so that feature alone does not reject the acid.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
17. Reject a hydroxyketone alternative
Candidate CH₃C(=O)CH(OH)CH₃ also has C₄H₈O₂. Compare its predicted OH-bearing proton count and adjacent methyl multiplicity with U1’s 4.12 q 2H and 1.25 t 3H.






Hint





The oxygen-bearing carbon is CH, not CH₂.









Worked explanation





The hydroxyketone has a one-H OH-bearing CH and a methyl adjacent to one H, commonly giving a doublet. It does not give the supplied two-H O–CH₂ quartet/three-H ethyl triplet pattern. Its OH adds another predicted difference.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
18. Distinguish support from proof
A supplied candidate fits formula, IR and simple NMR while two alternatives fail. Write an appropriately restrained identity conclusion and one remaining limitation.






Hint





Specify the compared candidates and the nature of the observations.









Worked explanation





The candidate best fits the supplied evidence among the tested structures. A finite comparison does not exclude every imaginable alternative, and real confidence depends on spectrum quality, assignment completeness and sample context.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
19. Check spectral provenance
An IR file is numerically generated for teaching and named ethyl_ethanoate.csv. Which claims can the plot support, and which claims about an actual laboratory isolate would be unjustified?






Hint





Separate a model demonstration from measured sample evidence.









Worked explanation





It can demonstrate a labelled functional-group pattern and plotting workflow. It cannot establish that a real isolate was measured, identified or pure. The filename records the intended teaching label, not independent experimental identity proof.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
20. Plan an independent next check
An unknown’s carbonyl IR fits both an ester and another carbonyl candidate. You can request either a molecular formula or repeat the same isolated peak label. Which is more informative here, and why?






Hint





Seek an observation that tests a different prediction.









Worked explanation





The formula adds an independent composition/unsaturation constraint. Repeating the same peak label without new data adds little. A full proton NMR could likewise test distinct connectivity predictions; choose evidence that discriminates the remaining alternatives.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
section: R task: present an IR comparison
text:
R task: present an IR comparison
Open the student project. The supplied data/ir.csv contains sample_id, wavenumber_cm1 and transmittance_percent. Plot the simulated ethyl ethanoate and ethanoic acid traces. Keep their sample labels so the plotted evidence can be traced back to the data.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
ir <- read_csv("data/ir.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
comparison <- ir |>
  filter(sample_id %in% c("ethyl_ethanoate", "ethanoic_acid"))
ggplot(comparison,
       aes(wavenumber_cm1, transmittance_percent, colour = sample_id)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  labs(x = "Wavenumber (cm−1)", y = "Transmittance (%)",
       colour = "Simulated sample") +
  theme_minimal()
Add a report caption explaining that these are simulated traces, that dips indicate absorption in a transmittance plot, and which region distinguishes the candidates. Use a descending wavenumber axis; it is conventional here and does not reverse the underlying physics. Check that transmittance values lie between 0 and 100. Do not fit a model or ask R to assign the unknown for you.






Interpretation check





The acid trace includes a very broad O–H region, while the ester trace lacks that broad feature. Both contain carbonyl absorption. The chemical comparison uses the functional groups expected from the candidate structures; the plot is a way to inspect and communicate the supplied observations. An exact carbonyl position is not a unique molecular fingerprint.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
Leave with
A fully annotated structure, a rejected alternative, and a knitted Rmd section with a labelled IR comparison. Read selected Solomons chapters 2 and 9 through the reading guide.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
Explore
Question: what changes when a candidate must explain a complete set of observations rather than only its molecular formula?
Allow 10 minutes: predict for 2, inspect competing candidates for 5, then write an assignment and limitation for 3. All traces are fixed simulated teaching data, not measured sample spectra.

Enable JavaScript to compare a drawn candidate against supplied formula, IR and NMR clues.




Predict
Unknown U1 is C₄H₈O₂. Could both an ester and a carboxylic acid fit the formula? Which observation would make a stronger comparison than the formula alone?
For simple first-order proton NMR here, \(n\) equivalent neighbouring H give \(n+1\) lines. Integration counts relative H area; a quartet’s four lines do not mean four H. In an IR transmittance trace, absorption appears as a dip.


Explore

Compare ethyl ethanoate and butanoic acid using Formula only.
Add the complete IR and identify which functional-group prediction changes.
Use all clues. Assign the 2H quartet, 3H triplet and remaining 3H singlet in U1 rather than merely selecting the green outcome.
Try Second unknown and test ethanol against dimethyl ether. Then reset.



Supplied data and worked check
U1 has carbonyl absorption without a broad O–H feature and proton signals 1.25 ppm triplet, 3H; 2.05 ppm singlet, 3H; 4.12 ppm quartet, 2H. Ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, accounts for an ethyl pair and an acetyl methyl singlet. Butanoic acid predicts acid O–H and lacks the O–CH₂/acetyl pattern.
U2 is C₂H₆O, with broad O–H, no carbonyl, and 1.18 ppm triplet, 3H; 3.65 ppm quartet, 2H; an exchangeable broad OH signal, 1H in this illustrative model. Ethanol fits; dimethyl ether has the same formula but no OH and would not give that proton pattern.


Model limits
Peak positions, shapes and exchange depend on conditions. The listed patterns are introductory first-order examples, not a general spectral solver. Green means the candidate fits the selected supplied evidence, not that every possible alternative is excluded or the sample is pure. A filename is not identity evidence. See the local spectroscopy exercises.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: A chemical route through this session
text:
A chemical route through this session
Locate each nitrogen pair before predicting proton transfer. Distinguish simple amines, amides and aromatic nitrogens, then combine acid and base sites in an amino acid.

45-minute budget: retrieval 4 min; N bond/charge examples and paired checks 8 min; basicity comparison 6 min; aromatic nitrogen reasoning 12 min; amino-acid charge cases 10 min; integrated check and exit 5 min. Total 45 min, including drawing and discussion.
Suggested 30 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Plan 45 minutes including short drawing and discussion intervals. Routine visual frames take roughly 40 seconds; worked checks need longer and some resolutions can be quicker. Treat timings as guidance, with room for questions.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
Retrieve the starting idea
Draw NH₃ with three bonds and a lone pair. What changes when it accepts H⁺?

Suggested 30 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Give students a short individual attempt. Worked answer: The pair becomes an N–H bond; NH₄⁺ has four bonds and positive charge.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
Count carbon substituents at nitrogen

Count carbon substituents on nitrogen, not total N bondsWhich number distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary amines?

Suggested 40 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Ask students to inspect the indicated molecular feature rather than read the answer caption. Worked answer: Count directly attached carbon groups: one, two or three. The neutral ordinary amines shown still have a lone pair.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Apply: count carbon substituents at nitrogen
text:
Apply: count carbon substituents at nitrogen
Classify CH₃NHCH₂CH₃.

Suggested 60 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Allow a brief paper or pair check within this slide. Worked answer: Secondary: two carbon substituents are attached to N, plus one H.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
Audit nitrogen before protonation

Count nitrogen bonds and its nonbonding pairHow many bonds and nonbonding electrons belong to neutral methylamine N?

Suggested 40 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Ask students to inspect the indicated molecular feature rather than read the answer caption. Worked answer: It has three single bonds and one nonbonding pair. That pair can form the new N–H bond.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
Resolve: audit nitrogen before protonation

Count nitrogen bonds and its nonbonding pairIt has three single bonds and one nonbonding pair. That pair can form the new N–H bond.

Suggested 30 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Use a second inspection focus: justify the result by the atom, charge, ratio or observation involved. Next application answer: +1. Ordinary ammonium N has four bonds and no nonbonding pair.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
Apply: audit nitrogen before protonation
Give the N formal charge after forming a fourth single bond.

Suggested 60 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Allow a brief paper or pair check within this slide. Worked answer: +1. Ordinary ammonium N has four bonds and no nonbonding pair.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
Use a real proton donor

Amine protonation creates four bonds and positive chargeWhat must accompany the new N–H bond if H–A supplies H?

Suggested 40 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Ask students to inspect the indicated molecular feature rather than read the answer caption. Worked answer: The N pair forms N–H while the H–A bonding pair moves to A. Products are ammonium and A⁻.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Resolve: use a real proton donor
text:

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
text:
1. What is the attacked atom?
In ethyl ethanoate reacting with hydroxide, identify the initial attacked atom and the electron pair that moves at the same time.






Check your answer





The nucleophile attacks acyl carbon. The C=O pi pair moves onto carbonyl oxygen. Directly attaching OH while retaining every carbonyl bond would give five bonds at carbon.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
text:
2. What is the intermediate charge?
Write the intermediate from OH⁻ addition to CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ and locate its negative charge.






Check your answer





CH₃C(O⁻)(OH)(OCH₂CH₃), net −1. Incoming hydroxide becomes a neutral OH substituent; original carbonyl O now carries the charge.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
section: 3. What is the final acid/base pair?
text:
3. What is the final acid/base pair?
After collapse in basic ester hydrolysis, can carboxylic acid and ethoxide be treated as the final predominant products?






Check your answer





No. Ethoxide deprotonates the much stronger acid to give carboxylate and ethanol. Acid work-up can later protonate the carboxylate.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
section: 4. Does acid plus amine directly give amide?
text:
4. Does acid plus amine directly give amide?
Predict the initial predominant reaction between ethanoic acid and methylamine in water.






Check your answer





Proton transfer gives ethanoate and methylammonium. Suitable activation or conditions are needed to form an amide; simply losing OH⁻ from the unactivated acid is not an adequate mechanism.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
section: 5. Why is the amide C–N bond less freely rotating?
text:
5. Why is the amide C–N bond less freely rotating?
Connect amide resonance to its geometry without treating resonance contributors as separate molecules.






Check your answer





Nitrogen pair donation into the carbonyl gives partial C–N double-bond character. The charge-separated contributor has O− and N+; both contributors describe one delocalised amide.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
section: 6. Can an aldehyde follow exactly the same substitution?
text:
6. Can an aldehyde follow exactly the same substitution?
Why is a tetrahedral aldehyde intermediate not normally converted to an acyl-substitution product by ejecting its carbon-bound hydrogen?






Check your answer





That would require loss of hydride, a very poor leaving group in this setting. Aldehydes normally undergo carbonyl addition rather than this acyl-substitution analogy.



Return to the exercises for any reasoning you could not reconstruct. Explain one corrected mistake in your own words.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text: Compare acids, esters and amides by drawing their addition and leaving-group steps. Work through 1–10 for core work, 11–16 for transfer and 17–20 for deeper checks. Allow roughly 2–3 hours across the unit, taking longer for complete mechanisms. Attempt each problem before using its hint, then compare your revised drawing with the worked explanation.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
Working refresher
An acyl carbon is carbonyl carbon in R–C(=O)–Y. An ester has Y=OR′ and an amide has Y=NR′R″. A nucleophile donates a pair to carbonyl carbon while the C=O pi pair moves to O, giving a four-single-bond tetrahedral species. A viable leaving-group step can then restore C=O. Draw proton transfers with explicit donors and acceptors. Formal-charge checks used here: ordinary O with two bonds is neutral, one bond/three pairs is −1, and three bond orders is +1. For compatible pKa estimates, proton-transfer K≈10^(product-acid pKa−reactant-acid pKa). A worked mechanism is shown in the lecture; every problem below supplies its own necessary species and constants.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
1. Identify four oxygen-containing families
Draw CH₃COOH, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, CH₃CONH₂ and CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃ with explicit C=O bonds. Classify each, circle each acyl carbon and explain which one lacks an acyl group.






Hint





An acyl group contains a carbonyl carbon attached to the substituent being compared.









Worked explanation





The structures are acid, ester, amide and ether. The first three share CH₃C(=O)–Y; the ether has no C=O and therefore no acyl carbon. Oxygen alone does not establish an ester.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
2. Read a condensed formula carefully
Expand HCOOCH₃ and CH₃OCH₃. Count the bonds to the carbon next to the first oxygen. Which compound can undergo the elementary carbonyl-addition pattern?






Hint





In HCOOCH₃ the first carbon is H–C(=O)–, not H–C–O–O.









Worked explanation





HCOOCH₃ is methyl methanoate, H–C(=O)–O–CH₃, an ester. CH₃OCH₃ is an ether. Only the ester contains the required carbonyl carbon for that addition pattern.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
3. Write the two addition arrows
For OH⁻ attacking CH₃C(=O)OCH₃, draw the hydroxide lone pair and both curved arrows. Show a valid intermediate with all charges and count carbon bond orders.






Hint





As the new C–O bond forms, the C=O pi pair must move.









Worked explanation





Draw OH pair→acyl C and C=O π→carbonyl O. The intermediate is CH₃C(O⁻)(OH)(OCH₃), with four single bonds at C and net −1. Incoming O is neutral OH; original carbonyl O is O⁻.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
4. Track three oxygen identities
Label ester carbonyl O as A, ester single-bond O as B and incoming hydroxide O as C. Draw the tetrahedral intermediate and identify which oxygen still bears a methyl group.






Hint





Carbon–oxygen bonds to substituents do not disappear during the addition step.









Worked explanation





The intermediate is CH₃C(O-A⁻)(O-CH₃-B)(OH-C). B remains attached to methyl. A bears the negative charge and C retains its original H. A label follows an atom, not a position on the page.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
5. Complete an elimination step
Starting from CH₃C(O⁻)(OH)(OCH₃), draw carbonyl re-formation and methoxide departure. Give the immediate acid and base products and their total charge.






Hint





One pair moves from O⁻ into C–O π; another moves from the C–OCH₃ bond to methoxy O.









Worked explanation





The immediate pair is CH₃COOH + CH₃O⁻. Total charge remains −1. Carbonyl is restored, and methyl stays bonded to its departing oxygen; the group is methoxide, not a free methyl carbanion.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
6. Add the missing acid–base step
After collapse gives CH₃COOH and CH₃O⁻, use approximate compatible aqueous pKa values 4.8 for CH₃COOH and 15.5 for CH₃OH. Draw proton transfer, state the favoured pair and estimate K = 10^(product-acid pKa − reactant-acid pKa).






Hint





The weaker acid has the larger pKa.









Worked explanation





Methoxide takes the acid proton to give CH₃COO⁻ + CH₃OH. K≈10^10.7≈5×10¹⁰ toward that pair. Stopping at neutral acid plus alkoxide misses a strongly favoured final proton transfer.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
7. Balance net base-promoted hydrolysis
Write the net equation for CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ with OH⁻. Include the protonation state present in a basic mixture and audit atoms and total charge.






Hint





Cancel intermediates, not final stoichiometric reagents.









Worked explanation





CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + CH₃CH₂OH. Both sides have C₄H₉O₃ and net −1. Hydroxide is consumed overall, unlike the regenerated OH⁻ in simple carbonyl hydration.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
8. Separate hydrolysis from acid work-up
The basic reaction mixture contains sodium ethanoate. Write its reacting anion with hydronium and give products. Does work-up form a new carbon skeleton?






Hint





A spectator sodium ion need not enter the proton-transfer step.









Worked explanation





CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺ → CH₃COOH + H₂O. The acid carbon skeleton is retained. Work-up changes protonation state; it is not an unexplained deletion of the negative charge.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
9. Reject five-bonded carbon
A student draws CH₃C(=O)(OH)OCH₃ as the intermediate after OH⁻ attack. Count bond orders at carbon and repair the structure.






Hint





A carbonyl double bond contributes two to the bond-order count.









Worked explanation





That carbon has C–CH₃, C=O, C–OH and C–OCH₃: total five bond orders. Replace C=O with C–O⁻ to give CH₃C(O⁻)(OH)(OCH₃). The paired electron movement both restores carbon valence and locates charge.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
10. Compare ester and aldehyde
Compare OH⁻ addition to CH₃CHO and CH₃COOCH₃. Draw both tetrahedral species and explain why an ordinary aldehyde does not normally undergo substitution by expelling H⁻.






Hint





Compare the substituent in the potential leaving-group position.









Worked explanation





The species are CH₃CH(OH)O⁻ and CH₃C(OH)(O⁻)(OCH₃). Methoxy can leave through an appropriate pathway; hydride is an extremely poor leaving group in these simple reactions. Similar first addition steps do not force the same later chemistry.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
11. Start acid-catalysed esterification
Use ethanoic acid, ethanol and hydronium. Draw carbonyl-oxygen protonation, then neutral ethanol attack with movement of the pi pair. Give the charge on each oxygen of CH₃C(OH)(OH)(OHEt).






Hint





The incoming ethanol oxygen gains a third bond; the protonated original carbonyl oxygen loses its pi bond.









Worked explanation





Protonation gives CH₃C(=OH⁺)OH plus water. Ethanol attack gives CH₃C(OH)(OH)(O⁺HEt). Original carbonyl O is now neutral OH, original acid OH is neutral and incoming oxygen is +1. Total charge is +1.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
12. Make the incoming oxygen neutral
For CH₃C(OH)(OH)(O⁺HEt), draw water removing the extra incoming-oxygen proton. Count bonds at that O after transfer and identify the catalyst-containing species produced.






Hint





The O–H bonding pair stays on the oxygen losing H⁺.









Worked explanation





Water pair→incoming-oxygen H; O–H pair→incoming O. Products include CH₃C(OH)(OH)(OEt) and H₃O⁺. Incoming O has two bonds and is neutral. Explicit proton donors/acceptors preserve both atoms and charge.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
section: 13. Create and remove a leaving group
text:
13. Create and remove a leaving group
From the neutral tetrahedral species, protonate an OH to OH₂⁺, then draw loss of water with carbonyl re-formation. Why is drawing direct OH⁻ loss inappropriate for this representative acidic pathway?






Hint





Protonation changes the identity and stability of the departing group.









Worked explanation





An OH₂⁺ substituent can depart as neutral H₂O while the other OH oxygen reforms C=O, initially giving a protonated ester. Deprotonation restores neutral ester and acid catalyst. Direct OH⁻ loss skips the activation central to this acid pathway.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
14. Distinguish catalyst from equilibrium change
For CH₃COOH + EtOH ⇌ CH₃COOEt + H₂O, predict the effect of removing water and separately the effect of adding an acid catalyst at fixed temperature.






Hint





One action changes composition; the other changes access to the reaction pathway.









Worked explanation





Removing water can shift the composition toward ester. A catalyst accelerates the forward and reverse approach without changing K for the same net reaction under fixed conditions. Faster equilibration does not imply a different equilibrium constant.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
section: 15. Check an oxygen label in the product
text:
15. Check an oxygen label in the product
In the standard esterification pathway, use ethanol labelled at oxygen as Et–O*H. Draw the labelled ester and say which bond links the labelled O to the acid-derived fragment.






Hint





The alcohol oxygen forms the new bond to acyl carbon.









Worked explanation





The ester is CH₃C(=O)OEt. O is the single-bond ester oxygen, directly attached to acyl carbon and ethyl. This follows the specified mechanism; do not track atoms solely by whether they are drawn above or beside carbon.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
16. Draw amide resonance correctly
Draw neutral CH₃CONH₂ and its C=N charge-separated contributor. Give all O/N charges, total charge and the correct connecting arrow type.






Hint





When N donates into C–N, the C=O pi pair moves onto O.









Worked explanation





CH₃C(=O)NH₂ ↔︎ CH₃C(O⁻)=NH₂⁺. Total charge stays zero. Use a resonance double-headed arrow, not equilibrium arrows: these describe one delocalised amide with fixed nuclei.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
17. Explain restricted amide rotation
Compare CH₃CH₂NH₂ with CH₃CONH₂. Explain why their C–N bonds differ in rotational freedom and why their N basicities should not be assumed equal.






Hint





Connect the real bond to its resonance contributors rather than declaring the C–N bond literally always double.









Worked explanation





Amide donation gives partial C–N double-bond character, restricting rotation and delocalising the N pair into C=O. A simple alkylamine lacks that same neighbouring carbonyl conjugation. The different electron availability changes protonation behaviour.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
18. Predict acid plus amine
For CH₃COOH + CH₃NH₂ in water, use pKa 4.8 for the acid and 10.6 for methylammonium. Give the initially favoured acid–base products and explain why this is not already amide synthesis.






Hint





Compare the reactant and product acids.









Worked explanation





CH₃COO⁻ + CH₃NH₃⁺ is favoured, with estimated K≈10^5.8. This is proton transfer. Forming CH₃CONHCH₃ would require suitable activation/conditions and a productive acyl-substitution pathway; the salt alone is not an amide.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
19. Read two biological linkages
A lipid fragment is R–C(=O)–O–glycerol and a peptide fragment is R–C(=O)–NH–R′. Identify each linkage, locate the electrophilic carbon and explain why their rates of hydrolysis need not match.






Hint





The carbonyl carbon is common; the substituent and stabilisation differ.









Worked explanation





The first is ester and the second amide. Nucleophilic acyl attack begins at carbonyl carbon. Amide resonance stabilisation, leaving-group behaviour, activation and reaction conditions differ, so a common motif does not imply equal reactivity.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
20. Audit an incomplete mechanism
A proposed ester hydrolysis drawing adds OH⁻, loses the ethoxy group, writes neutral acid as final product in base and omits every charge. List three independent repairs and explain one experimental claim this mechanism alone cannot establish.






Hint





Check valence, proton transfers and the difference between a model and observations.









Worked explanation





Move the C=O pi pair during addition; show O⁻ in the intermediate and ethoxide on collapse; include acid–base transfer giving carboxylate and ethanol in base. The mechanism alone cannot establish isolated yield, purity or the measured rate; those require observations.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
Consolidate your work
Choose one corrected error and explain what changed in your reasoning. Then complete the self-check. Reading is optional; all practice above is self-contained.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
Explore
Choose electron-pair steps for ester hydrolysis and follow the acid–base trap. Allow 7–10 minutes: predict first, change one input at a time and explain the result.

Explore the chemistry





Prediction, exploration and explanation
Predict (1 minute). For methyl ethanoate plus hydroxide in the supplied basic model, predict the first electron-pair operation. Which group at acyl carbon could leave after a tetrahedral intermediate forms?
Explore (4–5 minutes). Try addition, then inspect the tetrahedral intermediate. Test both plausible collapse directions: forward methoxide departure and reversal with hydroxide departure. Follow the forward route, then choose what happens to the transient acid–methoxide pair. Test a hydride or methyl leaving-group proposal and read why it fails.
Explain (2 minutes). Draw the accepted addition, collapse and acid–base steps. Use the supplied pKa values to explain why stopping with neutral acid plus methoxide misses the base-condition product. What additional operation would be needed to obtain neutral acid after the basic reaction?


Supplied model and its limits
The selected model is basic hydrolysis of CH₃C(=O)OCH₃. Addition makes a tetrahedral O⁻ intermediate; collapse can expel methoxide or reverse by expelling hydroxide. Forward collapse gives a transient acid–methoxide pair. Compatible illustrative pKa values are 4.8 for ethanoic acid and 15.5 for methanol, so the proton-transfer equilibrium constant is approximately 10^(15.5−4.8)≈5×10¹⁰ toward carboxylate + methanol. Acid work-up is outside the interactive sequence. No rates, real operating protocol or universal leaving-group ranking is inferred.


Carry the explanation into practice
Return to the local exercises. Keep your prediction, a corrected drawing or calculation, and two sentences stating what the model supports and what it leaves unresolved.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Explain why carbonyl carbon is electrophilic.
Follow addition and proton-transfer steps.
Recognise a hydrate, hemiacetal and acetal.


45-minute block budget (all pauses included): 0–5 min: polarity and geometry; 5–15 min: labelled hydration and catalyst accounting; 15–27 min: acid activation, alcohol attack and deprotonation; 27–34 min: hydrate/hemiacetal/acetal comparisons and water equilibrium; 34–40 min: ring closure, formula and stereocentre checks; 40–43 min: independent labelled mechanism; 43–45 min: recap. The brief predictions, individual drawing and board discussion occur inside these blocks, not in extra time. The 40-second metadata is a rough planning reference; spend longer on the identified drawings and merge explanations already understood.
Begin with the previous unit’s electron-pair and charge audit. Ask students to predict a product or bond change before displaying the worked drawing. These slides support discussion and paper drawing; the practice page supplies further explanations.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
Draw ethanal and distinguish its partial charges from formal charges. What is its carbonyl-carbon geometry?

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: The carbonyl is polar and planar
text:
The carbonyl is polar and planar

Ethanal has an oxygen-polarised carbonyl and approximately trigonal planar geometry at its carbonyl carbon.C=O polarity makes carbon electron-poor. Its π pair can move to oxygen when a nucleophile adds.

Partial charges are not formal charges. The neutral starting carbonyl has no formal positive carbon even though the carbon is electrophilic.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: Label the original and incoming oxygen
text:
Label the original and incoming oxygen

Label the original and incoming oxygenIdentify which O receives the pi pair and which brings its H into the tetrahedral intermediate.

A was carbonyl O and becomes O⁻ first, then OH. B was incoming hydroxide O and already carries H. Hydroxide is regenerated by water proton loss.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Follow the proton-transfer product

Label the original and incoming oxygenAfter water protonates A, draw both labelled OH groups and the regenerated base.

A was carbonyl O and becomes O⁻ first, then OH. B was incoming hydroxide O and already carries H. Hydroxide is regenerated by water proton loss.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
Add OH⁻ to CH₃CHO on paper. If C–O forms, which existing pair must move so carbon keeps four bond orders?

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Addition changes carbon geometry

Hydroxide adds to ethanal, giving a tetrahedral intermediate with alkoxide oxygen and a newly attached OH.Two coupled arrows form C–O and move the C=O π pair to oxygen. The total charge remains −1.

The carbon has four single bonds after addition. The original carbonyl oxygen bears the negative charge. Check atom identity rather than treating both oxygens as interchangeable.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: Compare acid and base entry steps
text:
Compare acid and base entry steps

Compare acid and base entry stepsName the first operation in base-catalysed versus acid-catalysed hydration.

Base route attacks carbon first; acid route protonates oxygen first. Strong basic anions are protonated in excess acid, so the route must respect acid–base chemistry.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Choose a compatible attacking species

Compare acid and base entry stepsUnder proton-rich conditions, why use a neutral water/alcohol nucleophile rather than assuming freely persistent OH⁻/RO⁻?

Base route attacks carbon first; acid route protonates oxygen first. Strong basic anions are protonated in excess acid, so the route must respect acid–base chemistry.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
Label the original carbonyl oxygen A and incoming hydroxide oxygen B. After addition, which one needs a proton?

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Proton transfer completes the hydrate

Water transfers a proton to the alkoxide, giving a geminal diol and regenerating hydroxide.The net reaction is carbonyl + water ⇌ hydrate. The base participates in the pathway and is regenerated.

Not every carbonyl is mostly hydrated at equilibrium. Substituents and conditions affect the equilibrium; mechanism and product proportion are different questions.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Count methanol oxygen bonds

Count methanol oxygen bondsAfter methanol bonds to carbon but still retains H, explain its formal charge.

Incoming O goes from two to three bonds and becomes +1. Water takes its H⁺ to give neutral hemiacetal and hydronium.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Neutralise with an explicit acceptor

Count methanol oxygen bondsDraw the water deprotonation that restores a two-bond oxygen and state its donor-derived product.

Incoming O goes from two to three bonds and becomes +1. Water takes its H⁺ to give neutral hemiacetal and hydronium.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
In a proton-rich aqueous medium, which carbonyl atom can accept H⁺? Draw the donor-derived water too.

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: Acid can activate the oxygen first
text:
Acid can activate the oxygen first

A carbonyl oxygen lone pair accepts a proton from hydronium, producing protonated carbonyl and water.Protonating oxygen increases carbonyl electrophilicity. Neutral water or alcohol can then be the attacking nucleophile.

Avoid drawing a strongly basic nucleophile freely coexisting in excess strong acid. For this route use neutral nucleophiles and explicit proton transfers.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: Keep both oxygens in the product
text:
Keep both oxygens in the product

Keep both oxygens in the productWhich labelled oxygen is OH and which belongs to OCH₃ after hemiacetal formation?

Original carbonyl A gives OH; methanol B gives OCH₃. Swapping labels would require additional bond-breaking/exchange chemistry beyond the drawn sequence.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Reject a silent atom exchange

Keep both oxygens in the productWhy cannot the two oxygen labels simply be swapped in the worked drawing?

Original carbonyl A gives OH; methanol B gives OCH₃. Swapping labels would require additional bond-breaking/exchange chemistry beyond the drawn sequence.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
Methanol attacks a protonated aldehyde. Before deprotonation, count the incoming oxygen’s bonds and predict its charge.

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: An alcohol oxygen supplies a pair
text:
An alcohol oxygen supplies a pair

Methanol attacks the protonated carbonyl; the pi pair moves to oxygen, and the incoming methanol oxygen becomes oxonium.The new tetrahedral species has OH and O⁺HCH₃ attached to the same carbon.

An incoming neutral oxygen changes from two to three bonds and acquires positive charge. The formerly protonated carbonyl oxygen becomes neutral OH after its pi pair returns.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: Classify by groups at one carbon
text:
Classify by groups at one carbon

Classify by groups at one carbonIdentify two OH versus OH+OR in the two structures. Which reagent supplies the extra carbon of the methoxy group?

Water adds no carbon and gives a hydrate. Methanol provides OCH₃ and gives a hemiacetal; local group identity and overall atoms both distinguish them.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: Use formula accounting as a check
text:
Use formula accounting as a check

Classify by groups at one carbonCompare aldehyde+water with aldehyde+methanol. Why are their products not the same class?

Water adds no carbon and gives a hydrate. Methanol provides OCH₃ and gives a hemiacetal; local group identity and overall atoms both distinguish them.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
After attack, choose the oxygen that must lose a proton to form a neutral hemiacetal. What base can take it?

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Deprotonate the incoming oxygen

Water accepts a proton from the methoxy oxonium group, forming a neutral hemiacetal and hydronium.A hemiacetal has OH and OR attached to the same carbon. The acid catalyst is regenerated.

Do not remove the proton from the wrong atom without considering the resulting structure. Ask students to label original carbonyl oxygen and incoming alcohol oxygen.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: Ring closure does not imply elimination
text:
Ring closure does not imply elimination

Ring closure does not imply eliminationCompare before/after formulas for the five-hydroxy aldehyde cyclisation.

The terminal alcohol oxygen becomes ring O; the original carbonyl O becomes OH. No net water is removed in hemiacetal addition/proton transfer.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Locate every ring atom

Ring closure does not imply eliminationDraw the six-membered ring and mark the oxygen that was the terminal OH versus the oxygen now in its OH substituent.

The terminal alcohol oxygen becomes ring O; the original carbonyl O becomes OH. No net water is removed in hemiacetal addition/proton transfer.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
At the same tetrahedral carbon compare OH+OR with OR+OR. Name the two product classes without changing the drawing.

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
One substitution changes the class

A hemiacetal carbon has one OH and one OR group; an acetal carbon has two OR groups.A second alcohol can ultimately give an acetal under acid catalysis, with water formed. Additional steps are required.

The left/right diagrams compare product classes; they do not represent a single elementary OH-to-OR substitution. Students are required to understand the hemiacetal steps first.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Four groups must be different

Four groups must be differentCompare the former carbonyl carbon after methanol addition to ethanal versus propanone.

Ethanal product hasCH₃, H, OH, OCH₃ and is stereogenic. Propanone product retains two identical methyl groups, so its tetrahedral carbon is not a simple stereocentre.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Separate tetrahedral from chiral

Four groups must be differentWhy can an addition change geometry without making a stereocentre?

Ethanal product hasCH₃, H, OH, OCH₃ and is stereogenic. Propanone product retains two identical methyl groups, so its tetrahedral carbon is not a simple stereocentre.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
Balance aldehyde+two alcohols⇌acetal+water. Predict which direction excess water favours and separate that from acid catalysis.

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Conditions control the equilibrium mixture

The acetal equilibrium can be shifted toward acetal by removing water or toward hydrolysis using excess water under acid catalysis.Acid speeds both directions. Changing composition can shift the equilibrium mixture; catalysis alone does not change K.

This is a composition argument, not an experimental recipe. Do not describe an equilibrium arrow as proof of equal concentrations.

section: A pathway does not give the equilibrium amount
text:
A pathway does not give the equilibrium amount

A pathway does not give the equilibrium amountIdentify what a valid hydration mechanism accounts for and what it does not calculate.

A pathway does not give the equilibrium amountWhat information would justify calling the hydrate the dominant solution form?

Need compatible equilibrium/structure/condition evidence. A valid accessible pathway does not establish100% conversion to hydrate.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
Draw HO(CH₂)₄CHO and connect the alcohol O to aldehyde C. How many atoms belong to the new ring?

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: An internal OH can close a ring
text:
An internal OH can close a ring

The terminal alcohol of 5-hydroxypentanal can add to its aldehyde to form a six-membered cyclic hemiacetal.Intramolecular addition conserves the molecular formula. The ring includes the attacking oxygen and the original carbonyl carbon.

Count the six ring atoms: oxygen plus five carbons. This provides a chemical bridge to sugar rings without assuming carbohydrate biochemistry.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
Compare CH₃CHO and CH₃C(=O)OCH₃. Which group attached at carbonyl C introduces a possible leaving-group pathway?

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: Ask what else is bonded to carbonyl carbon
text:
Ask what else is bonded to carbonyl carbon

An aldehyde bears H at its carbonyl carbon, while an ester bears OR that can participate in an addition–elimination pathway.Aldehydes and ketones ordinarily retain their H/carbon substituents during addition. Acyl derivatives introduce leaving-group chemistry next.

Do not imply that alkoxide departs freely from every tetrahedral intermediate. Protonation state, leaving-group ability and conditions determine the viable pathway.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Same pattern, different nucleophiles
Water gives a hydrate; an alcohol can give a hemiacetal; a hydride equivalent gives an alcohol after proton donation.
Locate the new bond in each product. Keep reagent scope and conditions explicit.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: A mechanism and an equilibrium answer different questions
text:
A mechanism and an equilibrium answer different questions
The mechanism accounts for the path and intermediates. The equilibrium describes the relative amounts of species under stated conditions.
Drawing an accessible hydrate does not prove it is the major species.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Account for each oxygen
Start with CH₃CHO and CH₃OH. Label the aldehyde oxygen A and alcohol oxygen B.
In the hemiacetal, which is OH and which is OCH₃? What would be wrong with exchanging their atom labels without an extra process?

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: Draw the hemiacetal sequence without the slides
text:
Draw the hemiacetal sequence without the slides
Start from CH₃CHO and CH₃OH under acid catalysis. Draw activation, attack and deprotonation, labelling both oxygen atoms throughout.

Reserve 2 minutes for a complete individual drawing, then compare one mechanism at the board. This is application of the previous steps, not a new reaction family.

Adjust to observed errors; the 40 second metadata is a planning guide, not a quota. Required paper practice and optional transfer are available in the exercises.

Use the same reasoning in practice
