title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 1. What does propan-2-ol give on selected oxidation?
text:
1. What does propan-2-ol give on selected oxidation?
Retain the carbon skeleton.






Check your answer





Propanone. The carbon bearing OH becomes a carbonyl carbon, while its two carbon substituents remain attached.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 2. Why is a tertiary alcohol a boundary case?
text:
2. Why is a tertiary alcohol a boundary case?
Explain the missing bond at the carbon bearing OH.






Check your answer





It has no C–H bond at that carbon. Simple conversion to C=O while retaining all three C–C bonds would overbond carbon. Harsh oxidation can involve C–C cleavage, outside this selected pattern.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 3. What comes immediately after hydride-equivalent addition?
text:
3. What comes immediately after hydride-equivalent addition?
A ketone receives H at carbon while its pi pair moves to oxygen. Name the species type before work-up.






Check your answer





An alkoxide. A subsequent proton transfer from an explicit donor produces the alcohol. Free hydride in water is not what the simplified H: minus drawing represents.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 4. Does an OH band prove which alcohol is present?
text:
4. Does an OH band prove which alcohol is present?
State a limitation of functional-group IR evidence.






Check your answer





No. Many compounds share that functional group, bands can overlap, and samples can contain water or mixtures. Combine multiple observations with structural and purity evidence.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 5. Which amount limits a one-to-one reaction?
text:
5. Which amount limits a one-to-one reaction?
Reactants are available as 10.0 and 15.0 mmol. Product coefficient is one.






Check your answer





The 10.0 mmol reactant limits product to 10.0 mmol. Compare amount divided by stoichiometric coefficient, rather than raw masses.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
text:
6. Does 66.6% isolated yield mean 66.6% conversion?
Explain one possible reason they differ.






Check your answer





No. Starting material may react but product may be lost during isolation; side products or impurities can also affect the relationship. Conversion, isolated yield and purity answer different questions.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the worked practice, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
Track alcohol and carbonyl transformations, check oxidation states, and connect reagent amounts to the evidence for a product. Use the lecture and demo to revisit a worked case.
Core 1–12: about 80–100 minutes. Transfer 13–20: an optional 45–65 minutes; choose problems that target the mistakes you want to resolve.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
section: Local refresher and worked starting example
text:
Local refresher and worked starting example
Selected primary alcohol oxidation gives aldehyde then acid; secondary alcohol gives ketone. Carbonyl reduction by a supplied suitable reagent gives an alkoxide then an alcohol after proton donation. For the carbon oxidation-state check, C–O bond order contributes+1, C–H−1, C–C0. For amounts use n=m/M and compare n/coefficient.
Worked starting example. Ethanol CH₃CH₂OH→ethanal CH₃CHO raises the changing carbon oxidation state from −1 to+1. In the reverse selected reduction, hydride-equivalent delivery forms CH₃CH₂O⁻ first; water can then donate H⁺ to give ethanol and OH⁻. Each stage has explicit atoms and charge.
Draw structures, identify the relevant atom and explain the reason. A name alone is insufficient where a mechanism or argument is requested.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
1. Classify the alcohol centre
Draw CH₃CH₂OH, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ and (CH₃)₃COH. Classify the OH-bearing carbon and count its attached H.






Hint





Count carbon neighbours and H at that particular carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





The centres are primary with two H, secondary with one H and tertiary with no H. These local differences determine whether the simple carbon-skeleton-retaining carbonyl oxidation pattern applies.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
2. Oxidise a primary alcohol once
Draw the selected net transformation ethanol → ethanal, preserving the carbon skeleton. Identify the changing C–O and C–H bond inventory.






Hint





Turn the alcohol-bearing carbon into a carbonyl carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





CH₃CH₂OH becomes CH₃CHO. The changing carbon loses a C–H bond overall and gains C–O bond order; O also loses its H. This is a net oxidation map, not an elementary one-step mechanism or a lab protocol.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
3. Oxidise the aldehyde further
Draw ethanal → ethanoic acid and explain why an aldehyde target requires controlled oxidation conditions.






Hint





Replace the aldehyde C–H with the acid C–OH in the net structure.









Worked answer and reasoning





CH₃CHO becomes CH₃COOH. Since the aldehyde can undergo further oxidation, an unspecified oxidation arrow does not guarantee that isolation stops there. Conditions and reagent scope matter.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
4. Oxidise a secondary alcohol
Predict the selected oxidation product of butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃. Name the functional group and give its condensed structure.






Hint





Retain both carbon substituents on the OH-bearing carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





The product is butan-2-one, CH₃C(=O)CH₂CH₃, a ketone. Forming C=O while removing the appropriate H atoms retains the four-carbon skeleton.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
5. Explain the tertiary boundary
Why would drawing (CH₃)₃C=O as the direct simple oxidation product of (CH₃)₃COH be invalid?






Hint





Count bond orders at the central carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





Three C–C single bonds plus C=O give bond-order sum five. The starting tertiary centre has no C–H for the usual alcohol-to-carbonyl change. Oxidative C–C cleavage can occur under other conditions, but that is a different transformation.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
6. Assign a carbon oxidation state
Use +1 per C–O bond order, −1 per C–H and zero per C–C to assign the changing carbon in ethanol, ethanal and ethanoic acid.






Hint





Double C=O contributes plus two.









Worked answer and reasoning





The values are −1, +1 and +3 respectively. Increasing oxidation state identifies oxidation even when simply counting oxygen atoms would miss the first change.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
7. Check a ketone carbon
Assign the carbonyl-carbon oxidation state in CH₃COCH₃ and the corresponding OH-carbon value in CH₃CH(OH)CH₃.






Hint





The ketone carbon has no attached H; the alcohol carbon has one.









Worked answer and reasoning





Propanone carbonyl C is +2 from C=O. Propan-2-ol carbinol C is 0 from +1 for C–O and −1 for C–H. The ketone-to-alcohol transformation lowers the carbon oxidation state by two.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
8. Reduce an aldehyde
Assume a suitable NaBH₄ reduction then proton-donor work-up of CH₃CH₂CHO. Predict the neutral organic product.






Hint





Carbonyl reduction preserves the carbon skeleton and adds H at carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





Propanal gives propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH. Hydride-equivalent delivery gives an alkoxide first; a proton donor supplies its O–H proton afterward.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
9. Reduce a ketone
Under the same selected reduction/work-up model, predict CH₃COCH₂CH₃ → product. Does the product have a stereocentre?






Hint





The former carbonyl carbon gains H and OH while retaining methyl and ethyl.









Worked answer and reasoning





The product is butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃. Its OH-bearing carbon has OH, H, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃, so it is a stereocentre. An achiral reagent/environment can allow both faces of the planar carbonyl to react.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
10. Draw the reduction arrows
For propanone, draw a simplified H:⁻ delivery step and the alkoxide. Explicitly state what H:⁻ represents.






Hint





Move the carbonyl pi pair onto oxygen as C–H forms.









Worked answer and reasoning





The product is (CH₃)₂CHO⁻; one pair forms C–H and the C=O π pair returns to O. H:⁻ means hydride-equivalent delivery from a reagent such as borohydride, not a claim that free hydride persists in aqueous solution.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
11. Finish the work-up
Use water to turn (CH₃)₂CHO⁻ into alcohol. Draw the donor and conjugate base instead of writing unexplained H⁺.






Hint





Water loses one H⁺ when it protonates the alkoxide.









Worked answer and reasoning





Alkoxide O attacks water H; the water O–H pair returns to O. Products are propan-2-ol and OH⁻, with net charge −1 conserved.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
12. Test reagent scope
A student transfers the selected NaBH₄ aldehyde/ketone rule directly to an ordinary ester and an amide. Why is that unsupported by this course toolkit?






Hint





Carbonyl groups belong to different functional classes with different reactivity.









Worked answer and reasoning





The supplied rule establishes aldehyde/ketone reduction under appropriate conditions. Esters and amides have different electronic and leaving-group chemistry; their behaviour cannot be inferred just from the shared C=O drawing. More reagent/condition information is required.









Note



Optional transfer starts here. Choose problems that address your own gaps; the core route remains1–12.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
13. Read two IR observations
A supplied teaching sample loses a broad 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ alcohol feature and gains strong absorption near 1715 cm⁻¹ after a proposed secondary-alcohol oxidation. Explain support and limitation.






Hint





Relate each observation to a functional group, then consider identity.









Worked answer and reasoning





The changes support loss of OH and formation of carbonyl, consistent with the proposed oxidation. They do not uniquely identify the ketone or establish purity; use additional structure and sample evidence.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
14. Calculate amounts by hand
A balanced 1:1 aspirin teaching reaction uses 1.3812 g acid at 138.12 g/mol and 1.53135 g anhydride at 102.09 g/mol. Calculate both mmol values and identify the limiting reagent.






Hint





Divide g by g/mol, multiply mol by1000, then compare amount/coefficient.









Worked answer and reasoning





The acid is 0.01000 mol=10.00 mmol and anhydride0.01500 mol=15.00 mmol. The acid limits the 1:1 reaction. Comparing raw grams would ignore the different molar masses.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
section: 15. Use a coefficient other than one
text:
15. Use a coefficient other than one
For the hypothetical balanced teaching stoichiometry 2 A + B → P, available amounts are 12 mmol A and8 mmol B. Calculate the maximum mmol P and identify the limit.






Hint





Compare n(A)/2 with n(B)/1.









Worked answer and reasoning





A permits 6 mmol reaction extent; B permits 8 mmol. A limits product to 6 mmol P. A larger molar amount can still limit when its stoichiometric coefficient is larger.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
16. Calculate theoretical mass
The aspirin teaching reaction can make10.00 mmol product with molar mass180.16 g/mol. Calculate theoretical mass in grams.






Hint





Convert mmol to mol before multiplying by g/mol.









Worked answer and reasoning





0.01000 mol×180.16 g/mol=1.8016 g. Using10 directly as mol would introduce a thousandfold error.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
17. Calculate isolated yield
Using theoretical mass1.8016 g and isolated mass1.20 g, calculate isolated yield. State a claim this value cannot establish.






Hint





Yield%=100×isolated/theoretical.









Worked answer and reasoning





The result is about 66.6%. It does not prove purity or conversion: isolation losses, unreacted material, side reactions and retained impurities require separate evidence.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
18. Repair a yield over 100percent claim
A wet isolated sample weighs1.95 g although the theoretical pure-product maximum is 1.8016 g. Should this establish109% chemical yield? Give a better interpretation.






Hint





The balance measures all material present, not only intended product.









Worked answer and reasoning





The apparent mass-based percentage is about 108%, but a pure-product yield above the stoichiometric maximum is inconsistent with the assumptions. Residual solvent/water, impurities or input/measurement errors should be investigated before reporting an actual product yield.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
19. Plan a one-step interconversion
Given ethanal and a target of ethanol, choose oxidation or the supplied carbonyl reduction/work-up. Draw the target and explain why further oxidation is wrong.






Hint





The target carbon has more C–H and less C–O bond order.









Worked answer and reasoning





Use the selected reduction followed by proton donation to give CH₃CH₂OH. Oxidation moves toward ethanoic acid instead, increasing rather than decreasing the changing carbon oxidation state.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
20. Assemble an evidence statement
A proposed propan-2-ol→propanone experiment gives an IR carbonyl band, one visible TLC spot and an isolated mass. Write two supported conclusions and two unresolved questions.






Hint





Separate functional-group evidence, chromatographic observation and chemical identity.









Worked answer and reasoning





The IR supports a carbonyl-containing sample; the TLC records one spot under its stated conditions. Neither alone proves pure propanone. Identity needs additional structural evidence, and purity/conversion require suitable separate checks; the isolated mass alone is not enough.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
section: R task: chemistry calculation in your report
text:
R task: chemistry calculation in your report
The balanced teaching equation is salicylic acid + acetic anhydride → aspirin + ethanoic acid, with all coefficients one. The shared CSV supplies reagent masses and molar masses. This is a calculation context, not a synthesis protocol. Keep the raw data unchanged.
The amount in mol is mass in g divided by molar mass in g/mol. Divide each reactant amount by its stoichiometric coefficient. The smallest available reaction extent limits the maximum product amount. Here aspirin’s coefficient is one and its supplied molar mass is 180.16 g/mol.
Predict which of 10.0 and 15.0 mmol will limit a 1:1 reaction, then add this code to your report:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
amounts <- read_csv("data/amounts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol,
         amount_mmol = amount_mol * 1000,
         extent_mol = amount_mol / stoich)
knitr::kable(amounts, digits = 4)
limiting_extent_mol <- min(amounts$extent_mol)
theoretical_product_mass_g <- limiting_extent_mol * 180.16
theoretical_product_mass_g
Knit the report. Give the limiting reagent, theoretical product amount in mmol and mass in g. Change a copy of the acetic anhydride input to 0.51045 g and predict the new limiting reagent before recalculating. Do not overwrite the original CSV to make this alternative scenario.






Numerical and chemical check





The supplied amounts are 0.0100 mol acid and 0.0150 mol anhydride. Salicylic acid limits the product to 10.0 mmol, corresponding to 1.8016 g aspirin. With 0.51045 g anhydride at 102.09 g/mol, anhydride is 5.00 mmol and limits product to 5.00 mmol, or 0.9008 g. Comparing masses alone would be wrong because the reagents have different molar masses. In a different balanced reaction, coefficients other than one must also be included.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
Explore
Use this explorer for about 7–10 minutes. Make a prediction first, change one input at a time, and record a chemical explanation rather than only a screenshot.

Explore the chemistry





Prediction, exploration and explanation
Predict (1–2 minutes). Assign the changing carbon in ethanol before checking. Use +1 per C–O bond order, −1 per C–H bond and 0 per C–C bond. Is your answer a formal charge?
Explore (3–4 minutes). Check ethanol, then use the selected-next-oxidation button to move through ethanal to ethanoic acid. Compare propan-2-ol with propanone. Finally inspect 2-methylpropan-2-ol and explain why the simple next-oxidation button is unavailable.
Explain (2 minutes). Show one full bond-count calculation. Why can oxidation happen without adding a new oxygen atom? Why would retaining all three C–C bonds while converting the tertiary centre to C=O give an invalid ordinary carbon?


Supplied model and its limits
The displayed value is the oxidation state of the changing carbon, not its formal charge. C–O bond order contributes +1, C–H −1, C–C 0. The supplied selected net maps are primary alcohol→aldehyde→acid and secondary alcohol→ketone. The tertiary centre has no attached H, so the simple carbon-skeleton-retaining map cannot be used. Other harsh, C–C-cleaving chemistry is outside this model; no laboratory conditions are supplied.


Continue with the exercises
Continue with the exercises. Keep your prediction, a corrected drawing or calculation, and two sentences stating what the model supports and what it leaves unresolved.

title: Self-check: Substitution
text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Substitution
text:
1. Which carbon is secondary?
Classify the carbon bearing Br in CH₃CH(Br)CH₂CH₃.






Check your answer





It is secondary because it is directly bonded to two carbon atoms. The molecule containing four carbons does not make the reacting centre tertiary.

title: Self-check: Substitution
text:
2. What does SN2 leave behind?
For OH⁻ + CH₃Br, give products and net charge.






Check your answer





CH₃OH + Br⁻; total charge is minus one. The C–Br pair goes to Br while hydroxide makes C–O.

title: Self-check: Substitution
section: 3. What happens when both concentrations double?
text:
3. What happens when both concentrations double?
Use the supplied simple SN2 rate law k[RX][Nu]. Keep temperature and solvent fixed.






Check your answer





The initial rate becomes fourfold because each concentration contributes a factor of two. This does not by itself predict a fourfold isolated yield.

title: Self-check: Substitution
section: 4. Does inversion always mean R becomes S?
text:
4. Does inversion always mean R becomes S?
Explain why priorities must still be checked after an SN2 replacement.






Check your answer





The reacting geometry inverts, but replacing one substituent can change CIP priorities. Assign the new priorities before translating geometry into an R/S label.

title: Self-check: Substitution
section: 5. What follows water capture in SN1?
text:
5. What follows water capture in SN1?
Water adds to a carbocation. Is the immediate product an ordinary neutral alcohol?






Check your answer





No. Oxygen has three bonds and formal charge plus one, giving a protonated alcohol. A base such as another water must remove a proton to give the neutral alcohol.

title: Self-check: Substitution
section: 6. Is every SN1 product exactly racemic?
text:
6. Is every SN1 product exactly racemic?
A carbocation is planar. What does that suggest, and what qualification is needed?






Check your answer





Both faces can be accessible, giving both configurations when a stereocentre forms. Ion pairs and the molecular environment can bias attack, so exact 50:50 is not universal.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the worked practice, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
Classify reacting carbons, draw substitution mechanisms and explain how the conditions affect the pathway. Use the lecture and demo to revisit a worked case.
Core 1–12: about 80–100 minutes. Transfer 13–20: an optional 45–65 minutes; choose problems that target the mistakes you want to resolve.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
section: Local refresher and worked starting example
text:
Local refresher and worked starting example
A nucleophile donates a pair to saturated carbon; a leaving group takes the old bonding pair. SN2 couples these changes and inverts the reacting geometry. SN1 ionises first and then captures a carbocation. Methyl/primary/secondary/tertiary counts carbon neighbours at the reacting carbon. Conditions determine which model applies.
Worked starting example. For OH⁻+CH₃Br, oxygen gains a C–O bond and becomes neutral in CH₃OH; Br receives the C–Br pair as Br⁻. No carbocation appears in this concerted example. A neutral incoming water or ammonia instead acquires positive charge before a later proton transfer.
Draw structures, identify the relevant atom and explain the reason. A name alone is insufficient where a mechanism or argument is requested.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
1. Classify four centres
Draw CH₃Br, CH₃CH₂Br, CH₃CH(Br)CH₃ and (CH₃)₃CBr. Classify each carbon bonded to Br and explain your counting rule.






Hint





Count carbon neighbours directly attached to the Br-bearing carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





The classes are methyl, primary, secondary and tertiary, with zero, one, two and three carbon neighbours respectively. The total carbon count of the whole molecule is not the classification criterion.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
2. Same formula, different accessibility
Draw 1-bromobutane and 2-bromobutane. Circle the reaction centre and compare backside crowding under otherwise comparable SN2 conditions.






Hint





Their formulas match; the local carbon environment differs.









Worked answer and reasoning





The terminal reacting carbon in 1-bromobutane is primary and generally less hindered than the secondary carbon in 2-bromobutane. This favours SN2 access for the primary example, without establishing a universal rate ratio.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
3. Construct the methyl mechanism
Draw the concerted OH⁻ + CH₃Br SN2 step, showing the leaving pair and net charge.






Hint





Both bond changes occur in one elementary step.









Worked answer and reasoning





OH lone pair → C and C–Br pair → Br produce CH₃OH + Br⁻. Total charge is −1. A methyl carbocation is not an intermediate in this model.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
4. Change the incoming group
Assume an SN2 displacement of CH₃Br by I⁻ in a suitable medium. Draw the bond changes and products without claiming the equilibrium position.






Hint





Use iodine as pair donor and keep bromide as the leaving group.









Worked answer and reasoning





The I pair forms C–I while C–Br breaks to Br⁻, producing CH₃I + Br⁻. The same electron-flow pattern applies. Conditions and relative activities are needed to discuss extent of reaction.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
5. Build an ether
Assume suitable dry SN2 conditions for CH₃CH₂O⁻ + CH₃CH₂Br. Draw the new bond and both products. Why is the organic product neutral?






Hint





The alkoxide oxygen changes from one bond to two.









Worked answer and reasoning





Products are CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃ and Br⁻. Oxygen donates its pair to carbon and becomes a neutral two-bond ether oxygen. Net charge remains −1, now carried by bromide.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
6. Let ammonia attack
Draw the first SN2 step of NH₃ + CH₃Br. A proposed answer CH₃NH₂ + Br⁻ is missing something: identify it.






Hint





The attacking nitrogen initially carries three H atoms.









Worked answer and reasoning





The immediate product is CH₃NH₃⁺ + Br⁻. Nitrogen gains a fourth bond and positive charge. Neutral methylamine requires a separate proton-transfer step; it cannot lose H without a proton acceptor.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
7. Finish the amine proton transfer
Draw the possible equilibrium proton transfer from CH₃NH₃⁺ to another NH₃. Show both arrows and all products; do not assume quantitative deprotonation.






Hint





Ammonia is the base in this second event.









Worked answer and reasoning





An NH₃ lone pair takes H from methylammonium; the original N–H pair returns to methylamine N. Products are CH₃NH₂ and NH₄⁺. Charge +1 is conserved, and the nitrogen roles differ between attack and deprotonation. This is a valid proton-transfer possibility, not a claim that equilibrium intrinsically favours complete deprotonation. Amounts and reaction conditions, including excess ammonia, affect the resulting mixture.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
8. Use the SN2 rate model
For rate=k[RX][Nu], predict the initial-rate factor when [RX] is doubled and [Nu] tripled at fixed temperature and solvent.






Hint





Multiply the independent concentration factors.









Worked answer and reasoning





The rate increases sixfold in the supplied simple model. The calculation describes initial kinetics and does not imply a sixfold equilibrium conversion or yield.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
9. Hold the rate constant
In the same rate model, [RX] is halved while [Nu] is doubled. Predict the rate factor and state the assumptions.






Hint





One factor offsets the other if k is unchanged.









Worked answer and reasoning





The predicted initial rate is unchanged: 0.5×2=1. Temperature, solvent and the applicable mechanism must remain comparable; changing those can change k or the mechanism.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
10. Reject an obstructed pathway
Compare CH₃CH₂Br and (CH₃)₃CBr for direct backside substitution by the same nucleophile. Why should a tertiary substrate not be assigned SN2 merely because the nucleophile is strong?






Hint





Draw the carbon groups around the reaction centre.









Worked answer and reasoning





Three carbon substituents strongly obstruct backside approach at the tertiary centre. A strong donor cannot remove this geometric requirement; elimination or a stepwise route may compete depending on conditions. Primary ethyl is much more accessible.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
11. Begin a tertiary SN1 route
For (CH₃)₃CBr in an ionising aqueous medium, draw C–Br heterolysis and label the product charges.






Hint





The departing group receives the entire C–Br pair.









Worked answer and reasoning





Products are (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻. The tertiary carbocation is more stabilised than a methyl cation, and the medium can stabilise separated charge. Ionisation does not yet specify the final capture or elimination outcome.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
12. Capture with water
Draw H₂O attack on (CH₃)₃C⁺. Count oxygen bonds in the immediate product.






Hint





Use a water lone pair, not a hydrogen, to make the new bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





The oxonium product is (CH₃)₃COH₂⁺. Oxygen has three bonds and charge +1. Writing the neutral alcohol at this stage would silently remove a proton.









Note



Optional transfer starts here. Choose problems that address your own gaps; the core route remains1–12.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
13. Obtain neutral alcohol
Use H₂O to deprotonate (CH₃)₃COH₂⁺. Include the species made from the base.






Hint





Water becomes hydronium after accepting H⁺.









Worked answer and reasoning





Products are (CH₃)₃COH and H₃O⁺. The base pair forms O–H and the original oxonium O–H pair returns to its oxygen. The net charge is +1 before and after.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
14. Balance the overall aqueous route
Combine tertiary ionisation, water capture and water deprotonation into one net equation starting from (CH₃)₃CBr. Include bromide.






Hint





Two waters appear in the explicit overall accounting.









Worked answer and reasoning





(CH₃)₃CBr + 2 H₂O → (CH₃)₃COH + H₃O⁺ + Br⁻. This represents the selected substitution path; it does not exclude competing elimination. Atoms and overall zero charge balance.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
15. Assign a particular inversion
Start with (S)-2-bromobutane and assume stereospecific SN2 replacement of Br by OH. Assign the product configuration by checking priorities rather than just changing the letter.






Hint





For each structure, rank the heteroatom group, ethyl, methyl and H.









Worked answer and reasoning





Both Br and OH are highest priority in their respective structures; ethyl outranks methyl and H is lowest. Backside geometric inversion therefore gives (R)-butan-2-ol in this particular example. A different replacement could change the priority order and the letter relationship.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
16. Explain two-face access
A planar carbocation reacts in an achiral medium to form a stereocentre. Explain why both configurations may form and why an exactly 50:50 mixture is not guaranteed in every SN1 reaction.






Hint





Distinguish an isolated planar model from an actual ion pair and environment.









Worked answer and reasoning





Both faces of a planar intermediate may be accessible. Nearby leaving-group ions or other environmental constraints can bias capture, so the geometric argument supports both-face reaction without promising an exact racemic ratio in every experiment.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
17. Activate an alcohol
Draw CH₃CH₂OH protonation by H₃O⁺ and name the better departing group after protonation. Do not assume a primary carbocation forms.






Hint





Change the oxygen protonation state before discussing departure.









Worked answer and reasoning





The alcohol gives CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺ plus H₂O. Neutral water is a better leaving group than hydroxide. That activation allows suitable substitution pathways, but a primary substrate still should not be forced into an unsupported SN1 carbocation model.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
18. Keep solvent claims controlled
A student predicts identical rates for CH₃Br + OH⁻ in every solvent because the two reactant formulas are unchanged. Give a chemically justified objection.






Hint





The medium can alter ion stabilisation and donor availability.









Worked answer and reasoning





Solvation changes the energies and effective reactivity of the charged nucleophile and transition state. Keeping formulas the same does not keep k unchanged. State solvent and temperature before transferring rate comparisons between experiments.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
19. Repair an atom-loss error
A proposed tertiary-water mechanism changes (CH₃)₃COH₂⁺ directly to (CH₃)₃COH and writes no other species. Add a valid missing step.






Hint





Supply a base and show where the departing proton goes.









Worked answer and reasoning





Another water takes H⁺ while the oxonium O–H pair returns to O, producing alcohol and H₃O⁺. The corrected step conserves H atoms and charge +1.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
20. Name the competing route
From (CH₃)₃C⁺ in water, draw removal of a β-H and the resulting alkene. How does this differ from water attack at carbon?






Hint





The C–H pair can form a C=C bond to the cationic centre.









Worked answer and reasoning





Water acting as base removes β-H, giving 2-methylpropene and hydronium through E1. Water acting as nucleophile at carbon instead starts the alcohol-forming SN1 path. The common intermediate permits competing outcomes.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
Check your progress
Choose one corrected drawing and explain what changed in its atoms, charge, geometry or evidence. Then complete the self-check. The reading guide is optional support; all required exercise information is supplied here.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
Explore
Use this explorer for about 7–10 minutes. Make a prediction first, change one input at a time, and record a chemical explanation rather than only a screenshot.

Explore the chemistry





Prediction, exploration and explanation
Predict (1–2 minutes). With [RX]=0.050 mol/L and [Nu]=0.100 mol/L, use the supplied illustrative constants below to calculate both initial rates. Predict what happens when only [Nu] doubles.
Explore (3–4 minutes). Hold [RX] fixed while changing [Nu], then hold [Nu] fixed while changing [RX]. Set nucleophile to zero, and then substrate to zero. Find the nucleophile concentration where the two model lines cross. Use the reset to return to the named starting case.
Explain (2 minutes). Which model changes with nucleophile concentration and why? Why does a crossing of these assumed laws not identify the real mechanism of an arbitrary substrate? Report rates with units.


Supplied model and its limits
Supplied models: v₁=k₁[RX] with k₁=0.010 s⁻¹; v₂=k₂[RX][Nu] with k₂ = 0.100 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. Concentrations are mol/L, and rates are mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. These constants are illustrative teaching inputs, not measured values for a named chemical. The two laws are compared as separate assumed pathways; this tool does not choose SN1/SN2 from substrate identity or calculate product competition.


Continue with the exercises
Continue with the exercises. Keep your prediction, a corrected drawing or calculation, and two sentences stating what the model supports and what it leaves unresolved.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Identify an electron-pair source and acceptor.
Draw valid arrows for an elementary step.
Distinguish intermediates, transition states and catalysts.


45-minute block budget (all pauses included): 0–4 min: recall lone pairs/valence; 4–12 min: proton transfer and concerted substitution; 12–21 min: carbonyl addition and charge repair; 21–29 min: neutral-nitrogen donors and proton accounting; 29–37 min: energy profiles, catalysis and reverse barriers; 37–42 min: labelled-atom drawing/application; 42–45 min: retrieval and recap. The brief predictions, individual drawing and board discussion occur inside these blocks, not in extra time. The 40-second metadata is a rough planning reference; spend longer on the identified drawings and merge explanations already understood.
Begin with the previous unit’s electron-pair and charge audit. Ask students to predict a product or bond change before displaying the worked drawing. These slides support discussion and paper drawing; the practice page supplies further explanations.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
Given CH₃OH and OH⁻, draw the pair that forms a new O–H bond. What second pair must move? Do not decide equilibrium position from arrows alone.

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Arrows follow electron pairs

A lone pair forms the new O–H bond while the original O–H bonding pair returns to oxygen.Every full-headed curved arrow starts at a lone pair or bond. Two arrows are needed for this proton transfer.

Point to each arrow tail and ask what pair was there before the step. Do not accept an arrow starting at a positive charge or at a bare hydrogen.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: A neutral base can become a cation
text:
A neutral base can become a cation

A neutral base can become a cationRead the new N–H bond in ammonia protonation. Identify both original electron pairs before writing products.

NH₃ donates its lone pair; H–Cl gives its pair to Cl. NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻ conserve net zero charge.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Audit the nitrogen after proton transfer
text:
Audit the nitrogen after proton transfer

A neutral base can become a cationDraw NH₄⁺ with four N–H bonds. Explain why four bonds and no lone pair require +1, then locate the opposite charge.

NH₃ donates its lone pair; H–Cl gives its pair to Cl. NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻ conserve net zero charge.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
Break the C–Br bond in CH₃Br formally by giving both electrons to Br. Which two charges must appear? Is a balanced drawing sufficient evidence of a fast reaction?

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Both bonding electrons can stay together
text:
Both bonding electrons can stay together

The C–Br bonding pair moves to bromine, giving formally separated positive and negative ions.Heterolysis gives the two bonding electrons to one atom. Charge separation must appear in the products.

This is bookkeeping, not a prediction that a methyl carbocation forms readily. Methyl substrates instead favour concerted substitution in the examples used here.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Count before using a charge label
text:
Count before using a charge label

Count before using a charge labelCompare three-bond NH₃ with four-bond NH₄⁺. Which available lone pair has become a bond?

Nitrogen has five valence electrons. Three bonds plus one pair is neutral; four bonds and no pair gives formal +1.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Transfer the counting rule to an attacking amine
text:
Transfer the counting rule to an attacking amine

Count before using a charge labelIf NH₃ adds a bond to CH₃ instead of H, predict CH₃NH₃⁺ before any later proton transfer.

Nitrogen has five valence electrons. Three bonds plus one pair is neutral; four bonds and no pair gives formal +1.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Name the donor and acceptor

A hydroxide lone pair is the source and the polar carbonyl carbon is an electron-pair acceptor.A nucleophile donates a pair to form a bond; an electrophile accepts it. A neutral molecule may be either.

This picture locates the source and acceptor. It is not a complete mechanism: the carbonyl pi pair must move too when the new bond forms.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: A new bond need not give a neutral product
text:
A new bond need not give a neutral product

A new bond need not give a neutral productRead the methyl–nitrogen bond formation. Explain why the immediate product retains three N–H bonds.

The next products are CH₃NH₂ and NH₄⁺. A separate proton acceptor is necessary to form neutral methylamine.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Choose the next chemical operation

A new bond need not give a neutral productDraw another NH₃ accepting a proton from CH₃NH₃⁺. Track the pair returning to methylamine N.

The next products are CH₃NH₂ and NH₄⁺. A separate proton acceptor is necessary to form neutral methylamine.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
Draw the immediate product when OH⁻ adds to CH₃CHO. Count every carbon bond order and place the charge before protonating anything.

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Do not give carbon five bonds
text:
Do not give carbon five bonds

Hydroxide addition moves the carbonyl pi pair to oxygen and makes a tetrahedral alkoxide.New C–O bond formation and C=O π-bond cleavage occur in the same elementary addition step.

Count the central carbon bond orders before and after. The product oxygen with one bond has three lone pairs and formal charge minus one.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Use each minimum as its own baseline
text:
Use each minimum as its own baseline

Use each minimum as its own baselineRead the forward and reverse barriers from reactants0, transition state +45 and products−20 kJ/mol.

Forward barrier 45, reverse 65. Endpoint free energy describes equilibrium; the barrier is needed for rate reasoning.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Distinguish favourable from fast

Use each minimum as its own baselineThe endpoint ΔG is −20 kJ/mol. Explain why a45 kJ/mol forward barrier still matters even though the products are lower.

Forward barrier 45, reverse 65. Endpoint free energy describes equilibrium; the barrier is needed for rate reasoning.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
For OH⁻ + CH₃Br, draw the new bond and the departing bond pair in one elementary step. What species must not be inserted between them?

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: One elementary step can use several arrows
text:
One elementary step can use several arrows

Two electron pairs move together in methyl bromide substitution by hydroxide.Concerted means one step with no intermediate between bond breaking and bond making.

The total charge remains minus one. There is no methyl carbocation minimum hidden in this concerted example.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Protons transfer; oxygen labels stay

Protons transfer; oxygen labels stayIdentify which oxygen remains bonded to CH₃ after methanol deprotonation.

A remains methoxide oxygen; B is water oxygen. Exchanging labels would imply C–O cleavage/new bonding not present here.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Use labels to reject an extra mechanism
text:
Use labels to reject an extra mechanism

Protons transfer; oxygen labels stayA proposed answer puts oxygen A into water. What additional bond changes would that require beyond proton transfer?

A remains methoxide oxygen; B is water oxygen. Exchanging labels would imply C–O cleavage/new bonding not present here.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
An alkoxide becomes alcohol after water is added. What happens to the proton-donor water? Write it rather than supplying an unexplained H⁺.

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: A proton must come from a species
text:
A proton must come from a species

Ethoxide receives a proton from water, and hydroxide is produced.Write the proton donor and its conjugate base. A work-up is a chemical step, not a source of unexplained H atoms.

Use this to prepare for carbonyl reduction. Students often draw the alkoxide directly as an alcohol and lose both the proton donor and charge.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Two contributors describe one ion

Two contributors describe one ionCompare the positions of C, O and H nuclei across ethanoate resonance contributors. What changes?

Resonance moves electron placement at fixed nuclei. Deprotonation changes atom membership and describes interconverting species.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Contrast a chemical equilibrium

Two contributors describe one ionNow write CH₃COOH⇌CH₃COO⁻+H⁺. Why does that relation require an equilibrium arrow instead?

Resonance moves electron placement at fixed nuclei. Deprotonation changes atom membership and describes interconverting species.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
Sketch one reaction step as a free-energy profile. Where is its transition state? Why is the horizontal axis not a clock?

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Transition states are energy maxima

A one-step free-energy profile has one maximum between reactants and products.The transition state is not an isolable intermediate. Its barrier helps determine the reaction rate.

The curve is schematic. The vertical axis is free energy, not concentration, and the horizontal axis is reaction progress, not elapsed time.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: A complete product includes its charge
text:
A complete product includes its charge

A complete product includes its chargeFind the original carbonyl oxygen in the tetrahedral addition product and count its single bond and three pairs.

No. Carbon has four single bonds and formal 0. Original oxygen is −1, preserving the starting net −1 charge.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Repair a wrong carbon charge

A complete product includes its chargeWould putting+1 at the tetrahedral carbon repair a missing oxygen-minus sign? Check the actual electrons and net charge.

No. Carbon has four single bonds and formal 0. Original oxygen is −1, preserving the starting net −1 charge.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
Sketch a two-step profile. Place the intermediate and both transition states. How would you measure the second step’s barrier?

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
An intermediate occupies a minimum

A two-step schematic path has two transition states and an intermediate free-energy minimum.Count steps by maxima, not by the number of curved arrows. An intermediate has a finite lifetime.

A minimum may be short-lived and difficult to observe. The diagram does not by itself specify whether it can be bottled.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Cancel species only after summing real steps
text:
Cancel species only after summing real steps

Cancel species only after summing real stepsAdd the two hydrate-forming equations and mark the alkoxide as intermediate.

The species OH⁻ is used and regenerated overall. Formal cancellation of species is net stoichiometry, not an assertion that individually labelled atoms cannot exchange through steps.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Identify the regenerated participant

Cancel species only after summing real stepsExplain why hydroxide is a catalyst here, while water is a net reactant. Is every oxygen atom necessarily the same after cancellation?

The species OH⁻ is used and regenerated overall. Formal cancellation of species is net stoichiometry, not an assertion that individually labelled atoms cannot exchange through steps.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
Can two different barriers join the same reactant/product free energies? Predict what this means for catalysis and equilibrium.

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Catalysis changes the pathway

Catalysed and uncatalysed paths have the same reactant and product energies but different barriers.A catalyst can increase the rate while leaving the overall equilibrium constant unchanged.

The drawn catalysed profile is simplified. Real catalysis often adds multiple elementary steps; the catalyst is regenerated overall.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Predict before the worked drawing
For OH⁻ + CH₃Br → CH₃OH + Br⁻, inventory C, H, O and Br and the total charge. Which omission is easiest to miss?

Allow about 25 seconds of individual drawing/thinking, then ask for one reason. Do not display the worked product yet. Use the following illustration to resolve the atom, charge or geometry issue.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Use an atom and charge audit
text:
Use an atom and charge audit

Substitution conserves C, H, O and Br and has total charge minus one on both sides.After every step, check valence, atoms and net charge. Add implied hydrogens when the audit is unclear.

An electron-flow arrow does not add atoms. A missing counterion may be a spectator, but the reacting species must still have correct individual charges.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Nucleophilicity and basicity ask different questions
text:
Nucleophilicity and basicity ask different questions
A base accepts a proton; a nucleophile attacks an electrophilic centre. The same species can do both, but the preferred outcome depends on the substrate and conditions.
Identify the atom attacked before naming the process.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Repair an impossible step
A student draws OH⁻ adding to a carbonyl but leaves the C=O double bond intact.
Draw all bonds to that carbon. Which electron pair must move, and where does the negative charge end up?

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Explain an energy diagram
Sketch a two-step path. Mark both transition states and the intermediate.
Which feature would change if a catalyst offers a faster path? Which endpoint energy difference stays the same?

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Use the same reasoning in practice
text:
Use the same reasoning in practice
Complete the exercises, then the self-check.
Optional textbook support: selected Solomons chapter 3 and 6 sections. The reading guide explains the provisional book mapping.

Session budget45 minutes:roughly27–29 minutes of concise explanations/visual inspection, about 11–13 minutes of individual drawing and predictions distributed through the sequence, and4–6 minutes of discussion/closing checks. Adjust to observed errors; the 40 second metadata is a planning guide, not a quota. Required paper practice and optional transfer are available in the exercise bank.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
text: Answer before opening each check. Give a reason or a drawing, not only a term.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 1. Is carbon attached to H, OH, CH₃ and CH₃ a stereocentre?
text:
1. Is carbon attached to H, OH, CH₃ and CH₃ a stereocentre?






Check your answer





No: the two methyl substituents are identical. A simple tetrahedral stereocentre requires four different substituents.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 2. Give lactic-acid CIP priorities for OH, COOH, CH₃ and H.
text:
2. Give lactic-acid CIP priorities for OH, COOH, CH₃ and H.






Check your answer





OH > COOH > CH₃ > H. Oxygen outranks carbon. For the carbon tie, the COOH carbon has O,O,O in the comparison, whereas CH₃ has H,H,H.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 3. Assign the lactic-acid Fischer with COOH top, CH₃ bottom, OH left and H right.
text:
3. Assign the lactic-acid Fischer with COOH top, CH₃ bottom, OH left and H right.






Check your answer





S. The 1→2→3 trace appears clockwise, but the lowest-priority H is horizontal and points toward the viewer, so invert.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 4. Can propene have E and Z forms?
text:
4. Can propene have E and Z forms?






Check your answer





No. Its terminal alkene carbon bears two identical H substituents. Each alkene carbon needs two different substituents.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 5. Must a molecule with two stereocentres be chiral?
text:
5. Must a molecule with two stereocentres be chiral?






Check your answer





No. A meso compound has stereocentres but is achiral because of its overall symmetry. Meso-tartaric acid is an example.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 6. What is the ee of 70% R and 30% S?
text:
6. What is the ee of 70% R and 30% S?






Check your answer





40% ee in favour of R. The major enantiomer makes up 70%, not 40%, of the two-enantiomer mixture.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 7. Does S establish negative optical rotation?
text:
7. Does S establish negative optical rotation?






Check your answer





No. R/S specifies configuration and (+)/(−) is a measured rotation sign; there is no universal mapping.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text: Draw and compare stereoisomers, assign R/S and E/Z, and explain each priority decision. Review the lecture when you need a drawing convention. Core 1–12: about 60–80 minutes with drawings and checks. Transfer 13–20: an optional 35–50 minutes for consolidation or later revision. Choose a smaller core subset when a practical session also includes R.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
1. Find a candidate centre
Draw CH₃CH(OH)COOH and list all four substituents at CH(OH). Is it a simple tetrahedral stereocentre?






Hint





Compare complete groups, not only their first atoms.









Worked check





It has OH, H, CH₃, COOH: four different groups. It is a tetrahedral stereocentre.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
2. Reject a false stereocentre
Compare CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ and explain why a wedge on OH cannot make the central carbon stereogenic.






Hint





Two methyl groups remain identical regardless of drawing style.









Worked check





The central carbon has two identical CH₃ groups, so it is not a simple stereocentre. Wedges describe geometry but do not change group identity.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
3. Rank the first attachment atoms
For a centre attached directly to Br, Cl, OH, H, give CIP priority. Do not use total group size.






Hint





Atomic number decides the first shell.









Worked check





Br>Cl>O(in OH)>H. This compares directly attached atoms, not the number of atoms in each substituent.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
section: 4. Resolve the carbon tie in lactic acid
text:
4. Resolve the carbon tie in lactic acid
Rank OH, COOH, CH₃, H. Explain the duplicate-atom convention for C=O in this comparison.






Hint





OH attaches through O; COOH and CH₃ both attach through C.









Worked check





OH>COOH>CH₃>H. For the carbon tie, COOH compares as O, O, O and methyl as H, H, H. The duplicate entry is bookkeeping, not an extra real O atom.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
5. Read a Fischer depth convention
Draw a cross with COOH top, CH₃ bottom, OH left, H right. Which bonds point toward and away from you?






Hint





Fischer is a convention, not an ordinary planar cross.









Worked check





Horizontal OH/H bonds point toward; vertical COOH/CH₃ bonds point away. The central crossing is the stereocentre carbon.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
6. Assign the left-OH Fischer
Use the preceding projection and priorities OH1, COOH2, CH₃3, H4. Trace 1→2→3 and assign R/S with justification.






Hint





The lowest-priority group is horizontal and therefore forward.









Worked check





The trace appears clockwise, but H4 points toward you, so reverse the apparent result. This configuration is S.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
7. Assign the mirror Fischer
Keep COOH top and CH₃ bottom, but put H left and OH right. Assign R/S and its relation to the preceding structure.






Hint





One interchange at a single stereocentre inverts configuration.









Worked check





The new projection is R. It is the nonsuperimposable mirror/enantiomer of the S-lactic-acid drawing, with unchanged connectivity.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
8. Rotate a Fischer by 180°
Rotate the entire S projection in the plane by 180°. State each new label position and whether configuration changes.






Hint





All four labels rotate together.









Worked check





CH₃ becomes top, COOH bottom, H left, OH right. The configuration stays S. A complete valid 180° Fischer rotation preserves configuration.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
9. Test a 90° Fischer rotation
Explain why simply rotating a Fischer cross 90° is unsafe as an identity operation.






Hint





It changes which group positions are interpreted as horizontal versus vertical.









Worked check





The implied toward/away pattern changes under the convention, so a 90° Fischer rotation changes the represented configuration. Redraw using a valid 3D transformation instead.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
10. Assign Z-but-2-ene
Draw CH₃CH=CHCH₃ with both methyl groups on the same side. Rank the groups at each end and assign E/Z.






Hint





Methyl carbon outranks H at each alkene carbon.









Worked check





The higher-priority groups are together, giving Z-but-2-ene. Rank each end independently rather than treating left-to-right page direction as a descriptor.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
11. Assign E-but-2-ene
Draw but-2-ene with methyls on opposite sides. Explain why ordinary single-bond rotation is not the relevant interconversion.






Hint





The arrangement is around a C=C bond.









Worked check





Opposite high-priority methyl groups give E. Interconversion requires changing the double-bond arrangement; it is not a freely rotating anti/gauche relationship.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
12. Check whether E/Z is defined
For CH₂=CHCH₃ and (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃, test the two-different-substituents requirement at both ends.






Hint





One identical pair at either end is enough to fail.









Worked check





Neither qualifies. Propene has H/H at one end; the second molecule has CH₃/CH₃ at one end. No E/Z descriptor applies to those double bonds.




Optional transfer and challenge
These extend the same concepts without assuming later reaction chemistry.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
13. Classify a four-pair set
Classify ethanol/ether, anti/gauche butane, R/S-lactic acid, and E/Z-but-2-ene by their structural relationship.






Hint





Ask connectivity, rotation, mirror relation in that order.









Worked check





Respectively: constitutional isomers; conformers; enantiomers; diastereomers. E/Z pairs are stereoisomers that are not mirror-related.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
14. Use a two-centre framework carefully
Use CH₃CH(Br)CH(Cl)CH₃ (2-bromo-3-chlorobutane), numbered from the Br end. Compare the supplied configurations (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) and (2R,3R)/(2R,3S). Classify their relationships; no new R/S assignment from a drawing is required.






Hint





Mirror inversion reverses every centre.









Worked check





RR/SS are enantiomers; RR/RS are diastereomers. The symmetry assumption prevents a hidden meso equivalence from invalidating the simple classification.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
15. Examine meso-tartaric acid
Draw a Fischer with COOH top/bottom and OH right/H left at both central carbons. Explain why two stereocentres do not force chirality.






Hint





Inspect the equivalence of its upper and lower halves.









Worked check





The whole structure has an internal symmetry relationship and is meso-tartaric acid, achiral despite stereocentres. Overall superimposability matters, not centre count alone.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
16. Reject an R, S shortcut
A student calls every molecule with one R and one S centre meso. Give the missing structural condition.






Hint





Descriptors do not establish equivalence of the two ends.









Worked check





The complete molecule must have appropriate symmetry/superimposability with its mirror. An unsymmetrical R, S molecule can be chiral.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
17. Calculate 70:30 excess
A pure two-enantiomer composition is 70 % R and 30 % S. Compute ee and explain why it is not 70%.






Hint





Subtract the two populations.









Worked check





ee=|70−30|=40% in favour of R. Major-enantiomer percentage and excess are different quantities; the excess is the imbalance after pairing equal R/S amounts.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
18. Recover composition from excess
Assume only R/S components. A sample has 80 % ee in favour of R. Solve for the two percentages.






Hint





Use R+S=100 and R−S=80.









Worked check





R=90% and S=10%. Adding equations gives 2R=180. Calling this 80 % R would give the wrong excess.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
19. Separate configuration and rotation
Does an R label establish positive optical rotation or a stronger receptor effect? State what each additional claim requires.






Hint





Configuration is assigned; rotation/effect is measured.









Worked check





No universal mapping connects R/S to(+)/(−) or biological magnitude. Optical rotation needs specified measurements; receptor effects require appropriate experimental evidence in a chiral environment.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
20. Distinguish ee from total purity
R:S is 95:5 among the measured enantiomeric components. Compute ee and explain whether solvent contamination is excluded.






Hint





The measured ratio may describe only a subset of all material.









Worked check





The enantiomeric excess is 90 % R. The ratio does not exclude solvent or other molecular impurities; enantiomeric composition and total chemical purity are separate questions.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
section: R task: distinguish percentage from enantiomeric excess
text:
R task: distinguish percentage from enantiomeric excess
Question: how unbalanced is each supplied two-enantiomer mixture? The simulated table data/enantiomers.csv contains sample identifiers and percentages of R and S. This model assumes R and S are the only components being counted and have no missing composition. First check that R% + S% = 100.
For this model, ee_percent = abs(R_percent - S_percent). Report the major enantiomer too. Predict the ee for E1 (70% R, 30% S) before running the code.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
mixtures <- read_csv("data/enantiomers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(total_percent = R_percent + S_percent,
         ee_percent = abs(R_percent - S_percent),
         excess = case_when(R_percent > S_percent ~ "R",
                            S_percent > R_percent ~ "S",
                            TRUE ~ "racemic"))
knitr::kable(mixtures, digits = 1)
ggplot(mixtures, aes(sample_id, ee_percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#176b91") +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Enantiomeric excess (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
Write one sentence about each sample, specifying both composition and ee. If a sample has 80% ee in favour of R, calculate R% and S% by solving R + S = 100 and R − S = 80. Explain why the graph alone does not establish sample purity or optical-rotation sign.






Numerical and chemical check





E1 has 40% ee in favour of R; E2 (50:50) is racemic, 0% ee; E3 (95:5) has 90% ee in favour of R. An 80% R ee corresponds to 90% R and 10% S. Enantiomeric composition does not establish the absence of other chemical contaminants. Without a validated composition measurement and suitable assumptions this is only a calculation on supplied data. R/S alone does not give optical-rotation sign or a biological effect.

Explore

Loading interactive…This interactive needs JavaScript. The exploration instructions and linked exercises below remain available.




Explore

Assign the initial configuration yourself using OH > COOH > CH₃ > H. State whether H points toward or away before interpreting the clockwise/counterclockwise trace.
Interchange one selected pair and reassign. Interchange a second pair and explain why two interchanges can restore the original configuration. Compare with the left/right mirror operation.
Reset before testing 180° and 90° page-layout rotations separately. Explain why a 90° Fischer layout operation is not equivalent to rigidly turning the actual molecule in three dimensions.



Take-away
Write a valid rule for assigning configuration from a Fischer projection, including the lowest-priority-group correction. Why does this tool predict no optical-rotation sign?


Model and limits
Each horizontal Fischer bond points toward the viewer and each vertical bond away. All operations rearrange the same four lactic-acid groups in that convention. A 180° in-plane Fischer rotation preserves configuration; a 90° layout rotation changes the implied configuration. R/S describes geometry, not measured (+)/(−) optical rotation.

1. Where does the first arrow start?
In hydroxide deprotonation of an alcohol, should an electron-flow arrow begin at hydroxide oxygen’s lone pair, at the acidic hydrogen, or at the product?






Check your answer





At the hydroxide lone pair. The arrow ends at the acidic H. A second arrow moves the original O–H bonding pair onto the alcohol oxygen.

Check your answer





CH₃NH₂, neutral. Losing a positive proton reduces the net charge by one.

They are representations of one delocalised ion, not two equilibrating ions. Electron placement differs; nuclear positions and connectivity do not.

The ratio A⁻/HA is 0.1, so the fraction is 0.1/1.1, about 9.1%.

Draw CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O with relevant lone pairs and both curved arrows.

One pair goes to H; the original O–H pair stays on acid O.









Worked check





Hydroxide pair→acidic H, acid O–H bond→acid O. Net charge is−1 before and after. The proton moves while its original bonding pair stays behind.

text:
2. Name both conjugate pairs

Hint





Pair species differing by one H⁺.









Worked check





CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻ and H₂O/OH⁻ are the pairs. Reactants are acid and base; water is the base’s conjugate acid, ethanoate the acid’s conjugate base.

3. Protonate methylamine
Draw CH₃NH₂ + H–A → CH₃NH₃⁺ + A⁻ with two arrows and all N lone pairs/charges.






Hint





N starts with three bonds and a pair.









Worked check





N pair→H; H–A bond→A. N ends with four bonds/no lone pair/charge+1. Total charge is conserved because A becomes−1.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
4. Remove H⁺ from ammonium
Draw NH₄⁺ losing one H⁺ and identify the formula, charge and lone-pair count of the conjugate base.






Hint





Keep the N–H bonding pair on N.









Worked check





The conjugate base is neutral NH₃ with three N–H bonds and one lone pair. Losing H⁺ decreases charge by one without removing the bonding electrons.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
5. Compare conjugate-base stabilisation
Draw ethoxide and both equivalent ethanoate contributors. Use the supplied aqueous pKa 16 for ethanol and 4.8 for ethanoic acid to identify the stronger acid.






Hint





Explain the base structure before citing the numbers.









Worked check





Ethanoate distributes negative charge over two equivalent O atoms; ethoxide lacks that equivalent delocalisation. Ethanoic acid is stronger, consistent with its lower pKa.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
6. Reject a false resonance contributor
A proposed contributor moves a hydrogen from one O to another. Explain why this is not merely resonance.






Hint





Resonance changes electron placement while preserving nuclei.









Worked check





Moving H changes a nuclear position and bonding pattern, describing a proton transfer or tautomeric change. It is not another contributor to the same fixed-nucleus species.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
7. Estimate forward equilibrium
For CH₃COOH + CH₃NH₂ ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + CH₃NH₃⁺, use acid pKa 4.8 and product-acid pKa 10.6. Apply K≈10^(product−reactant acid pKa).






Hint





Subtract in the stated order.









Worked check





K≈10^5.8≈6.3×10⁵. Products contain the weaker acid and are strongly favoured in the compatible aqueous approximation. This does not give a reaction rate.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
8. Reverse the equilibrium
Write the reverse of the preceding equation and estimate its K.






Hint





A reversed equation has reciprocal K.









Worked check





CH₃COO⁻+CH₃NH₃⁺⇌CH₃COOH+CH₃NH₂ has K≈1/(6.3×10⁵)≈1.6×10⁻⁶. Using the same large K for both directions is inconsistent.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
9. Control an inductive comparison
Supplied aqueous pKa values are 4.8 for CH₃COOH and 2.9 for ClCH₂COOH. Draw the conjugate bases and explain the trend.






Hint





The changed substituent is electron withdrawing.









Worked check





Cl substitution stabilises the nearby carboxylate through inductive electron withdrawal, making the acid stronger. Compare within compatible conditions; the Cl is not a resonance contributor moving between atoms.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
10. Convert ratio into fraction
At pH 3.8 for a monoprotic acid of pKa 4.8, use r=10^(pH−pKa) and fraction=r/(1+r).






Hint





The fraction denominator includes both forms.









Worked check





r=0.1; fraction=0.1/1.1≈0.0909=9.09%. A ratio of 0.1 does not equal exactly 10% of the total population.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
11. Explain the midpoint
At pH=pKa, calculate r and the ionised fraction. Describe definite molecular species rather than half-protonated molecules.






Hint





10^0=1.









Worked check





r=1 and fraction=0.5. Equal HA and A⁻ concentrations coexist; each species is HA or A⁻, not an individual molecule halfway losing a proton.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
12. Go one unit above pKa
For pKa 4.8 at pH 5.8, calculate r and fraction. Check direction against the previous two cases.






Hint





The ratio multiplies by ten for each pH unit.









Worked check





r=10 and fraction=10/11≈0.9091. The conjugate-base fraction increases as pH increases, consistent with deprotonation being favoured.




Optional transfer and challenge
These extend the same concepts without assuming later reaction chemistry.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
13. Go two units above pKa
For the same acid at pH 6.8, calculate fraction and explain why it is not exactly 100%.






Hint





Use r=100, then include HA in the denominator.









Worked check





fraction=100/101≈0.9901. The model retains a small HA population; a strongly favoured form need not be exclusive.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
section: 14. Compare two acids at one pH
text:
14. Compare two acids at one pH
At pH 4.8 compare supplied pKa 4.8 and 6.0. Use fraction=1/(1+10^(pKa−pH)).






Hint





The weaker acid has the higher pKa.









Worked check





Fractions are 0.5 and approximately 0.0594. At the same pH the lower-pKa acid is more deprotonated. This comparison uses the stated monoprotic dilute aqueous model.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
15. Repair a reversed curve
A student’s fraction_A_minus decreases as pH increases after coding 1/(1+10^(pH−pKa)). Explain the sign error.






Hint





Evaluate the code far above pKa.









Worked check





The exponent is reversed for the A⁻ fraction. Use pKa−pH in this denominator. The student’s expression instead gives the complementary HA fraction under the model.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
16. Separate equilibrium from kinetics
A proton-transfer estimate has K=10⁶. Does that number alone give seconds needed to reach equilibrium?






Hint





Compare state preference with pathway barrier.









Worked check





No. K describes equilibrium proportions/activities under the model, not the time scale. Reaction kinetics require additional mechanistic and rate information.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
17. Use water in both roles
Write one proton-transfer example with water accepting H⁺ and another with water donating H⁺. Identify the resulting conjugates.






Hint





Use H–A and a sufficiently basic B⁻ as generic partners.









Worked check





H–A+H₂O⇌A⁻+H₃O⁺ shows water accepting. B⁻+H₂O⇌BH+OH⁻ shows water donating. Relative extents depend on compatible acid/base strengths.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
section: 18. Check total charge in a mechanism
text:
18. Check total charge in a mechanism
A drawing turns neutral HA and neutral B into A⁻ and neutral BH. Find the missing formal charge.






Hint





The reactant net charge is zero.









Worked check





BH must be BH⁺ when B accepts H⁺ in this generic transfer. A⁻ plus BH⁺ preserves net zero. Drawing neutral BH would lose a unit of total charge.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
19. Distinguish speciation and titration
A graph plots fraction A⁻ against a supplied pH grid. Explain why its x-axis cannot simply be relabelled mL of added base.






Hint





pH is an input here; titrant volume would require a mass-balance model.









Worked check





A titration relation must connect added amount, total volume and equilibria to pH. The speciation curve computes fraction at specified pH and does not supply that connection.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
20. Set an extraction boundary
At high aqueous pH an acid is mostly A⁻. List missing information needed to predict mass in an organic phase.






Hint





Speciation is only one part of a two-phase calculation.









Worked check





Partition coefficients for relevant species, phase volumes, starting amount and losses are needed. Aqueous fraction alone does not determine organic recovery or isolated yield.

title: Day 3: Exercises — Acids, bases and ionisation
section: R task: how much of the acid is ionised?
text:
R task: how much of the acid is ionised?
Question: for a monoprotic acid with supplied pKa 4.8, how does its aqueous ionised fraction change between pH 1 and 9? This is a calculated teaching model, not measured acid dissociation data. Use the dilute-solution approximation.
The ratio is \(r=[A^-]/[HA]=10^{pH-pK_a}\), so the fraction is \(r/(1+r)=1/(1+10^{pK_a-pH})\). pH, pKa and the fraction are dimensionless. At pH = pKa predict 0.5. At one pH unit above pKa predict 10/11.
Add the following to your report, below a sentence stating your prediction:
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
ionisation <- data.frame(pH = seq(1, 9, by = 0.1)) |>
  mutate(fraction_A_minus = 1 / (1 + 10^(4.8 - pH)))
ggplot(ionisation, aes(pH, fraction_A_minus)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#176b91", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "pH", y = "Fraction present as A−") +
  theme_minimal()
1 / (1 + 10^(4.8 - c(3.8, 4.8, 5.8)))
Knit the report. Explain why the curve rises, why its midpoint is 4.8, and why a fraction of 0.909 does not mean each molecule is 90.9% deprotonated. Change pKa to 6.0, predict the shift and then compare the curves. State why the plot alone cannot predict extraction recovery into an organic solvent.






Numerical and chemical check





At pH 3.8, 4.8 and 5.8 the fractions are approximately 0.0909, 0.5 and 0.9091. A larger pKa shifts the midpoint to higher pH; this weaker acid needs higher pH to achieve the same fraction. Fractions describe a population of molecular species. Extraction needs partition coefficients and phase volumes as well as aqueous ionisation. The supplied curve is not a titration curve: pH is the input, not the calculated consequence of adding a specified titrant volume.

1. Recover a five-carbon line
Draw an unbranched four-segment skeletal zigzag with only single bonds. Label each carbon CH₃ or CH₂ and obtain its molecular formula.






Hint
