title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
Use bond polarity, intermolecular interactions and IR observations to explain the structures below. Use the lecture and the refresher below when needed.
Core 1–12: about 60–80 minutes with drawings and checks. Transfer 13–20: an optional 35–50 minutes for consolidation or later revision. Choose a smaller core subset when the session also includes R.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
1. Assign two kinds of charge
Draw ethanol with O lone pairs. Mark C–O partial charges and calculate O formal charge. Explain why the two labels differ.






Hint





Unequal sharing differs from a Lewis integer count.









Worked check





C is δ+ and O δ− in the C–O bond. Ethanol O has formal charge zero with two bonds/two pairs. A partial charge is not a whole added electron.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
2. Combine dipoles geometrically
Sketch linear O=C=O and bent H₂O. Indicate bond-dipole directions toward O and predict each molecular sum.






Hint





Equal opposite vectors cancel; angled ones need not.









Worked check





CO₂ dipoles cancel by symmetry. Bent water has a nonzero net dipole. Polar bonds alone do not establish a polar molecule.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
3. Draw a donor–acceptor contact
Draw ethanol and water and mark one O–H···O hydrogen bond. Distinguish the covalent and intermolecular connections.






Hint





The donor supplies the H; the acceptor supplies a lone pair.









Worked check





Either molecule can donate OH to the other O. Covalent O–H stays within a molecule, while the H···O contact is dashed and does not change connectivity.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
4. Let ether accept
Draw CH₃OCH₃ with water as a hydrogen-bond partner. Which molecule supplies H? Can pure ether provide an O–H donor?






Hint





Ether O has two C neighbours and no attached H.









Worked check





Water donates an O–H hydrogen to ether O. Ether can accept but has no O–H donor; oxygen presence alone does not imply donor ability.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
section: 5. Compare amines by their actual bonds
text:
5. Compare amines by their actual bonds
For CH₃NH₂, (CH₃)₂NH and (CH₃)₃N, identify N–H donor bonds and the neutral N acceptor pair.






Hint





Count N–H before counting carbon substituents.









Worked check





All three neutral amines have a lone-pair acceptor. The first two have N–H donor bonds; trimethylamine lacks N–H and cannot donate at N.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
6. Test a protonated amine
Draw CH₃NH₃⁺ and compare its N donor/acceptor inventory with CH₃NH₂.






Hint





The original lone pair has become a bond.









Worked check





Methylammonium has N–H donors but no ordinary N lone-pair acceptor. It is not a neutral amine with the same available pair.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
7. Explain a controlled boiling comparison
Ethanol and dimethyl ether share C₂H₆O. Their approximate normal boiling temperatures are 78 ° C and−24 ° C. Explain a structural reason for the difference.






Hint





Keep molecular size and pressure comparable.









Worked check





Ethanol forms an OH donor/acceptor network; the ether lacks an OH donor. This supports stronger liquid intermolecular attractions in ethanol, not stronger covalent C–O bonds.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
8. Separate boiling from decomposition
A student says boiling ethanol breaks C–O bonds. Rewrite their claim to identify which interactions are normally overcome.






Hint





Ask whether vapour molecules still have the same connectivity.









Worked check





Boiling separates largely intact ethanol molecules by overcoming intermolecular attractions. C–O cleavage would be a chemical transformation, not ordinary vapour formation.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
9. Compare related alcohols in water
Draw methanol and hexan-1-ol CH₃(CH₂)₅OH. Explain which is more water compatible and what a single-OH rule misses.






Hint





Balance the polar site against nonpolar size.









Worked check





Methanol is more water compatible. The longer alcohol has a much larger hydrocarbon region per OH group. The prediction is qualitative and depends on conditions.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
10. Read an IR transmission feature
A complete IR transmission trace dips strongly near 1715 cm⁻¹. Name the axes and explain what the dip means.






Hint





Less transmission corresponds to more absorption.









Worked check





The horizontal coordinate is wavenumber; the vertical coordinate is transmittance. The dip supports absorption near 1715 cm⁻¹, often a carbonyl feature, without uniquely identifying a molecule.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
11. Change the plotting convention
A second graph shows an upward band at the same wavenumber but labels its y-axis absorbance. Is it contradictory evidence?






Hint





The ordinate changes the feature direction.









Worked check





No. An absorbance band points upward while transmission decreases for the same absorption. Interpret axes before calling a plot wrong.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
12. Choose among three candidates
Unknown has strong C=O near 1715 cm⁻¹ and no broad alcohol OH region in suitable data. Candidates: ethanol, propanone, dimethyl ether. Choose and justify.






Hint





Draw the functional groups predicted by each.









Worked check





Propanone best fits this list: it has C=O and lacks OH. The other candidates lack carbonyl. This restricted comparison does not establish absolute identity or purity.




Optional transfer and challenge
These extend the same concepts without assuming later reaction chemistry.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
13. Reject a unique-carbonyl claim
A student identifies propanone from one C=O band. Draw another three-carbon carbonyl compound and explain the limitation.






Hint





An aldehyde can contain the same total carbon count.









Worked check





Propanal CH₃CH₂CHO also contains C=O. One broad-region observation is shared by many structures; further spectral and other evidence is required.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
14. Inspect sample contamination
An intended ether sample has a broad OH feature. Give two explanations consistent with limited evidence without choosing one as certain.






Hint





A feature can belong to the target or another component.









Worked check





The sample could contain an OH-bearing impurity or water; the target assignment could also be wrong. More observations are needed to distinguish these explanations.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
15. Distinguish alcohol and acid OH
Draw ethanol and ethanoic acid. Which has a neighbouring carbonyl, and how can the expected broad IR regions differ?






Hint





Acid OH is part of C(=O)OH.









Worked check





Ethanoic acid has OH adjacent to carbonyl and often an especially broad acid-OH region around 2500–3300 cm⁻¹. Alcohol OH is commonly broad around 3200–3600 cm⁻¹; exact shapes depend on conditions.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
16. Check an ester inventory
For CH₃COOCH₃, identify the carbonyl and single-bonded O. Does the molecule have any O–H donor?






Hint





Write each oxygen bond explicitly.









Worked check





It has two oxygen environments able to accept hydrogen-bond contacts in this simple treatment, but no OH donor. It is an ester, not an alcohol plus an unrelated ether.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
17. Interpret ion hydration
Compare CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻ in water. Name an interaction made especially important by the latter charge.






Hint





Water is polar even though neutral overall.









Worked check





Carboxylate can engage in ion–dipole hydration. The neutral acid also interacts with water, but formal charge changes the interaction pattern. Exact solubility still needs conditions and additional thermodynamics.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
18. Repair an IR-to-solubility shortcut
Rewrite: “It absorbs IR, so it must dissolve in water.” Give separate valid claims about IR and solubility.






Hint





A changing vibrational dipole is not an entire solution free energy.









Worked check





IR absorption probes suitable vibrational transitions. Water solubility depends on the balance of interactions, size, charge, condensed-phase structure and conditions. A band alone does not establish it.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
19. Use two observations together
Unknown is one of propan-1-ol or propanal. Suitable IR has C=O and no broad alcohol OH. Give one prediction for each candidate and a restrained conclusion.






Hint





Test both presence and absence.









Worked check





The alcohol predicts OH and lacks C=O; the aldehyde predicts C=O and lacks alcohol OH. Propanal fits the two observations among this pair; further evidence would address identity beyond this list.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
20. Name the missing extraction inputs
A monoprotic acid becomes mostly ionised in water at high pH. Why can that fact alone not predict mass recovered into an organic solvent?






Hint





Two phases require a partition model and their quantities.









Worked check





Aqueous speciation supplies only species ratios. Partition coefficients, phase volumes, starting amount and losses affect recovered mass. More ionisation is not a complete recovery calculation.

Explore

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text: Draw Newman projections and cyclohexane chairs, then explain how a rotation changes the view and energy. Review the lecture when you need a drawing convention. Core 1–12: about 60–80 minutes with drawings and checks. Transfer 13–20: an optional 35–50 minutes for consolidation or later revision. title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
1. Define the viewing bond
Number CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ C1–C4 and look C2→C3. Identify front/rear C and the three groups on each.






Hint





Nearest carbon is front.









Worked check





C2 is front, attached to C1 methyl and two H; C3 is rear, attached to C4 methyl and two H. Both carbon sets must be drawn.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
2. Draw anti-butane
Keep front CH₃ at 12 o’clock; place rear CH₃ at 6 o’clock and complete both H sets in a Newman projection. State methyl dihedral.






Hint





Each carbon has three projected bonds 120° apart.









Worked check





The methyl dihedral is 180°. Front H at 4/8 and rear H at 2/10 give a staggered arrangement. Anti names the methyl relationship.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
3. Draw one gauche arrangement
From anti, rotate only the rear set 120° while front stays fixed. State the resulting methyl dihedral and whether eclipsed.






Hint





A120° change from 180° reaches 60° modulo a full turn.









Worked check





Rear methyl reaches 2 or 10 o’clock depending direction, giving±60° to front methyl. The structure remains staggered and is gauche.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
4. Find both gauche minima
Draw the +60° and−60° methyl arrangements along C2→C3. Explain what stays identical.






Hint





Use rear methyl at 2 and 10 with front methyl at 12.









Worked check





Both preserve connectivity and are equivalent in energy in an achiral environment for ordinary butane. They are distinct conformations, not constitutional isomers.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
5. Draw an eclipsed view
Draw ethane along C–C with front/rear C–H bonds aligned. How does it differ from a staggered view?






Hint





Compare a 0° and 60° bond-set offset.









Worked check





Eclipsed projected bonds align; staggered bonds are offset 60°. The atoms do not form extra bonds just because their projected positions overlap.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
6. Count ethane energy minima
A qualitative full-turn ethane profile has eclipsed maxima every 120°. Locate the staggered minima between them.






Hint





Start with a maximum at 0°.









Worked check





Minima occur at 60°,180°,300°. The three are equivalent because the substituents are H. Numerical barriers cannot be extracted from an uncalibrated schematic.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
7. Compare butane minima
For ordinary butane, anti is lower than gauche. Explain the methyl-group arrangement and why lower does not mean exclusive.






Hint





Compare larger-group separation, then remember thermal populations.









Worked check





Anti separates the methyl groups more favourably. Gauche remains a possible populated conformation. A finite energy difference does not make the higher state mathematically absent.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
8. Separate conformer from constitutional isomer
Compare anti/gauche butane with butane/2-methylpropane. Identify which relationship changes bonded neighbours.






Hint





Trace carbon connectivity before reading the view.









Worked check





Anti/gauche retain one connected chain and differ by rotation. 2-methylpropane has a branched carbon framework, so it is a constitutional isomer of butane.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
9. Read a cyclohexane sketch
Explain why a regular hexagon for cyclohexane does not prove a flat molecular geometry. Name a common low-energy conformation.






Hint





A skeletal drawing first establishes connectivity.









Worked check





The polygon gives a six-carbon ring. Cyclohexane usually adopts nonplanar chair conformations; the flat drawing does not encode all 3D positions.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
10. Track axial-up through a flip
Draw/build methylcyclohexane with axial-up methyl. Perform a chair flip and label the same methyl both ways.






Hint





Axial/equatorial changes; up/down does not.









Worked check





It becomes equatorial-up. Follow the whole ring rather than reversing one drawn bond. The process changes conformation while preserving configuration.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
11. Track axial-down through a flip
Repeat with an axial-down substituent. Does down become up?






Hint





Use the same rule with the other side of the ring.









Worked check





Axial-down becomes equatorial-down. A ring flip exchanges axial/equatorial without changing the side of the ring.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
12. Preserve a cis relation
Two labelled substituents are both up before a chair flip. State their cis/trans relationship before and after.






Hint





Cis/trans describes sides, not axiality.









Worked check





They are cis before and remain cis after. Up/up remains up/up even though axial/equatorial occupancy changes.




Optional transfer and challenge
These extend the same concepts without assuming later reaction chemistry.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
13. Preserve a trans relation
One substituent is up and one down. Can choosing a different chair make this pair cis?






Hint





Track each substituent’s side through the motion.









Worked check





No. They are trans and remain trans. A conformation change cannot silently change the up/down configuration.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
14. Explain methylcyclohexane preference
Compare axial and equatorial methyl chairs. Name an unfavourable interaction reduced in the equatorial form.






Hint





Think of groups at the 1,3 positions relative to an axial substituent.









Worked check





Equatorial methyl avoids the unfavourable 1,3-diaxial interactions present for axial methyl. This explains a preference, not that the axial form is impossible.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
15. Check Boltzmann-model units
Use ΔG=3500 J/mol, R=8.314462618J/(molK), T=298.15 K. Compute RT and explain why ΔG/(RT) can appear in exp().






Hint





Both numerator and denominator must have the same units.









Worked check





RT≈2478.96 J/mol; ΔG/(RT)≈1.412 is dimensionless. Mixing kJ/mol with J/(molK) without conversion would produce a wrong exponent.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
16. Normalise a two-state model
Given weights wA=1 and wB=0.244, calculate fractions. Are these already percentages?






Hint





Divide each weight by their total 1.244.









Worked check





Fractions are about 0.804 and 0.196, or 80.4% and 19.6%. Relative weights need not sum to one; fractions do.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
17. Test zero energy difference
In a two-state model with degeneracy included, ΔG(A)=ΔG(B)=0. What equilibrium fractions result?






Hint





Both exponentials equal one.









Worked check





The two weights are 1 and 1; normalising gives 0.5 and 0.5. The qualification about degeneracy matters when grouping multiple conformations into one state.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
18. Shift the energy reference
Add 1000 J/mol to both supplied relative state energies. Explain whether normalised fractions change.






Hint





Both weights receive the same multiplicative factor.









Worked check





Fractions stay unchanged because exp(−1000/RT) multiplies every weight and cancels in their normalisation. Only the relative difference matters for the ratio.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
19. Distinguish equilibrium from rate
Two systems have the same state free-energy difference but different interconversion barriers. Must they have identical rotation rates?






Hint





A state difference and an activation barrier are distinct quantities.









Worked check





No. The equilibrium preference can match while rates differ because barriers differ. An equilibrium population does not by itself determine a time scale.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
20. Identify a model boundary
A supplied two-state free-energy table already includes degeneracy. Should you independently multiply one weight by two because you remember two gauche views?






Hint





Avoid counting the same state multiplicity twice.









Worked check





No. The supplied convention already accounts for that effect. Adding it again changes the intended model. Distinguish a physical conformer inventory from an explicitly supplied effective-state model.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
section: R task: turn supplied free energies into a population
text:
R task: turn supplied free energies into a population
Question: in a deliberately simplified two-state model, how much of each conformer would be present at equilibrium? The file data/conformers.csv contains relative free energies, ΔG, in J/mol, for A and B: 0 and 3500. These values are supplied teaching values and already include any degeneracy; they are not measured energies for the qualitative butane curve above.
At temperature \(T=298.15\) K and \(R=8.314462618\) J/(mol K), use \(w_i=\exp[-\Delta G_i/(RT)]\) and \(p_i=w_i/\sum_jw_j\). The ratio in the exponent is dimensionless. A is the lower-free-energy state, so predict A will have more than half the population.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
conformers <- read_csv("data/conformers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(weight = exp(-delta_G_J_mol / (8.314462618 * 298.15)),
         fraction = weight / sum(weight))
knitr::kable(conformers, digits = 4)
ggplot(conformers, aes(conformer, fraction)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#176b91") +
  labs(x = "Conformer", y = "Predicted equilibrium fraction") +
  theme_minimal()
sum(conformers$fraction)
Add the result to your Rmd report. Check the sum and the direction. As a transfer task, replace 3500 with 0 in a copied data object, predict the answer and recompute. Then set both input energies 1000 J/mol higher, keeping their difference unchanged. What happens to the normalised fractions?






Numerical and model check





At 298.15 K, A has fraction about 0.804 and B about 0.196 (rounding depends on constants). Equal free energies give equal fractions. Adding the same constant to both energies multiplies every weight by the same factor, which cancels on normalisation, leaving fractions unchanged. The calculation assumes the two states adequately describe the system at equilibrium. It does not predict the speed of rotation; an activation free energy would be needed for rates.

No. Interconversion rates depend on activation barriers, while the equilibrium ratio depends on the free-energy difference of the states.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text: Draw electron-pair movements and audit atoms, bond orders and formal charges at every step. Core 1–12: about 80–100 minutes. Transfer 13–20: an optional 45–65 minutes; choose problems that target your mistakes.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Local refresher and worked starting example
text:
Local refresher and worked starting example
Full-headed curved arrows move electron pairs. Start each tail on a lone pair or bond; end at an atom or new-bond location. Ordinary carbon has total bond order four. A transition state is a free-energy maximum and an intermediate a minimum. All drawings must conserve atoms and net charge.
Worked starting example. For OH⁻+CH₃Br, move an oxygen lone pair to methyl C and the C–Br pair to Br in one step. Products CH₃OH+Br⁻ have the same atoms and net charge −1. This is our worked SN2 electron-accounting pattern.
Draw structures, identify the relevant atom and explain the reason. A name alone is insufficient where a mechanism or argument is requested.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
1. Follow a proton transfer
Draw CH₃OH + OH⁻ ⇌ CH₃O⁻ + H₂O, including both curved arrows and every reacting oxygen lone pair. Audit all atoms and net charge.






Hint





Begin at a hydroxide lone pair; also move the methanol O–H bond pair.









Worked answer and reasoning





The hydroxide pair forms its new O–H bond while the methanol O–H pair returns to methanol oxygen. Both sides contain C₁H₅O₂ and total charge −1. This draws a possible proton transfer; its equilibrium position needs compatible acid-strength data.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
2. Repair a proton arrow
A student draws an arrow from the H of H₃O⁺ to the oxygen of NH₃. Identify two errors and replace the step with a valid ammonia protonation drawing.






Hint





Which atom does ammonia contain, and which species supplies the electron pair?









Worked answer and reasoning





Ammonia contains nitrogen, not oxygen. The pair starts on nitrogen and points to a hydronium H; the donor O–H pair returns to O. Products are NH₄⁺ and H₂O, preserving charge +1. Arrows follow pairs, not the proton path.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
3. Construct a methyl substitution
Draw OH⁻ + CH₃Br → CH₃OH + Br⁻ as one elementary SN2 step. Explain why two arrows do not imply two steps.






Hint





Pair donation to carbon and departure of Br occur together.









Worked answer and reasoning





The hydroxide lone pair forms C–O and the C–Br pair goes to Br in the same concerted event. There is one barrier and no intervening carbocation. Both sides have net charge −1.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
4. Draw the reverse bond changes
As a formal electron-accounting exercise, draw Br⁻ attacking the methyl carbon of CH₃OH with OH⁻ departing. Explain why balanced arrows do not establish that this reverse event is experimentally favourable.






Hint





Keep the bond-pair directions valid, then evaluate the leaving group.









Worked answer and reasoning





A Br lone pair points to methyl C and the C–O bond pair points to O, producing CH₃Br and OH⁻. Atoms and charge balance, but hydroxide is a poor leaving group. Electron accounting is necessary; energies and conditions still determine plausibility.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
5. Locate the electrophile
Draw CH₃CHO with oxygen lone pairs and partial charges. Mark the usual attacked atom in hydroxide addition and distinguish partial from formal charge.






Hint





Unequal sharing in C=O leaves one atom relatively electron-poor.









Worked answer and reasoning





O is δ− and carbonyl C is δ+. Hydroxide attacks C while the π pair moves to O. The neutral starting Lewis structure has formal charge zero at both atoms; δ+ is not a carbocation formula.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
6. Repair five bond orders
A proposed product of OH⁻ addition to CH₃CHO retains C=O and adds C–OH while keeping C–H and C–CH₃. Count carbon bond order, then repair the step.






Hint





The carbonyl π pair cannot remain a bond if an extra sigma bond forms.









Worked answer and reasoning





The proposed carbon has bond-order sum five. Moving the C=O π pair to O gives CH₃CH(OH)O⁻, a four-single-bond carbon and net charge −1. Show both arrows in the addition step.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
7. Track hydride-equivalent addition
Represent a hydride equivalent from NaBH₄ as H:⁻ for a simplified step. Add it to CH₃COCH₃; draw both arrows and the immediate product, not the worked-up alcohol.






Hint





The incoming H makes C–H; the original carbonyl oxygen receives the π pair.









Worked answer and reasoning





The product is (CH₃)₂CHO⁻. H-delivery forms C–H while C=O becomes C–O⁻. H:⁻ is a shorthand for delivery from the reagent, not free hydride present in water; protonation is a later step.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
8. Supply a missing proton donor
A drawing changes (CH₃)₂CHO⁻ directly to (CH₃)₂CHOH without another species. Complete it using water, including all products and arrows.






Hint





Water must become its conjugate base after losing H⁺.









Worked answer and reasoning





Alkoxide O donates a pair to water H; the water O–H pair returns to water O. Products are propan-2-ol and OH⁻. Net charge remains −1, and no H appears without a source.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
9. A neutral nucleophile gains charge
Draw NH₃ + CH₃Br → CH₃NH₃⁺ + Br⁻ as an SN2 electron-flow step. Count nitrogen bonds and lone pairs before and after.






Hint





Neutral ammonia has three bonds and one pair available for the new bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





The N pair forms N–C as the C–Br pair moves to Br. Nitrogen now has four bonds, no lone pair and formal charge +1. Total charge is zero on both sides; neutral methylamine would require a later deprotonation.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
section: 10. Base or nucleophile in this event?
text:
10. Base or nucleophile in this event?
Compare OH⁻ attacking CH₃Br at carbon with OH⁻ removing H⁺ from H₃O⁺. Draw each step and name the role in each.






Hint





Classify the particular attacked atom rather than permanently labelling OH⁻.









Worked answer and reasoning





Attack at methyl C forms methanol and bromide: OH⁻ acts as nucleophile. Attack at H of hydronium produces two waters: OH⁻ acts as base. Both use pair donation, but they ask different chemical questions.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
11. Heterolysis as bookkeeping
Draw formal C–Br heterolysis for CH₃Br and assign both product charges. Then explain why that picture alone is not a suitable SN1 proposal for methyl bromide.






Hint





Give the entire bond pair to Br, then consider the methyl cation.









Worked answer and reasoning





Formal products are CH₃⁺ and Br⁻. This conserves net charge zero, but the methyl carbocation is extremely poorly stabilised. A charge-balanced drawing does not establish a readily accessible intermediate; methyl SN2 avoids it.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
12. Count steps in a profile
Sketch a reaction profile containing two maxima separated by one minimum. Label every maximum and the intervening minimum. How many elementary steps are depicted?






Hint





A step goes from one minimum to the next through a maximum.









Worked answer and reasoning





Two transition states separate reactants, an intermediate and products, so two elementary steps are shown. The number of curved arrows within either step can be greater than one.









Note



Optional transfer starts here. Choose problems that address your own gaps; the core route remains1–12.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
13. Choose the higher barrier
Two alternative paths start from the same reactants and have activation free energies 15 and 25 kJ/mol at the same temperature. Which path is kinetically favoured, all else comparable? Is either final product proportion specified?






Hint





Compare barriers for rate; distinguish endpoint energies for equilibrium.









Worked answer and reasoning





The 15 kJ/mol path has the lower activation barrier and is faster under the stated comparison. The barrier values alone do not specify the relative equilibrium amounts of final products, which require their thermodynamic relationship.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
14. Calculate a reverse barrier
A one-step schematic has reactants at 0, transition state at +45 and products at −20 kJ/mol. Give forward barrier, reverse barrier and overall ΔG.






Hint





Measure each barrier upward from its own starting minimum.









Worked answer and reasoning





Forward ΔG‡ is 45 kJ/mol; reverse is 45−(−20)=65 kJ/mol; overall ΔG is −20 kJ/mol. A reaction can be thermodynamically favourable yet have a substantial forward barrier.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
15. Add a catalytic path
On the preceding profile, add a catalytic path with its highest relevant barrier at +25 kJ/mol while retaining the same endpoints. Explain what changes and what does not.






Hint





A different path need not alter reactant or product state energies.









Worked answer and reasoning





The catalysed path offers a lower barrier and can speed reaction. The endpoint ΔG remains −20 kJ/mol, so catalysis alone does not change the equilibrium constant for the same net reaction and conditions. A real catalytic path may have several steps.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
16. Separate equilibrium from time
A sample has not reached equilibrium after ten minutes, but its eventual equilibrium composition is known. Can that composition alone tell you the half-time? Explain using a profile.






Hint





An endpoint energy difference does not specify the height of the route between endpoints.









Worked answer and reasoning





No. Different barriers can connect the same reactant/product free energies. Equilibrium information constrains relative state stabilities; rates need kinetic information such as the relevant activation barriers and rate laws.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
17. Audit a missing charge
A student writes OH⁻ + CH₃CHO → CH₃CH(OH)O with all atoms shown but no product charge. Repair the oxygen electron count and explain why assigning a +1 carbon would not solve it.






Hint





The original carbonyl oxygen now has only one bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





The original carbonyl oxygen is O⁻ with three lone pairs, giving CH₃CH(OH)O⁻. Carbon has four single bonds and formal charge zero. Placing +1 on carbon would not follow from the electron movement or preserve net charge −1.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
18. Resonance or reaction?
Draw the two equivalent ethanoate contributors, keeping all nuclei fixed. Contrast their relation with CH₃COOH → CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺.






Hint





One comparison moves electrons only; the other removes a nucleus from the species.









Worked answer and reasoning





Ethanoate contributors differ in which C–O is drawn double and which O carries formal negative charge; they describe one delocalised ion. Acid dissociation changes which atoms belong to the acid species. Use a resonance double-headed arrow for contributors and an equilibrium arrow for dissociation.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
19. Preserve atom identity
Label methanol oxygen A and hydroxide oxygen B in methanol deprotonation. Which oxygen belongs to methoxide and which to the newly formed water?






Hint





A proton transfers; an oxygen atom does not move from one molecule to the other.









Worked answer and reasoning





A remains the oxygen of CH₃O⁻; B becomes the oxygen of H₂O. Assigning A to water would imply additional bond changes not present in a simple proton transfer.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
20. Build a two-step explanation
Using only CH₃CHO, OH⁻ and H₂O, draw base-catalysed formation of CH₃CH(OH)₂. Cross out the catalyst from the net equation and name the intermediate.






Hint





First add hydroxide, then use water to protonate the alkoxide.









Worked answer and reasoning





Addition gives CH₃CH(OH)O⁻; water then protonates that alkoxide and regenerates OH⁻. The net equation is CH₃CHO + H₂O ⇌ CH₃CH(OH)₂. The alkoxide is an intermediate, while hydroxide is regenerated overall.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Check your progress
Choose one corrected drawing and explain what changed in its atoms, charge, geometry or evidence. Then complete the self-check. The reading guide is optional support; all required exercise information is supplied here.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Explore
A 5–10 minute exploration, using a prediction before each control change. The diagram and result update locally; no network service is used.

Predict first
Before choosing arrows, identify the electron source and the electron-poor destination in a supplied proton transfer. Can a full-headed electron-pair arrow begin at an isolated H⁺?
Loading interactive…This interactive needs JavaScript. The exploration instructions and linked exercises below remain available.




Explore

Repair the hydroxide/ethanoic-acid step. Choose both pair movements, set the total product charge and check. Follow the original acid O–H pair rather than treating an arrow as the proton’s path.
Select carbonyl addition. Compare moving the π pair to O with keeping C=O unchanged as OH⁻ makes a new bond. Check the carbon bond-order count.
Select amine protonation. Count N bonds before and after, then explain where hydronium’s original O–H pair goes. Use the valid-step preset only after making your own attempt.



Take-away
For one step, state both pair origins, both destinations and the total charge check. Which proposed intermediate would violate ordinary carbon valence?


Model and limits
Full-headed curved arrows represent electron pairs. Deliberately invalid proposals are included for repair and labelled as such; they are not proposed stable products. The carbonyl case isolates its initial elementary addition only, without claiming a final isolated hydrate yield. A valid ordinary tetrahedral carbon has four bond orders.
Continue with the exercises.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: 1. Where may a full-headed curved arrow start?
text:
1. Where may a full-headed curved arrow start?
Choose a lone pair, an ordinary atom label without a specified electron pair, or a positive charge. Explain the electron accounting.






Check your answer





Start at a lone pair or a bond containing the pair being moved. A positive charge is an acceptor cue, not an electron-pair source.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: 2. One arrow or two for carbonyl addition?
text:
2. One arrow or two for carbonyl addition?
OH⁻ forms a new bond to carbonyl carbon. What must happen to the C=O π pair?






Check your answer





It moves to oxygen in the same addition step. Otherwise the carbon would have total bond order five. The original carbonyl oxygen becomes an alkoxide.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
3. Are two arrows two steps?
The methyl SN2 drawing has two curved arrows. Does it have two elementary steps?






Check your answer





No. Both pair movements occur in one concerted elementary step. Step counting depends on the mechanistic intermediates and barriers, not the number of arrows.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
4. What distinguishes an intermediate?
On a schematic free-energy profile, is an intermediate a maximum or a minimum? How does it differ from a transition state?






Check your answer





An intermediate is a minimum between elementary steps and has a finite lifetime. A transition state lies at a barrier maximum and is not an isolable species.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: 5. What must a proton donor leave behind?
text:
5. What must a proton donor leave behind?
An alkoxide takes a proton from water. Give both products and check charge.






Check your answer





The products are an alcohol and OH⁻. Net charge starts and ends at minus one. Writing only alcohol would omit the donor-derived conjugate base.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: 6. Does a catalyst favour products at equilibrium?
text:
6. Does a catalyst favour products at equilibrium?
A catalyst lowers a kinetically relevant barrier. Does that change the equilibrium constant for the same reaction and conditions?






Check your answer





No. It changes the pathway and can speed approach to equilibrium in both directions. The same reactant/product endpoint free-energy difference determines the same equilibrium constant.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the exercises, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Explain a concerted SN2 and a stepwise SN1 example.
Predict inversion at a reacting stereocentre.
Justify a pathway using substrate and conditions.


45-minute block budget (all pauses included): 0–4 min: reacting-centre classification; 4–14 min: SN2 arrows, inversion and rate model; 14–21 min: steric access and leaving-group activation; 21–32 min: SN1 ionisation, capture and deprotonation; 32–39 min: face access, net accounting and competing routes; 39–43 min: independent mechanism drawing; 43–45 min: recap. The brief predictions, individual drawing and board discussion occur inside these blocks, not in extra time. The 40-second metadata is a rough planning reference; spend longer on the identified drawings and merge explanations already understood.
Begin with the previous unit’s electron-pair and charge audit. Ask students to predict a product or bond change before displaying the worked drawing. These slides support discussion and paper drawing; the practice page supplies further explanations.

text:
Both collision partners affect the rate

A schematic straight line shows initial SN2 rate proportional to nucleophile concentration at fixed substrate.For this simple model: rate = k[substrate][nucleophile]. Doubling one concentration doubles initial rate when the other is fixed.

This is a mechanistic model diagram, not measured data. Rate laws are evidence for mechanisms, but a single dependence does not prove every microscopic detail.

text:
Which conditions support each example?
Methyl bromide + hydroxide: accessible carbon and a strong pair donor support the SN2 model.

Neither is a universal rule for every solvent and temperature.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
Locate the reacting atoms, draw elimination and addition steps, and use geometry to explain the products. Use the lecture and demo to revisit a worked case.
Core 1–12: about 80–100 minutes. Transfer 13–20: an optional 45–65 minutes; choose problems that target the mistakes you want to resolve.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
section: Local refresher and worked starting example
text:
Local refresher and worked starting example
Alpha means the carbon carrying the leaving group and beta an adjacent carbon. E2 couples base attack at β-H, C–H pair donation to C–C and leaving-group departure; a suitable anti-periplanar arrangement has180° H–C–C–leaving-group dihedral. Addition consumes an alkene pi bond. The ionic HBr cases here explicitly exclude peroxides.
Worked starting example. In a formal E2 step RCH₂CH₂Br+B⁻→RCH=CH₂+BH+Br⁻, three pairs move together: B→H, C–H→C–C and C–Br→Br. This balances atoms and charge, but a particular primary substrate may favour competing substitution under actual conditions.
Draw structures, identify the relevant atom and explain the reason. A name alone is insufficient where a mechanism or argument is requested.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
1. Find every beta carbon
Draw 2-bromobutane and mark α and all β carbons. Explain the local definition.






Hint





Alpha is the carbon carrying the leaving group.









Worked answer and reasoning





C2 is α; C1 and C3 are β because they are directly adjacent to C2. Alpha/beta labels are relative to this functional site, not permanent names for the molecule.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
2. List possible alkene connectivities
From formal HBr elimination of 2-bromobutane, draw but-1-ene and but-2-ene and show which β site produces each.






Hint





Remove H from either neighbouring carbon, without moving the carbon skeleton.









Worked answer and reasoning





Loss from C1 forms C1=C2, but-1-ene. Loss from C3 forms C2=C3, but-2-ene. This inventories possible connectivity, not product proportions in unspecified conditions.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
3. Test the E/Z prerequisite
Draw the preceding two alkene products and decide which can be E/Z.






Hint





Each end of a double bond needs two different substituents.









Worked answer and reasoning





But-2-ene can be E or Z because each alkene carbon bears CH₃ and H. But-1-ene has two H on one end, so it cannot have an E/Z descriptor.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
4. Construct an E2 electron-flow step
Assume a suitable anti conformation of 2-bromopropane and a strong base B⁻. Draw the three arrows and complete the products.






Hint





Base→β-H; C–H→C–C; C–Br→Br.









Worked answer and reasoning





Products are propene, BH and Br⁻. All three pair movements are concerted in E2; no carbocation is inserted. Net charge remains −1. The conformation must support the reacting geometry.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
5. Reject methyl elimination
Explain why CH₃Br cannot undergo ordinary β-elimination to an alkene. Contrast it with CH₃CH₂Br as a formal bond inventory.






Hint





Count carbon atoms before searching for a β-H.









Worked answer and reasoning





Methyl bromide has no β-carbon. Ethyl bromide has one and can formally lose HBr to form ethene; however, a primary substrate with a strong nucleophile can favour SN2, so the inventory does not establish a dominant pathway.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
6. Read a Newman projection
Looking from the β-carbon toward the α-carbon, put the front reacting H at twelve o’clock and rear Br at six. Give the H–C–C–Br dihedral.






Hint





Opposing clock positions are separated by half a turn.









Worked answer and reasoning





The dihedral is 180°, an anti-periplanar arrangement. The front bond starts at the dot and the rear bond at the circle. Reversing which carbon is viewed first requires redrawing the projection consistently.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
7. Rotate without changing connectivity
Starting from that anti view, rotate only the rear carbon by 60°. Is the same H/Br pair still anti? Has the molecule become a constitutional isomer?






Hint





A torsion changes spatial arrangement around one bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





The selected pair is no longer at 180°. Connectivity and substituent identities remain unchanged, so this is a conformational change, not a constitutional isomerisation.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
8. Fix a two-arrow E2 proposal
A drawing moves the base pair to β-H and the C–Br pair to Br, but never moves C–H electrons. What is missing?






Hint





Account for the pair left behind when H departs as H⁺.









Worked answer and reasoning





The C–H pair must form the new C–C π bond. Otherwise the proposed bond inventory and electron count do not describe the alkene. Draw all three arrows in the same elementary step.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
9. Separate accessible from favoured products
A student lists all β sites, then claims each gives equal alkene amounts. Give two reasons that conclusion is unsupported.






Hint





Consider geometry and the identities of base and substrate.









Worked answer and reasoning





Different sites can have different access to anti geometry and give differently substituted alkenes; steric properties of the base and other conditions also affect relative pathways. Possible products need not be equally probable.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
10. Draw E1 after ionisation
Use (CH₃)₃C⁺ and water to draw β-H loss, with both electron-pair arrows and all products.






Hint





Water supplies a pair to H while C–H supplies the alkene π pair.









Worked answer and reasoning





The products are (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ and H₃O⁺. This deprotonation follows prior ionisation in an E1 pathway. It is not the concerted C–Br-breaking E2 event.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
11. Contrast E1 with E2
Compare an E1 route from a tertiary bromide in water with an E2 model using a strong base. State the order of bond breaking and the presence or absence of a carbocation.






Hint





Ask whether loss of the leaving group is a separate elementary step.









Worked answer and reasoning





E1 ionises first to a carbocation, then loses β-H. E2 couples base attack, C–H cleavage and C–leaving-group cleavage in one step, without a carbocation intermediate. Conditions and competing routes must still be considered.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
12. Choose the attacked atom
For a secondary bromide with a reagent that can act as nucleophile and base, draw a carbon-attack possibility and a β-H-removal possibility.






Hint





The alternatives differ first in where the donated pair goes.









Worked answer and reasoning





Pair donation to saturated carbon with leaving-group departure gives substitution; donation to β-H with C–H electrons forming C=C gives elimination. A reagent label alone does not choose between them.









Note



Optional transfer starts here. Choose problems that address your own gaps; the core route remains1–12.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
13. Protonate propene in two ways
For ionic HBr addition without peroxides, draw both formal carbocation connectivities possible after protonating propene.






Hint





H can attach at either alkene carbon, leaving the positive site at the other.









Worked answer and reasoning





Terminal H addition gives secondary CH₃CH⁺CH₃; internal H addition gives primary CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺. The secondary route is favoured in the selected model because its intermediate is more stabilised.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
14. Complete bromide capture
Starting from CH₃CH⁺CH₃ and Br⁻, draw pair donation and name the organic product.






Hint





The cationic carbon needs the new bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





A bromide lone pair forms C–Br, giving 2-bromopropane. Carbon becomes tetrahedral and neutral. The HBr addition sequence is protonation followed by capture, not a single arbitrary placement of H and Br.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
15. Audit HBr addition
Balance propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane at the formula level and count the local bonds that change.






Hint





A pi bond is consumed while two sigma bonds are made.









Worked answer and reasoning





C₃H₆ + HBr gives C₃H₇Br. The C=C π bond and H–Br bond are consumed overall while C–H and C–Br form; the original C–C sigma bond remains.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
16. Recognise a symmetric alkene
Predict the connectivity of ionic HBr addition to ethene. Is there a distinct regioisomeric alternative?






Hint





The two alkene carbons are equivalent by symmetry.









Worked answer and reasoning





The product is bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br. Exchanging which equivalent carbon receives H gives the same connectivity, so there is no distinct regioisomeric product in this example.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
17. Read bromonium opening
Draw a three-membered C–Br⁺–C bridge and Br⁻ approaching a carbon from the opposite side. Show which bridge bond pair returns to Br.






Hint





New C–Br formation opens the corresponding C–Br bridge bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





Bromide attacks carbon from the back of the bridge, and that carbon–bridge-Br pair returns to the bridging Br. This yields two C–Br bonds with anti addition in the representative mechanism.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
18. Compare HBr with Br₂
Why should the free-carbocation HBr picture not be copied unchanged when explaining anti Br₂ addition?






Hint





Compare the intermediates, not just the two letters Br in the reagents.









Worked answer and reasoning





The bromonium bridge changes access to the two faces and its backside opening explains anti addition. A freely planar carbocation picture omits this bridge and does not provide the same stereochemical explanation.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
19. Identify a false reverse reaction
A student calls every addition the reverse of the corresponding laboratory elimination under the same conditions. Rewrite the claim carefully.






Hint





Distinguish net bond inventory from microscopic path and operating conditions.









Worked answer and reasoning





Addition consumes a pi bond and elimination creates one, so some net transformations can be related. Their useful reagents, mechanisms, equilibrium conditions and competing processes may differ; the names alone do not establish an exact reverse under identical conditions.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
20. Explain a complete branch point
A tertiary carbocation is formed in water. Draw both capture leading to alcohol and deprotonation leading to alkene, including proton-transfer products.






Hint





Water can attack carbon or act as base at β-H.









Worked answer and reasoning





Carbon capture gives an oxonium ion, then water deprotonation gives alcohol plus H₃O⁺. β-H removal gives alkene plus H₃O⁺ directly from the cation. Both follow the same early ionisation, so seeing ionisation alone does not settle the product ratio.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
Explore
Use this explorer for about 7–10 minutes. Make a prediction first, change one input at a time, and record a chemical explanation rather than only a screenshot.

Explore the chemistry





Prediction, exploration and explanation
Predict (1 minute). Keep front H1 at twelve o’clock. At which rear-Br angle will H1–Cβ–Cα–Br be 180°? Repeat mentally for H2 at four o’clock.
Explore (3–4 minutes). Choose a reacting front hydrogen and rotate the rear carbon. Find anti alignment without the preset, then use “Align selected H anti” to check. Change the selected H without changing rotation. Does the same conformation remain eligible for that different H?
Explain (2–3 minutes). Draw one aligned Newman view on paper, then the three E2 electron-pair arrows and possible ethene product. Explain what stays unchanged during rotation and why alignment alone does not establish reaction speed or the dominant pathway.


Supplied model and its limits
The explicit substrate is bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br. View from its beta CH₃ (front) to alpha CH₂Br (rear). Front hydrogens stay fixed at 0°, 120° and 240°; rear Br and its two H atoms rotate together. A ±10° teaching window labels near 180° as near anti; it is not a kinetic threshold or reaction probability. This is a geometry model only: suitable nucleophiles can make primary bromoethane favour substitution instead of elimination.


Continue with the exercises
Continue with the exercises. Keep your prediction, a corrected drawing or calculation, and two sentences stating what the model supports and what it leaves unresolved.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 1. Can CH₃Br give an ordinary beta-elimination?
text:
1. Can CH₃Br give an ordinary beta-elimination?
Draw the carbon skeleton before answering.






Check your answer





No. There is no beta carbon, and therefore no beta-H that could be removed to form an adjacent C=C bond.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 2. How many pair arrows describe E2?
text:
2. How many pair arrows describe E2?
Identify the source and destination of each.






Check your answer





Three: base lone pair to beta-H; C–H bond pair into the C–C pi bond; C–leaving-group pair onto the leaving group. These describe one concerted elementary step.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
text:
3. What is anti-periplanar?
State the H–C–C–Br dihedral angle in the preferred simple anti arrangement.






Check your answer





180 degrees. The reacting C–H and C–Br bonds lie in one plane on opposite sides of the viewed C–C bond. A Newman drawing must specify front and rear bonds.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 4. Which alkenes follow formal elimination from 2-bromobutane?
text:
4. Which alkenes follow formal elimination from 2-bromobutane?
List constitutional possibilities and note the E/Z case.






Check your answer





But-1-ene and but-2-ene. The latter can be E or Z; but-1-ene has two H atoms at its terminal alkene carbon and cannot have E/Z configurations.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 5. Why does ionic HBr addition favour 2-bromopropane from propene?
text:
5. Why does ionic HBr addition favour 2-bromopropane from propene?
Assume no peroxides and use the supplied carbocation model.






Check your answer





Protonation giving a secondary carbocation is favoured over the alternative primary carbocation. Bromide then captures that intermediate, giving the observed connectivity in this model.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 6. Why is the Br₂ route a different drawing?
text:
6. Why is the Br₂ route a different drawing?
Name the key bridged intermediate and the relative opening geometry.






Check your answer





A bromonium intermediate can be opened by opposite-side bromide attack, giving anti addition. A free-carbocation HBr mechanism should not be copied unchanged for this process.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the worked practice, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

What will you be able to explain?

45-minute block budget (all pauses included): 0–5 min: alcohol/carbonyl transformation map; 5–13 min: local oxidation-state comparisons and tertiary boundary; 13–23 min: reduction plus proton-transfer drawing; 23–29 min: OH activation and IR evidence; 29–39 min: paper amount, yield and purity comparisons; 39–43 min: target-based route choice; 43–45 min: recap. The brief predictions, individual drawing and board discussion occur inside these blocks, not in extra time. The 40-second metadata is a rough planning reference; spend longer on the identified drawings and merge explanations already understood.

A secondary alcohol has a hydrogen on its OH-bearing carbon; a tertiary one has three carbon substituents instead.A tertiary alcohol lacks the required carbinol C–H bond for the simple alcohol → carbonyl transformation without C–C cleavage.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text: Draw carbonyl-addition mechanisms, track oxygen atoms and check each proton transfer. Use problems 1–12 for core work (about 80–100 minutes); choose from 13–20 for optional transfer work (another 45–65 minutes), focusing on the steps you need to practise.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
section: Local refresher and worked starting example
text:
Local refresher and worked starting example
The polar C=O bond makes carbon electrophilic. Addition forms a new bond to carbon while the pi pair goes to oxygen, yielding a tetrahedral species. Proton transfers use actual donors/bases. Hydrate=two OH; hemiacetal=OH+OR; acetal=OR+OR at one carbon. Full-headed arrows move pairs, and R/S requires a defined 3D view.
Worked starting example. OH⁻ adds to CH₃CHO with OH pair→C and C=O pair→O, giving CH₃CH(OH)O⁻. Water then donates H to that alkoxide and becomes OH⁻. The hydrate is neutral CH₃CH(OH)₂; net reaction is aldehyde+water⇌hydrate, not spontaneous loss of oxygen or creation of a proton.
Draw structures, identify the relevant atom and explain the reason. A name alone is insufficient where a mechanism or argument is requested.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
1. Separate partial and formal charge
Draw neutral CH₃CHO with oxygen lone pairs, δ labels and formal charges.






Hint





Unequal electron sharing need not create integer Lewis charges.









Worked answer and reasoning





O is δ− and carbonyl C δ+, while their ordinary neutral Lewis formal charges are both zero. Partial charge explains polarity; it is not a pre-existing carbocation formula.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
2. Count carbonyl geometry
Draw CH₃COCH₃ and count its carbonyl-carbon neighbours and bond orders. State the approximate geometry before addition.






Hint





There are three bonded atoms but one double bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





Carbonyl C has three atom neighbours and total bond order four, approximately trigonal planar. Confusing neighbour count with bond-order sum can produce an incorrect valence audit.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
3. Draw hydroxide addition
For CH₃CHO+OH⁻, draw two coupled arrows and the tetrahedral intermediate.






Hint





The carbonyl pi pair must move when the new bond forms.









Worked answer and reasoning





OH lone pair→C and C=O pair→O give CH₃CH(OH)O⁻. Carbon has four single bonds, and the original carbonyl oxygen bears the negative charge.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
4. Track oxygen labels
Label carbonyl O as A and incoming hydroxide O as B in the preceding step. Which becomes O⁻ and which is OH?






Hint





The incoming hydroxide keeps its H during C–O bond formation.









Worked answer and reasoning





A becomes O⁻ after receiving the π pair. B is the newly attached OH. Oxygen identities must not be exchanged without extra chemical steps.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
5. Complete hydration
Use water to protonate the preceding alkoxide, drawing all products.






Hint





Water becomes hydroxide when it loses H⁺.









Worked answer and reasoning





The alkoxide pair takes H from water while the water O–H pair returns to O. Products are CH₃CH(OH)₂ and OH⁻. Hydroxide used in the first step is regenerated overall.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
6. Write the net hydrated equation
Combine hydroxide addition and proton transfer, then cancel the regenerated catalyst.






Hint





OH⁻ occurs on both sides of the two-step sum.









Worked answer and reasoning





The net equation is CH₃CHO+H₂O⇌CH₃CH(OH)₂. The alkoxide is an intermediate and hydroxide a catalyst in this model. This does not specify which side dominates equilibrium.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
7. Activate with acid
Draw protonation of CH₃CHO oxygen by H₃O⁺ with both arrows and the charge on the product.






Hint





The carbonyl oxygen lone pair accepts a proton; hydronium loses it as water forms.









Worked answer and reasoning





Products are CH₃CH=OH⁺ and H₂O. The protonated oxygen has three bond orders and positive formal charge; carbon becomes more electrophilic. Do not assign an unexplained extra H to carbon.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
8. Choose a compatible nucleophile
For excess acidic methanol, should the selected elementary attack use neutral CH₃OH or freely persistent CH₃O⁻? Explain.






Hint





Check the strong base against the proton-rich medium.









Worked answer and reasoning





Neutral methanol is the suitable nucleophile for the selected acid-catalysed route. Methoxide is strongly basic and would be protonated in such a medium, so assuming it freely persists ignores acid–base chemistry.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
9. Attack the activated carbonyl
Draw methanol addition to CH₃CH=OH⁺, including movement of the carbonyl pi pair. Count incoming oxygen bonds afterward.






Hint





The formerly carbonyl oxygen becomes neutral OH; incoming methanol oxygen gains a bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





The intermediate is CH₃CH(OH)(O⁺HCH₃). Incoming oxygen has three single bonds and charge +1; original oxygen now has two single bonds and is neutral. Net charge +1 is retained.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
10. Finish the hemiacetal
Use water to deprotonate CH₃CH(OH)(O⁺HCH₃). Identify the group that loses H and all products.






Hint





Neutralise the oxygen that has three bonds.









Worked answer and reasoning





Water accepts H from the incoming methanol-derived oxonium group, giving CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃ and H₃O⁺. The product is a neutral hemiacetal, and acid is regenerated.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
11. Classify four products
Classify CH₃CHO, CH₃CH(OH)₂, CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃ and CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂ by local functional pattern.






Hint





Count OH and OR groups attached to the same carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





They are aldehyde, hydrate, hemiacetal and acetal respectively. One OH plus one OR defines the hemiacetal; two OR groups define the acetal. An ether elsewhere in a molecule is not enough.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
12. Reject an unexplained acetal jump
A proposed arrow converts a hemiacetal OH directly into OCH₃ without another species or intermediate. Explain why it is incomplete.






Hint





A poor leaving group and a new incoming alcohol both need accounting.









Worked answer and reasoning





Acetal formation requires additional acid-mediated activation, loss of water, alcohol addition and proton transfers. Merely swapping labels omits bond changes, atom sources and charge bookkeeping.









Note



Optional transfer starts here. Choose problems that address your own gaps; the core route remains1–12.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
13. Balance acetal formation
Balance CH₃CHO+CH₃OH⇌CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂+H₂O by finding the required methanol coefficient.






Hint





The acetal contains two methoxy groups.









Worked answer and reasoning





Two methanol molecules are required: CH₃CHO+2CH₃OH⇌CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂+H₂O. Carbon, oxygen and hydrogen then balance. Acid catalyses the path and is not consumed in the net equation.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
14. Change water composition
For that acid-catalysed equilibrium, predict the direction favoured by excess water and explain the acid role separately.






Hint





Water is on the product side of acetal formation.









Worked answer and reasoning





Excess water can favour hydrolysis toward carbonyl plus methanol. Acid accelerates interconversion in both directions without changing K for the same net reaction and conditions. Changing composition and adding catalyst are different operations.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
15. Count a cyclic hemiacetal ring
Draw HOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CHO and link its terminal alcohol O to aldehyde carbon through the hemiacetal pattern. Count ring atoms.






Hint





The attacking oxygen becomes part of the ring.









Worked answer and reasoning





The ring contains one oxygen and five carbons, six atoms total. The original carbonyl oxygen becomes OH at the former aldehyde carbon. Leaving the terminal oxygen outside the ring would lose the actual new C–O bond.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
16. Audit cyclisation formula
Compare the molecular formula before and after neutral cyclic hemiacetal formation from 5-hydroxypentanal. Is water lost overall?






Hint





Addition and proton transfer do not require removal of a whole molecule.









Worked answer and reasoning





The formula remains C₅H₁₀O₂. No net water is lost in hemiacetal cyclisation. Confusing this with later acetal formation would incorrectly subtract H₂O.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
17. Compare carbonyl substituents
Draw CH₃CHO and CH₃C(=O)OCH₃. Which has an oxygen-based substituent at carbonyl C that can participate in a suitable addition–elimination route?






Hint





Inspect the group bonded directly to the carbonyl carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





The ester has OCH₃; the aldehyde has H. Appropriate acyl substitution can involve departure of an oxygen-based group, whereas treating H⁻ as a normal leaving group is not a sound explanation for ordinary aqueous aldehyde addition.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
section: 18. Ask whether a new stereocentre forms
text:
18. Ask whether a new stereocentre forms
Methanol forms a hemiacetal from ethanal. List the four substituents at the former carbonyl carbon and test for a stereocentre.






Hint





The carbonyl carbon becomes tetrahedral.









Worked answer and reasoning





The groups are CH₃, H, OH and OCH₃, four different groups, so a stereocentre forms. Both faces of a planar aldehyde may react in an achiral environment; an R/S result needs an actual 3D product drawing.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
19. Contrast a symmetric ketone
Methanol adds to propanone to give(CH₃)₂C(OH)OCH₃. Does the former carbonyl carbon become a stereocentre?






Hint





Compare the identities of its two carbon groups.









Worked answer and reasoning





No. Its groups include two identical CH₃ groups, in addition to OH and OCH₃. Becoming tetrahedral is not alone sufficient for a simple stereocentre.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
20. Separate pathway from population
A student draws a valid hydrate mechanism and concludes the sample must be100% hydrate. Explain what evidence is missing.






Hint





A route describes how species interconvert; an equilibrium describes their relative amounts.









Worked answer and reasoning





A plausible mechanism does not supply the equilibrium constant or species concentrations. Structure, solvent, temperature and equilibrium evidence determine the mixture. The hydrate can be accessible without being the dominant form.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
Check your progress
Choose one corrected drawing and explain what changed in its atoms, charge, geometry or evidence. Then complete the self-check. The reading guide is optional support; all required exercise information is supplied here.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
Explore
Track oxygen labels and formal charges through hydrate and hemiacetal formation. Allow 7–10 minutes: predict first, change one input at a time and explain the result.

Explore the chemistry





Prediction, exploration and explanation
Predict (1 minute). Label aldehyde oxygen A and incoming nucleophile oxygen B. During initial hydroxide addition, which oxygen becomes negative? During methanol attack on a protonated aldehyde, which oxygen temporarily becomes positive?
Explore (4–5 minutes). Compare hydrate and hemiacetal routes. Step forward and backward, select each oxygen, and assign its formal charge plus the proton-transfer role entering that state. Use the check feedback. Pay special attention to oxygen C in water/hydronium and to the fact that addition itself is not a proton-transfer step.
Explain (2 minutes). Draw one labelled complete sequence. In base-catalysed hydration, why can the regenerated OH⁻ have oxygen C even though the incoming OH⁻ had oxygen B? In the acid route, which water accepts the final proton, and where is the catalyst at the end?


Supplied model and its limits
A always denotes the original carbonyl oxygen; B the incoming hydroxide or methanol oxygen; C the hydronium/water proton-transfer partner. The hydrate route has net charge −1 across all explicit species; the acid-catalysed hemiacetal route has net charge +1. Atom labels track identities, while catalyst regeneration means regeneration of a species, not necessarily the same individually labelled oxygen. These simplified paths do not predict equilibrium composition or supply operating instructions.


Carry the explanation into practice
Return to the local exercises. Keep your prediction, a corrected drawing or calculation, and two sentences stating what the model supports and what it leaves unresolved.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 1. Is delta-plus the same as formal plus one?
text:
1. Is delta-plus the same as formal plus one?
Explain the labelled carbon in a neutral aldehyde.






Check your answer





No. Partial positive charge describes unequal electron density in the polar bond. The ordinary neutral Lewis structure assigns formal charge zero to the carbonyl carbon.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 2. Which oxygen becomes O minus on initial hydroxide addition?
text:
2. Which oxygen becomes O minus on initial hydroxide addition?
Label carbonyl oxygen A and hydroxide oxygen B.






Check your answer





A becomes alkoxide after receiving the carbonyl pi pair. B becomes the newly bonded OH group. The intermediate is tetrahedral and has net charge minus one.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 3. Why add to protonated carbonyl under acid conditions?
text:
3. Why add to protonated carbonyl under acid conditions?
Name the nucleophile in the methanol example and the purpose of O protonation.






Check your answer





Neutral methanol is the nucleophile. Protonating carbonyl oxygen increases carbonyl carbon electrophilicity. Drawing a strongly basic nucleophile freely present in excess strong acid would require reconsidering acid–base reactions.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
text:
4. Which is the hemiacetal?
Choose CH₃CH(OH)₂, CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃ or CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂.






Check your answer





CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃: one OH and one OR group at the same carbon. The first is a hydrate and the third an acetal.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 5. Does a cyclic hemiacetal lose water?
text:
5. Does a cyclic hemiacetal lose water?
Consider 5-hydroxypentanal closing by internal OH attack and proton transfers.






Check your answer





No net water is lost. The molecular formula is unchanged. Its six-membered ring contains the terminal alcohol oxygen and five carbon atoms; the original carbonyl oxygen becomes OH.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 6. How does water affect acetal equilibrium?
text:
6. How does water affect acetal equilibrium?
For aldehyde + two alcohols ⇌ acetal + water under acid catalysis, predict the direction favoured by excess water.






Check your answer





Excess water can favour hydrolysis toward aldehyde and alcohol. Acid catalyses the pathway in both directions and does not itself change the equilibrium constant.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the exercises, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
section: A chemical route through this session
text:
A chemical route through this session
Use carbonyl addition as the starting pattern. Today we ask what makes a tetrahedral species collapse, how proton transfers enable leaving groups, and why amides differ.

45-minute budget: retrieval and motif reading 4 min; worked basic hydrolysis with drawing checks 13 min; acid-catalysed esterification 11 min; amide/salt comparison 7 min; paired integrated case and correction 8 min; exit explanation 2 min. Total 45 min, including drawing and discussion.
Suggested 30 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Plan 45 minutes including short drawing and discussion intervals. Routine visual frames take roughly 40 seconds; worked checks need longer and some resolutions can be quicker. Treat timings as guidance, with room for questions.

text:
Retrieve the starting idea
Draw CH₃CHO and CH₃COOCH₃. Which one has an oxygen-based substituent directly attached to acyl carbon?

Suggested 30 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Give students a short individual attempt. Worked answer: The ester has OCH₃ where the aldehyde has H. Both carbonyl carbons accept nucleophiles, but their leaving-group options differ.

Balance CH₃COOCH₃ + OH⁻ products.

Is one net reaction arrow evidence for one elementary step?

Acid activation protonates carbonyl oxygenWhich atom is protonated first in the representative acid-catalysed pathway?

Suggested 40 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Ask students to inspect the indicated molecular feature rather than read the answer caption. Worked answer: Carbonyl oxygen accepts H⁺ from a donor such as hydronium, increasing carbon electrophilicity. The protonated oxygen has +1 charge.

Count oxygen bond orders in C=OH⁺.

Neutral ethanol adds to the activated acyl carbonAfter ethanol attacks activated carbonyl, where is the positive charge?

Suggested 40 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Ask students to inspect the indicated molecular feature rather than read the answer caption. Worked answer: The incoming ethanol oxygen has three single bonds and is positive. Original carbonyl O becomes neutral OH.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
section: Resolve: let a neutral alcohol attack
text:
