title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text: Use nitrogen lone pairs, conjugate-acid strengths and aromatic electron counts to explain the structures and reactions. Work through 1–10 for core work, 11–16 for transfer and 17–20 for deeper checks. Allow roughly 2–3 hours across the unit. Attempt each problem before using its hint, then compare your revised reasoning with the worked explanation.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
Working refresher
A neutral ordinary amine N has three single bonds and a lone pair; ammonium N has four bonds and formal charge +1. Primary/secondary/tertiary amines have one/two/three carbon substituents on N. Proton-transfer arrows go from base pair to H and from donor H–A bond to A. A larger compatible conjugate-acid pKa means a stronger base; K≈10^(product-acid pKa−reactant-acid pKa). For simple aromatic rings first check planar cyclic conjugation, then count 4 n +2 pi electrons. Pyridine has a separate non-pi N pair; pyrrole uses its N pair in the sextet. In dominant-form pH reasoning, protonated forms predominate below a site’s pKa and deprotonated forms above it. See the local lecture for molecular drawings.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
1. Classify carbon substitution at N
Draw CH₃NH₂, CH₃NHCH₃ and (CH₃)₃N with lone pairs. Classify them as primary, secondary or tertiary and count N–H bonds.






Hint





Count carbon groups directly bonded to N, not the total molecular carbon count.









Worked explanation





They are primary with two N–H, secondary with one N–H and tertiary with zero N–H. Each neutral ordinary amine has three single bonds at N and one lone pair.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
2. Separate tertiary from quaternary
Compare (CH₃)₃N, (CH₃)₃NH⁺ and (CH₃)₄N⁺. Give carbon-substituent count, N–H count and formal charge for each.






Hint





A protonated tertiary amine still has three carbon groups; quaternary means four carbon groups.









Worked explanation





The three species have respectively 3/0/0, 3/1/+1 and 4/0/+1 for carbon groups/N–H/charge. Only the neutral first species has an available ordinary N lone pair.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
3. Draw protonation with a donor
Draw CH₃NH₂ + H₃O⁺ → products using both curved arrows. Count the N bond number before and after and audit net charge.






Hint





The N pair attacks H; the donor O–H pair returns to oxygen.









Worked explanation





Products are CH₃NH₃⁺ and H₂O. N changes from three bonds plus a pair to four bonds/+1. Net charge +1 is conserved; a positive proton is transferred rather than an electron being removed from N.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
4. Draw the reverse proton transfer
For CH₃NH₃⁺ + OH⁻, draw deprotonation with both arrows and identify the conjugate acid/base pairs.






Hint





Hydroxide is the pair donor and the ammonium N–H bond is the pair returned to N.









Worked explanation





CH₃NH₂ + H₂O form. The pairs are methylammonium/methylamine and water/hydroxide. Net charge zero on each side; the newly neutral N regains its lone pair.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
5. Compare supplied conjugate-acid pKa values
Ethylammonium has approximate aqueous pKa 10.7 and anilinium 4.6. Rank the corresponding neutral bases and state what larger conjugate-acid pKa means.






Hint





A weaker conjugate acid has a stronger conjugate base under comparable conditions.









Worked explanation





Ethylamine is stronger than aniline. Ethylammonium loses H⁺ less readily, so its neutral base binds a proton more favourably in the corresponding comparison. These values do not alone determine all nucleophilic reaction rates.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
6. Estimate a nitrogen-to-nitrogen proton transfer
For PhNH₃⁺ + EtNH₂ ⇌ PhNH₂ + EtNH₃⁺, use pKa 4.6 and 10.7 for the acids. Estimate K and identify the favoured side. Ph means phenyl; Et means ethyl.






Hint





Use 10^(product-acid pKa − reactant-acid pKa).









Worked explanation





K≈10^6.1≈1.26×10⁶ toward aniline and ethylammonium. Approximate pKa values must be compatible in solvent and conventions. This equilibrium estimate is not a rate prediction.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
7. Distinguish amine from amide
Draw CH₃CH₂NH₂ and CH₃C(=O)NH₂. Identify the N directly connected to carbonyl and explain why its pair differs in availability.






Hint





Only one pair can overlap directly with the neighbouring C=O system.









Worked explanation





The second is an amide. Its N pair delocalises into the carbonyl, contributing partial C–N double-bond character. The first is a simple amine without this direct carbonyl conjugation; treating both as equally basic would ignore structure.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
8. Audit an amide contributor
Write CH₃C(O⁻)=NH₂⁺, count N bond orders and sum formal charges. Explain why this drawing is not an independently equilibrating isomer of neutral ethanamide.






Hint





N has a C=N double bond and two N–H single bonds.









Worked explanation





N has four bond orders and +1; O is −1, giving net zero. The neutral and charge-separated drawings are resonance contributors to one molecule with fixed nuclei, not two species undergoing a chemical equilibrium.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
9. Explain aniline conjugation
Compare PhNH₂ with PhCH₂NH₂, where Ph is a benzene ring. Which N pair can overlap directly with the aromatic pi system, and what structural interruption appears in the other?






Hint





The intervening CH₂ is an ordinary saturated carbon.









Worked explanation





Aniline PhNH₂ has N directly attached to the aromatic system. In PhCH₂NH₂, the sp³ CH₂ interrupts that direct conjugation. Other substituent and solvation effects can remain; the structural comparison does not claim that only one effect ever controls basicity.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
10. Check aromatic requirements
For benzene and cyclohexane, state whether a continuous cyclic pi system exists. For benzene count pi electrons and find n in 4 n + 2.






Hint





A ring of sigma bonds is not sufficient.









Worked explanation





Benzene has a planar continuous pi system and six electrons, giving n=1. Cyclohexane lacks continuous pi conjugation and is nonaromatic, not automatically antiaromatic.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
11. Avoid double-counting pyridine electrons
In pyridine, N supplies one electron to the ring pi system and has a separate lone pair outside it. Should the pair be included when counting the aromatic sextet? Predict the effect of protonating that pair.






Hint





Separate the electron in the p orbital from the two in the non-pi lone-pair orbital.









Worked explanation





Do not add the separate pair to the aromatic count. Its protonation makes pyridinium, and the sextet can remain. N becomes positive; the ring skeleton and pi electron count remain consistent with aromaticity.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
12. Count pyrrole electrons
A five-membered pyrrole ring has two C=C units and an NH whose pair joins the cyclic pi system. Count the contributions and explain why the N pair is less available than pyridine’s separate pair.






Hint





Each double bond contributes two pi electrons.









Worked explanation





Two C=C units supply four electrons, and N contributes its pair of two, giving six. Removing that pair from its aromatic role by ordinary N protonation costs stabilisation, so pyrrole N is much less basic than pyridine N in this comparison.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
13. Repair an aromaticity claim
A student says “Both pyridine and pyrrole contain one nitrogen, so they must have equal basicity.” Give a structural correction using the two lone-pair roles.






Hint





Atom count does not locate the pair’s orbital role.









Worked explanation





Pyridine keeps a non-pi pair available for N–H bond formation; pyrrole’s pair supplies part of the aromatic sextet. Their protonation equilibria differ because the pair environments differ, despite both molecules containing N.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
14. Draw glycine at low pH
Use supplied pKa 2.3 for COOH and 9.6 for NH₃⁺. Draw the predominant glycine form at pH 1 and give every formal charge and net charge.






Hint





At pH well below a pKa, the site’s protonated form predominates.









Worked explanation





H₃N⁺CH₂COOH predominates: N is +1, carboxyl group neutral, net +1. Dominant-form drawings are approximations; minority forms still exist.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
section: 15. Draw glycine between its pKa values
text:
15. Draw glycine between its pKa values
Using the same supplied pKa values 2.3 and 9.6, draw predominant glycine at pH 6. Explain “zwitterion” and whether net zero implies no formal charges.






Hint





Apply the pH comparison separately to COOH and ammonium.









Worked explanation





H₃N⁺CH₂COO⁻ predominates. COOH has mostly lost H while ammonium mostly retains it. Opposing formal charges sum to zero, so it is a zwitterion; it is not entirely uncharged at every site.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
16. Draw glycine at high pH
With pKa values 2.3 and 9.6, draw the predominant form at pH 12. Show the proton transfer from the pH 6 form to hydroxide and audit charge.






Hint





At sufficiently high pH, ammonium can lose a proton while carboxylate remains.









Worked explanation





H₂NCH₂COO⁻ predominates. Zwitterion + OH⁻ → H₂NCH₂COO⁻ + H₂O. N returns to neutral three-bonded form; total charge is −1 on both sides.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
section: 17. Calculate a simple amine protonation ratio
text:
17. Calculate a simple amine protonation ratio
For B + H⁺ ⇌ BH⁺, use pKa(BH⁺)=10.0 and [B]/[BH⁺]=10^(pH−pKa). At pH 9 and 11 calculate the ratios and fraction present as BH⁺.






Hint





Convert ratio r=B/BH⁺ to protonated fraction 1/(1+r).









Worked explanation





At pH9, r=0.1 and protonated fraction≈0.909. At pH11, r=10 and fraction≈0.0909. A higher pH reduces the protonated fraction; a ratio is not itself a population fraction.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
18. Explain coexistence near pKa
For the same simple amine with pKa(BH⁺)=10.0, predict fractions at pH10. Does every molecule carry half a positive charge?






Hint





At equal pH and pKa, the concentration ratio is one.









Worked explanation





The populations of B and BH⁺ are equal under the model, each about 50%. Individual molecules are in one protonation state or the other; the population average does not mean each N is half protonated.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
19. Separate equilibrium from kinetics
Two species have different conjugate-acid pKa values. A student infers which attacks every carbon electrophile fastest. State what the pKa comparison supports and name two missing factors for a rate prediction.






Hint





Basicity compares proton-transfer equilibrium; nucleophilicity is a kinetic property.









Worked explanation





The data compare basicity under compatible conditions. Substrate steric/electronic structure, solvent, leaving group and the particular nucleophile’s solvation can change rates. pKa alone cannot supply a universal nucleophilic-rate ranking.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
20. Integrate a peptide-like fragment
For H₂NCH₂C(=O)NHCH₃, identify the simple amine-like N and the amide N. Explain which structural feature you would inspect first before predicting protonation and why the two sites should not be treated identically.






Hint





Follow each N’s directly attached atom: is it a carbonyl carbon?









Worked explanation





The left H₂N site is not directly attached to C=O; the right NH is the amide N. Carbonyl conjugation delocalises the amide pair and changes its basicity. The molecule can contain more than one chemically distinct nitrogen environment.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
Consolidate your work
Choose one corrected error and explain what changed in your reasoning. Then complete the self-check. Reading is optional; all practice above is self-contained.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
Explore
Question: why can the same pH leave one nitrogen base mainly neutral and another mainly protonated?
Use this activity for about 8 minutes: predict for 2 minutes, explore for 4, then explain your result for 2.

Enable JavaScript to compare the supplied molecular species and aqueous ionisation model.




Predict
The supplied approximate aqueous conjugate-acid pKa values are methylammonium 10.6, anilinium 4.6, and pyridinium 5.2. For a base B and its conjugate acid BH⁺,
\[f_{BH^+}=\frac{1}{1+10^{pH-pK_a}}.\]
Before moving a control, predict the fraction BH⁺ at pH = pKa and at one pH unit below it. Predict which base is most protonated at pH 7.


Explore

Use At supplied pKa for each molecule. Explain the common midpoint.
Compare all three molecules at pH 7 while keeping the environmental pH fixed.
For one molecule, move pH two units upward. Follow both the curve and the drawn neutral/protonated molecular forms.
Use Reset to reconstruct the original state.



Explain and check
At pH = pKa, half the population is BH⁺. One unit below gives \(1/(1+0.1)=10/11\), about 90.9%. At pH 7, methylamine is much more protonated than aniline or pyridine under this model. Higher pH decreases BH⁺, because deprotonated B becomes favoured.
A 50% fraction describes two populations of molecular species; it does not mean that every nitrogen has half a proton. The ring drawings use implicit carbon/hydrogen conventions; the N–H count and charge are shown explicitly.


Model limits
These are supplied, approximate compatible aqueous pKa values in a dilute one-site model. Substituents, solvent, temperature and activities can alter behaviour. The plot predicts neither extraction recovery nor the rate of a nucleophilic reaction. See the local nitrogen exercises for lone-pair and charge explanations.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
text:
1. Is a tertiary amine charged?
Trimethylamine has three methyl groups on N. State its charge before and after accepting one proton.






Check your answer





Neutral (CH₃)₃N has three N–C bonds and one lone pair. Its conjugate acid (CH₃)₃NH⁺ has four bonds and charge +1.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
section: 2. Which pKa belongs in a basicity comparison?
text:
2. Which pKa belongs in a basicity comparison?
Conjugate-acid pKa values are 10.7 for ethylammonium and 4.6 for anilinium. Which neutral base is stronger in comparable aqueous conditions?






Check your answer





Ethylamine. Its conjugate acid is the weaker acid with larger pKa. Basicity is an equilibrium property and is not a universal nucleophilic-rate ranking.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
text:
3. Is cyclohexane aromatic?
It is a six-membered ring. Explain why this is insufficient.






Check your answer





It has no continuous cyclic p-orbital network. It is nonaromatic; being cyclic does not imply aromaticity or antiaromaticity.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
section: 4. Which nitrogen pair is in the sextet?
text:
4. Which nitrogen pair is in the sextet?
Compare pyridine and pyrrole nitrogen lone pairs.






Check your answer





The pyridine lone pair lies outside its aromatic pi system. The pyrrole pair supplies two of the six aromatic pi electrons, making ordinary N protonation much less favourable.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
section: 5. Does net zero mean no charge?
text:
5. Does net zero mean no charge?
Draw glycine in its predominant form near pH 6 with supplied pKa values 2.3 and 9.6.






Check your answer





H₃N⁺–CH₂–COO⁻ has N charge +1 and carboxylate charge −1, giving net zero. It is a zwitterion, not an entirely uncharged molecule.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
section: 6. Is peptide nitrogen a simple amine?
text:
6. Is peptide nitrogen a simple amine?
Identify the neighbouring structural feature that changes its electron availability.






Check your answer





Peptide nitrogen is directly attached to a carbonyl as part of an amide. Its pair delocalises into C=O, unlike the pair in a simple alkylamine.



Return to the exercises for any reasoning you could not reconstruct. Explain one corrected mistake in your own words.

title: Structure from spectra
section: A chemical route through this session
text:
A chemical route through this session
Treat a structure as a hypothesis. Use a formula, functional-group evidence and simple one-dimensional NMR to test candidates; all supplied spectra today are simulated.

45-minute budget: retrieval 3 min; formula constraints 5 min; IR comparisons 8 min; worked proton-NMR assignment with paired checks 13 min; carbon-NMR check 6 min; candidate elimination and explanation 8 min; exit check 2 min. Total 45 min, including interpretation and discussion.
Suggested 30 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Plan 45 minutes including short drawing and discussion intervals. Routine visual frames take roughly 40 seconds; worked checks need longer and some resolutions can be quicker. Treat timings as guidance, with room for questions.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Retrieve the starting idea
For C₄H₈O₂, can two different connectivities share the same molecular formula?

Suggested 30 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Give students a short individual attempt. Worked answer: Yes. The formula constrains atoms and unsaturation, but spectra test arrangement and environments.

title: Structure from spectra
section: Start with a constraint, not a guess
text:

A formula constrains but does not specify connectivityWhat does C₄H₈O₂ leave undecided?

Suggested 40 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Ask students to inspect the indicated molecular feature rather than read the answer caption. Worked answer: Several connectivities fit the formula. Ethyl ethanoate and butanoic acid both account for one degree of unsaturation.

title: Structure from spectra
section: Resolve: start with a constraint, not a guess

text:

Calculate (2×4 + 2 − 8)/2.

Suggested 60 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Allow a brief paper or pair check within this slide. Worked answer: One degree of unsaturation. Oxygen does not enter this simple C/H/O expression.

title: Structure from spectra

One degree of unsaturation can be a ring or a double bondCould one degree correspond to a saturated ring instead of C=O?

Suggested 40 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Ask students to inspect the indicated molecular feature rather than read the answer caption. Worked answer: Yes. A ring or one double bond can account for one degree. Spectra must locate the structural feature.

title: Structure from spectra

text:

Suggested 60 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Allow a brief paper or pair check within this slide. Worked answer: No. It constrains possibilities but does not specify functional-group connectivity.

title: Structure from spectra

Suggested 40 seconds; adjust to the explanation and class response. Ask students to inspect the indicated molecular feature rather than read the answer caption. Worked answer: A decrease in transmitted light at that wavenumber indicates absorption. The axis decreases left to right by convention.

title: Structure from spectra
text:

title: Structure from spectra

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
Plan short transformations, calculate the possible product amount and decide what the observations support.
Core exercises 1–10: begin here. Transfer 11–16: apply the same ideas to new cases. Further checks 17–20: use these to investigate mistakes and revise. Allow roughly 2–3 hours across the unit, with more time for complete mechanism drawings. Attempt each problem before opening its hint, then compare your reasoning with the worked explanation.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
Working refresher
Keep these calculations distinct: amount n=m/M; reaction extent available from a reagent is n divided by its balanced coefficient; maximum product amount is limiting extent times the product coefficient.1 mol=1000 mmol. Theoretical product mass is product amount×product molar mass. Apparent isolated yield=100×isolated mass/theoretical product mass, interpreted as product yield only if the weighed mass is product. Yield does not measure purity or conversion. For TLC, Rf=spot-centre distance/front distance, both from the same origin; the ratio is dimensionless and depends on conditions. All masses/plates here are teaching data rather than a protocol. The lecture and practical report guide supply worked examples.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
1. Plan a two-step functional-group route
Starting with ethanol, propose a route through ethanoic acid to ethyl ethanoate. Identify the separate ethanol portion needed in the second step and name each transformation.






Hint





The acid-derived and alcohol-derived fragments need not come from the same reacting molecule.









Worked explanation





Oxidise one ethanol portion to ethanoic acid, then use a separate ethanol portion in esterification. The first change is oxidation and the second acyl substitution. Conditions and work-up require suitable choices; this is a planning example, not a protocol.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
2. Choose an oxidation endpoint
Ethanol can give ethanal and then ethanoic acid under appropriate oxidation conditions. Explain why a target labelled ethanal needs more information than an unspecified [O] arrow.






Hint





Further oxidation is a possible competing transformation.









Worked explanation





Conditions must favour forming and isolating the aldehyde rather than proceeding to acid. A target name does not guarantee selectivity or purity, and product evidence is still needed after the reaction.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
3. Convert mass with visible units
A teaching amount table gives 1.3812 g salicylic acid and M=138.12 g/mol. Calculate mol and mmol, showing unit cancellation.






Hint





Divide mass by molar mass;1 mol=1000 mmol.









Worked explanation





1.3812 g/(138.12 g/mol)=0.01000 mol=10.00 mmol. Grams cancel. Converting mmol into mol requires dividing by 1000, which matters before multiplying by a molar mass in g/mol.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
4. Compare a second reagent
For 1.53135 g acetic anhydride at 102.09 g/mol, calculate amount. In a 1:1 reaction with 10.00 mmol acid, identify the limiting reagent and justify without comparing masses.






Hint





The balanced reaction has coefficients one for both starting reagents.









Worked explanation





Anhydride amount is 0.01500 mol=15.00 mmol. Acid has the smaller n/coefficient,10/1 versus 15/1, and limits theoretical product. A larger mass alone would not establish excess.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
5. Handle coefficients explicitly
For the illustrative equation 2A+B→P, starting amounts are 10 mmol A and 8 mmol B. Find limiting reagent and maximum P amount; explain why simply taking min(10,8) is wrong.






Hint





Compare n divided by reactant coefficient.









Worked explanation





A supplies 10/2=5 mmol reaction extent while B supplies 8/1=8 mmol. A limits and at most 5 mmol P forms. Taking the minimum raw amount ignores that two A units are required per product.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
6. Include a product coefficient
For 2A+B→2P with 10 mmol A and 8 mmol B, find maximum P amount. Compare with the previous equation 2A+B→P using the same inputs.






Hint





The limiting extent is multiplied by the product coefficient.









Worked explanation





A still limits extent to 5 mmol. With product coefficient 2, maximum P=10 mmol; with coefficient 1 it is 5 mmol. Extent and product amount are not universally the same number.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
7. Change the limiting reagent
In the 1:1 aspirin teaching reaction, acid stays 10.00 mmol but anhydride mass is 0.51045 g at 102.09 g/mol. Identify the new limiter and predict product mol and mass with M=180.16 g/mol.






Hint





Recompute the changed amount before reusing the original limiter label.









Worked explanation





Anhydride is 0.00500 mol=5.00 mmol and now limits. Theoretical aspirin is 0.00500 mol, giving 0.9008 g. The original 10 mmol acid is now in excess for the desired reaction.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
8. Calculate theoretical mass
A1:1 teaching reaction has 10.0 mmol limiting reagent and product M=180.16 g/mol. Calculate the theoretical mass and state what assumptions the upper bound contains.






Hint





Convert 10.0 mmol to 0.0100 mol before multiplying.









Worked explanation





Theoretical mass is 1.8016 g before final rounding. It assumes the balanced desired transformation and complete use of limiting reagent toward that product; it does not establish actual conversion, recovery or purity.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
9. Calculate apparent isolated yield
For theoretical mass 1.8016 g and isolated material 1.20 g, calculate 100×isolated/theoretical. State the chemical assumption behind calling it product yield.






Hint





The numerator must represent product mass for the interpretation to hold.









Worked explanation





The apparent isolated yield is 66.6%. Interpreting this as product yield assumes the weighed material is product with appropriate identity/purity; solvent or impurities can inflate its mass.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
10. Predict a changed numerator
Theoretical mass remains 1.8016 g. Compare isolated masses 1.10 g and 1.20 g. Calculate both apparent yields and say which upstream quantities should remain unchanged.






Hint





Only isolated mass changes in the numerator.









Worked explanation





The yields are 61.1% and 66.6%. Starting-reagent amounts, limiting extent and theoretical mass should stay fixed. A report that changes those without changing the inputs has a dependency error.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
11. Critique a yield above 100 percent
Theoretical mass is 1.8016 g but a sample weighs 1.95 g. Calculate the apparent yield and name two plausible classes of explanation without diagnosing a unique cause.






Hint





An apparent yield can expose a questionable mass or model assumption.









Worked explanation





The value is about 108.2%. Residual solvent/water or other impurities can add mass; a weighing, input or stoichiometry error is another possibility. It is not evidence of creating extra product atoms beyond the balanced maximum.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
12. Separate yield and purity
One isolate has low apparent yield but the supplied spectra are consistent with the target; another has high apparent yield and major extra NMR signals. Explain why yield cannot rank their purity.






Hint





Yield measures recovered amount relative to a theoretical amount, not composition.









Worked explanation





A small recovered amount can be relatively pure, while a large mass can include impurities. Purity needs composition evidence; yield and identity/purity are different claims. The facts do not give exact purities of either sample.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
13. Compute two Rf values
A TLC origin is 0 cm, solvent front 5.0 cm, starting-material spot 1.2 cm and product-reference spot 3.2 cm. Calculate both Rf values and give units.






Hint





Rf=distance from origin to spot centre divided by distance from origin to solvent front.









Worked explanation





The values are 0.24 and 0.64, dimensionless. Both distances must use the same baseline and units; the numbers are conditional on stationary phase, eluent and other conditions.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
14. Read a crude TLC lane
Under the same conditions, a crude lane has spots at 1.2 cm and 3.2 cm with front 5.0 cm; reference lanes match those positions. Write a restrained interpretation and one limitation.






Hint





Matching retention supports comparison but is not a unique molecular fingerprint.









Worked explanation





At least two detected components are present, with retention consistent with the references. Co-migration or invisible components remain possible; spot matching alone does not uniquely establish identity or quantitative conversion.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
15. Recognise missing information
A TLC image records a spot 3.0 cm above baseline but no solvent-front position. Can Rf be calculated? What observation is missing, and why should a typical front distance not be invented?






Hint





A ratio needs both numerator and denominator.









Worked explanation





Rf cannot be determined reliably. The actual front travel from the same baseline is missing. A presumed usual distance would substitute an invented observation and could give a false retention value.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
16. Test the single-spot purity claim
A and B each run at Rf 0.64 in one eluent, and their mixture shows one spot. Explain how this can happen and propose a useful follow-up kind of evidence.






Hint





The separation method may fail to resolve different compounds.









Worked explanation





Co-migration can give one retention feature for a mixture. A suitable changed separation condition or independent spectral assessment can test composition. One spot is not a guarantee of purity, and detection can miss some components.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
17. Track the aspirin functional-group change
Salicylic acid has adjacent aromatic COOH and OH groups. In the teaching aspirin target, the phenolic oxygen becomes O–C(=O)CH₃ while COOH remains. State which group changes and why acid O–H evidence may persist.






Hint





Not every oxygen-containing group is consumed by phenolic acetylation.









Worked explanation





Phenolic OH is converted to an acetate ester. The carboxylic acid remains, so acid-region features can persist in the target. Acid O–H alone does not uniquely establish unreacted salicylic acid.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
18. Interpret an extra NMR signal
An isolate has a plausible mass-based yield and one TLC spot but an extra major NMR signal group. Give two possibilities and a targeted next check without naming a definite impurity.






Hint





The identity/purity assumption should be tested against independent evidence.









Worked explanation





Residual solvent or another component, including starting material, could contribute; assignment error is also possible. Compare full integrations/assignments and suitable references or use a discriminating separation. Do not discard contradictory spectra because yield looks plausible.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
19. Audit a report dependency
A student changes isolated mass from 1.20 g to 1.10 g and the report also changes theoretical product mol from 0.0100 to 0.0090. Starting-reagent masses were unchanged. Identify the error and the correct dependency.






Hint





The theoretical maximum comes from starting materials, not from recovered mass.









Worked explanation





Theoretical mol must remain 0.0100 under the unchanged reaction inputs. Isolated mass only changes the apparent yield numerator. Reconstruct calculations from saved raw inputs and keep the independent measurements separate.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
20. Write a supported conclusion
Supplied teaching evidence gives theoretical mass 1.8016 g, isolate 1.20 g, crude TLC two spots and a product-like simulated IR comparison. Write a conclusion separating amount, reaction evidence and remaining identity/purity limits.






Hint





Avoid allowing one observation to answer every question.









Worked explanation





Apparent isolated yield is 66.6% under the product-mass assumption. Crude TLC shows at least two detected components, and the labelled teaching IR illustrates consistent functional groups. These observations do not uniquely prove a real isolate’s identity or purity, especially when the trace is simulated.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
section: R task: results that update when a mass changes
text:
R task: results that update when a mass changes
In the student project, save a results section containing the amount table, limiting-reagent reasoning, theoretical mass and isolated yield. Reuse code from the report guide or adapt this transparent calculation:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
amounts <- read_csv("data/amounts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol,
         extent_mol = amount_mol / stoich)
theoretical_product_mol <- min(amounts$extent_mol)
theoretical_mass_g <- theoretical_product_mol * 180.16
isolated_mass_g <- 1.20
isolated_yield_percent <- 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g
knitr::kable(amounts)
isolated_yield_percent
The amounts.csv table contains the two starting reagents. If adding product or solvent rows later, select the relevant starting reagents before min(). Inspect the table and check the units. Write the numerical yield using inline R in the report, not by typing a second independent copy of the number. Add your TLC table and an interpretation distinguishing evidence for reaction, identity and purity. Change the isolated mass to 1.10 g, predict the direction of change, and Knit again before restoring the original teaching value.






Reproducibility check





At 1.10 g the apparent isolated yield becomes about 61.1%. Every dependent result should change when knitted. If a copied number remains 66.6%, it is no longer linked to the saved calculation. Correctness also requires the right stoichiometry and trustworthy primary observations; automatic updating alone cannot supply either.



Finish with two sentences stating what the observations support and what remains uncertain. Optional reading: selected Solomons chapters 8, 12 and 17; see the reading guide.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
Explore
Question: what does an Rf calculation tell you, and what information is lost if the solvent front was not recorded?
Allow 7 minutes: predict for 2, adjust the plate for 3, then explain the limits for 2. Distances are supplied hypothetical teaching measurements.

Enable JavaScript to vary distances from the origin and inspect the TLC ratio.




Predict
Rf is spot-centre distance divided by solvent-front distance, both measured from the same origin. Predict the value for 3.20 cm and 5.0 cm. Predict the value for a spot halfway to the front and state its units.


Explore

Change front and spot distances. Follow the geometrical plate as well as the reported ratio. The spot control stays between origin and front.
Use Spot halfway to front at more than one front distance.
Select Front unrecorded. Explain why spot height alone is insufficient.
Compare one known component with two components with the same retention. Can the visible plate distinguish those scenarios?



Explain and check
\(Rf=3.20/5.0=0.64\). A halfway spot gives 0.5, independent of the numerical front distance. The ratio is dimensionless. Without an actual recorded front, the denominator is unknown and the tool correctly declines to invent an Rf.
Two components can co-migrate and produce the same visible feature. The composition selector supplies a counterexample; the plate alone did not measure that component count. One spot therefore does not prove purity.


Model limits
Rf depends on stationary phase, eluent and other conditions, so matching retention is not a unique identity code. Detection can also miss components. Use matched conditions and appropriate independent structural/composition evidence. The geometric model does not simulate molecular adsorption or provide operating instructions. See the local practical evidence guide.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
1. Which reagent limits?
A 1:1 reaction uses 10.0 mmol A and 15.0 mmol B. How much product can form stoichiometrically?






Check your answer





At most 10.0 mmol of the stated 1:1 product under the assumed desired transformation. A limits; leftover B does not increase that maximum.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
2. What if coefficients differ?
For 2A + B → P, with 10 mmol A and 8 mmol B, identify the limiting reagent and maximum P amount.






Check your answer





Compare 10/2 = 5 mmol with 8/1 = 8 mmol. A limits and at most 5 mmol P forms. Comparing amounts without coefficients would be misleading.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
3. What does 1.20 g mean?
Theoretical mass is 1.8016 g. Calculate apparent isolated yield and state its purity assumption.






Check your answer





100×1.20/1.8016 ≈ 66.6%. The calculation treats isolated mass as product mass; impurities or solvent can bias that assumption.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
4. What is Rf?
A spot travels 3.2 cm and solvent front 5.0 cm from the origin. Calculate Rf and give units.






Check your answer





Rf = 0.64, dimensionless. Both distances must be measured from the same origin; the ratio depends on separation conditions.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
5. Does one spot establish purity?
Give two reasons a mixture might show only one TLC spot.






Check your answer





Distinct compounds can co-migrate, and a component may not be detected by the chosen visualisation. One spot under one condition does not uniquely identify or prove purity.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
6. What should change after Knit?
You change isolated mass from 1.20 to 1.10 g. Predict the effect and the approximate new yield.






Check your answer





The yield decreases to about 61.1%. Tables and inline computed values should update from saved inputs; manually copied numbers may not.



Return to the exercises for any reasoning you could not reconstruct. Explain one corrected mistake in your own words.

title: Reading organic structures
text:
About this lecture
Two bottles are both labelled C₂H₆O. One is the alcohol in beer and boils at 78 °C. The other is a spray-can propellant that boils at −24 °C. Same atoms, different molecules. Only the structure tells them apart.
Today we learn to read structures fluently:

Drawings: formula, condensed and skeletal, and what each one hides
Hidden atoms: every corner is a carbon; valence implies the H
Functional groups: the local patterns that decide behaviour
Formal charge: an electron count that keeps a drawing honest
Names and amounts: basic naming, and grams to moles

The rest of the course assumes you can read a structure at a glance.

Open with the two bottles. Ethanol and dimethyl ether really do share the formula C2H6O, yet one is a liquid you can drink (in moderation) and the other is a gas used in spray cans and as a diesel substitute. The 100-degree gap in boiling point is something we’ll explain tomorrow with hydrogen bonding; today the point is simply that the arrangement of atoms, not the list of atoms, is the molecule. Frame the lecture as learning a language: by the end, a skeletal drawing should read as fast as a sentence. Mention that most of this is review-plus-sharpening of general chemistry, but organic chemists use a shorthand that hides most atoms, and that shorthand is what trips people up.

title: Reading organic structures
text:
One formula, two molecules

Ethanol and dimethyl ether are constitutional isomersMolecules with the same formula but different connectivity are constitutional isomers.

Point at the oxygen in each. In ethanol, oxygen carries a hydrogen; in dimethyl ether, it sits between two carbons. That single difference in who is bonded to whom gives a liquid versus a gas at room temperature. Molecules with the same formula but different connectivity are constitutional isomers. The word “connectivity” is the key word of the whole lecture: a structure is a statement about which atoms are bonded to which. Everything else (left/right on the page, the angle you draw it at) is presentation.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Three ways to write the same molecule
text:
Three ways to write the same molecule

Ethanol as molecular formula, condensed structure and skeletal structure
Molecular formula C₂H₆O tells you what is there. It’s good for mass and amount, but useless for identity.
Condensed CH₃CH₂OH tells you the connectivity in a single line of text.
Skeletal is the drawing chemists actually use. It’s fast, and it puts the functional groups up front.


Each representation answers a different question. The molecular formula is what a mass spectrometer or an elemental analysis gives you; the condensed formula is convenient in text and in R code (you’ll type these into data frames); the skeletal structure is the working language of every paper and textbook. Stress that the condensed and skeletal forms contain identical information. Also stress that HOCH2CH3 and CH3CH2OH are the same molecule written in opposite directions. Writing a formula backwards does not create an isomer.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Skeletal structures hide most of the atoms
text:
Skeletal structures hide most of the atoms

Pentane as a skeletal zigzag and with every atom drawnRules: every end and corner is a carbon. Hydrogens on carbon are not drawn: add enough to give each carbon four bonds. Heteroatoms (O, N, …) and the H on them are drawn.

Try it: how many carbons are in an unbranched zigzag with four line segments?

Five. Segments are bonds, not atoms. The molecule is pentane, C₅H₁₂.



This is the single most important reading skill of the course. Walk along the pentane line: end, corner, corner, corner, end, five carbons. Then fill hydrogens: the ends have one carbon neighbour, so three H each; the inner carbons have two, so two H each. 3+2+2+2+3 = 12. Give students 20 seconds for the try-it before revealing. The classic error is counting the line segments (four) instead of the vertices (five). Heteroatoms are always written out, and so is any H attached to them. That’s why the skeletal ethanol on the previous slide shows “OH”.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Branches and rings: same counting rule
text:
Branches and rings: same counting rule

Butane, 2-methylpropane and cyclobutaneA branch point has three carbon neighbours, so it carries one H. A ring uses one more C–C bond and costs two H.

Try it: in 2-methylpropane, how many H are on the central carbon?

One. It has three carbon neighbours, so 4 − 3 = 1 H. The three CH₃ ends supply the other nine.



Extend the counting rule from chains to branches and rings. Draw butane and 2-methylpropane on the board side by side: both C4H10, but the branched one boils lower (about −12 °C versus about 0 °C). Shape matters even among hydrocarbons, which we’ll revisit tomorrow. The ring point is a preview: each ring, like each double bond, removes two hydrogens from the saturated formula. Students who internalise “H = 4 minus bonds to carbon” never need to memorise formulas.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Double and triple bonds change the hydrogen count
text:
Double and triple bonds change the hydrogen count

Ethane, ethene and ethyne with every hydrogen drawnA neutral carbon has a bond-order sum of four, not four neighbours. Each extra bond between two carbons removes one H from each.

Try it: start from butane, C₄H₁₀, and put in one C=C. What’s the formula?

C₄H₈. Each end of the new double bond loses one H.



Count bonds, not neighbours. An ethene carbon has three neighbours (one C and two H) but its bond-order sum is 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Point out the pattern C2H6 → C2H4 → C2H2: every extra bond costs two hydrogens. This is the “degree of unsaturation” idea that will become a tool in spectroscopy week: from a formula alone you can count rings plus pi bonds. Notice that C4H8 is also the formula of cyclobutane from the previous slide, another case where a formula leaves a choice.

This is why skeletal drawings use zigzags: they approximate the real 109.5° and 120° angles, and a triple bond is drawn as a straight line through the carbons. Shape matters for everything that follows: polarity and boiling point (Day 2), and stereochemistry and enzyme binding (Week 2). Keep it practical: students should be able to look at any carbon and say “tetrahedral”, “planar” or “linear” from its bonds. Hybridisation labels (sp3, sp2, sp) can be mentioned as names for these three cases without going into orbital theory today.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Functional groups: the parts that react
text:
Functional groups: the parts that react

Six functional groups in real moleculesA functional group is identified by its local connectivity, not just by which elements are present.

Most of a molecule is an inert carbon-hydrogen scaffold. The functional groups are where the chemistry happens, and each family has characteristic reactivity that the rest of the course is organised around. Ground each family in something students have smelled or used. The take-home message is in the last line: an ether, an acid and an ester all contain oxygen, but they’re recognised by what the oxygen is attached to. Teach students to look at the neighbours of each heteroatom.

title: Reading organic structures
text:
Reading around a carbonyl

The neighbour of C=O decides the familyFind the C=O, then look at its other neighbour. An OH or OR with no C=O next to it is just an alcohol or ether.

Try it: is CH₃C(=O)NH₂ an amine or an amide?

Amide. The N sits directly on the carbonyl carbon, which makes it much less basic than an amine. That difference comes back in Week 4.



The carbonyl, C=O, is the most important functional group in biochemistry and the course. Read the condensed notation carefully: in CH3C(=O)OH the parentheses mean the oxygen hangs off the carbon with a double bond, so there are two different oxygens. A frequent mistake is calling HOCH2CH2OH (ethylene glycol, two OH groups) an acid because it has two oxygens. It’s a diol, because neither OH is on a carbonyl. Peptide bonds in proteins are amides, which is a good reason to care about the amine/amide distinction.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Formal charge: count the electrons each atom owns
text:
Formal charge: count the electrons each atom owns

Water, hydroxide and hydronium with bonds, lone pairs and charges\text{formal charge} = \text{valence electrons} - \text{lone-pair electrons} - \text{bonds}
Hydroxide O: 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. Hydronium O: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1.

The formula is the usual V minus N minus B/2, written in a form students can apply by eye: count lone-pair electrons, count bonds. Emphasise that charges are part of the structure. Omitting a charge is a drawing error, not a simplification. Tomorrow’s acid-base unit lives entirely on this: when O–H loses a proton, the bonding pair stays on oxygen, so oxygen gains a lone pair and a negative charge.

title: Reading organic structures
section: The normal states, so charges jump out
text:
The normal states, so charges jump out

Learn the neutral column. Any atom that doesn’t match it carries a charge.

Try it: amino acids in your cells exist as H₃N⁺–CH₂–COO⁻ (glycine). Which atoms carry the charges, and why?

N has four bonds, so it’s +1. One O has one bond and three lone pairs, so it’s −1. The molecule is neutral overall: a zwitterion.



Experienced chemists don’t calculate formal charges. They recognise deviations from the neutral pattern instantly, and this table is the shortcut. Carbocations and carbanions are previews of the mechanism unit. The glycine zwitterion connects to biochemistry and to acids and bases on Day 3: at physiological pH, amino acids are charged at both ends. Ask students to point at the exact atom, not just say “the molecule is charged”.

title: Reading organic structures
section: A valence audit catches impossible structures
text:
A valence audit catches impossible structures
Before you trust any drawing, including your own, check every atom:

Carbon: bond-order sum exactly 4 (unless a charge is shown).
N, O: compare with the neutral pattern, and write the charge if they differ.
Hydrogen: exactly one bond.


Try it: a proposed reaction intermediate keeps C=O and adds three single bonds at the same carbon. Is that possible?

No. 2 + 3 = 5 bonds to carbon. For a new group to attach, the C=O π bond must open first. That’s the key step of every carbonyl addition in Week 3.



This is the habit that saves the most marks on the exam. Students under time pressure draw five-bonded carbons, especially when adding a nucleophile to a carbonyl. Make the audit a reflex: after drawing anything, run a finger over each atom and count. The try-it deliberately previews mechanism: the reason a carbonyl’s pi bond breaks when a nucleophile adds is exactly this valence limit.

title: Reading organic structures
text:
Naming: just enough to communicate

Butan-1-ol numbered from the OH end
Find the longest chain containing the group: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, …
Number from the end nearest the group.
Add the ending: -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid, …


Try it: name CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃.

Butan-2-ol. Numbering from the right puts OH on C2. “Butan-3-ol” is the same molecule, numbered the wrong way.



We teach naming only as far as needed to talk about molecules unambiguously; nobody will be asked to name a complex natural product. Propan-1-ol versus propan-2-ol is the essential contrast: the number says where the group sits, and moving it creates an isomer with a different name. Common names (acetic acid, acetone) will appear alongside systematic ones; the reading guide lists the ones we use.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Putting it together: two molecules from biology
text:
Putting it together: two molecules from biology

Glycine and lactic acidRead every atom, group by group: count each C–H, N–H and O–H separately, and don’t add an H to the carbonyl carbon.

Try it: write the molecular formulas of glycine and lactic acid.

Glycine C₂H₅NO₂ (2 N–H + 2 C–H + 1 O–H). Lactic acid C₃H₆O₃ (3 + 1 C–H on carbon, 1 + 1 O–H). Note the central carbon of lactic acid has only one H.



This slide combines everything: identify groups, count hidden hydrogens, respect the carbonyl carbon’s valence. The common error in lactic acid is giving the central carbon two hydrogens, forgetting that OH takes one of its four bonds. Lactic acid also has a carbon with four different groups, which is a teaser for stereochemistry in Week 2: there are two mirror-image lactic acids, and your muscles make only one of them.

title: Reading organic structures
section: From a structure to an amount
text:
From a structure to an amount

1.3812 g of salicylic acid divided by 138.12 g/mol gives 0.01000 moln = \frac{m}{M} \qquad \text{grams} \div \frac{\text{g}}{\text{mol}} = \text{mol}
The structure gives the formula, the formula gives M, and the balance gives m. In R: 1.3812 / 138.12 → 0.01.

The lab connection: every synthesis and titration in the practical starts from a weighed mass, and reactions happen in moles, not grams. The chain is structure → formula → molar mass → amount. Keep units visible so the grams cancel. Salicylic acid is the starting material for aspirin, which students will meet again. The R line is a deliberate nudge: today’s exercise has a short R task doing exactly this with a small data table, and the habit of keeping units in comments starts here.

The summary is the revision sheet; recite the reading procedure once: find the vertices, fill hydrogens to four bonds, name the functional groups by their neighbours, check charges against the neutral patterns. Close the loop with the opening hook. Tomorrow answers the boiling-point question from the first slide, and the answer is hydrogen bonding, which only ethanol can do because only ethanol has O–H. Point students to the exercises: the core problems are required, and the transfer ones are optional.
